items.title: Force, Distance, Work, and Mechanical Advantage
items.description: A Principles of Engineering lesson: Force, Distance, Work, and Mechanical Advantage.
items.searchText: POE Lesson 1.3: Force, Distance, Work, and Mechanical Advantage | LockwoodSTEM POE Lesson 1.3: Force, Distance, Work, and Mechanical Advantage | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.3 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.3 Force, Distance, Work, and Mechanical Advantage Focus question: How can force and distance measurements prove whether a mechanism provides mechanical advantage? Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Mechanical advantage is evidence. It compares input and output force or distance so a design claim can be tested. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can calculate work and mechanical advantage using measured force and distance data from a mechanism. Evidence Work and mechanical advantage calculation set Success Looks Like Calculations use correct units and connect force-distance tradeoffs to mechanical advantage and efficiency. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Measure force and distance Record input and output force and travel over the same mechanism cycle. 2. Calculate performance Determine work, actual mechanical advantage, and efficiency. 3. Interpret the tradeoff Explain why increased output force requires increased input distance or another cost. Lesson Interactive Analyze Force, Distance, Work, and Mechanical Advantage A mechanism uses 25 N of input force over 0.80 m to move an 80 N load through 0.20 m. Calculate the performance values. Measured Data 25 N Input force 0.80 m Input distance 80 N Output force 0.20 m Output distance Use W = Fd, AMA = output force ÷ input force, and efficiency = output work ÷ input work × 100. Your Analysis Input work (J) Output work (J) Actual mechanical advantage Efficiency (%) Best conclusion Choose The mechanism increases force by requiring more input distance and losing some energy. The mechanism creates additional energy. The output moves farther than the input. Check Activity Complete all four calculations and choose the conclusion supported by the data. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Work and Mechanical Advantage Calculation Set Complete one evidence table for a tested or provided mechanism. Show input work, output work, actual mechanical advantage, and efficiency with units. Write one conclusion connecting the results to the force-distance tradeoff. Exit Ticket Mission Debrief 1 One way today’s lesson connects to an aerospace mechanism or VEX rover system. 2 One type of evidence you could use to support a design decision. 3 One question you still have about mechanisms, energy, power, or the Unit 1 challenge. items.searchText: POE Lesson 1.12: Design Brief: VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge | LockwoodSTEM POE Lesson 1.12: Design Brief: VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.12 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.12 Design Brief: VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge Focus question: How do engineers interpret a design brief before building a mechanism? Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission A strong design brief turns a broad challenge into criteria, constraints, deliverables, and testable evidence. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can interpret a design brief and identify the problem, criteria, constraints, and deliverables for the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Evidence Problem statement, criteria/constraints list, and initial test plan notes Success Looks Like The annotated brief separates the problem, criteria, constraints, deliverables, and required evidence without rewriting them as vague goals. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Read for the mission problem Identify the user, task, environment, and failure that the design must address. 2. Separate requirements Classify measurable criteria, fixed constraints, deliverables, and evidence. 3. Plan verification Connect every important criterion to a specific test method. Lesson Interactive Parse the Rover Challenge Brief Classify each requirement so the team knows what must be achieved, what cannot change, what must be submitted, and what evidence is required. items.searchText: POE Lesson 1.8: Work, Power, and Efficiency in Mechanical Systems | LockwoodSTEM POE Lesson 1.8: Work, Power, and Efficiency in Mechanical Systems | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.8 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.8 Work, Power, and Efficiency in Mechanical Systems Focus question: How do work, power, and efficiency help engineers evaluate a mechanical system? Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Efficiency compares useful output work to input work; losses reveal friction, flex, slipping, or poor alignment. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can calculate work, power, and efficiency using measured input and output data from a mechanical system. Evidence Work, power, and efficiency data sheet Success Looks Like Work, power, and efficiency are calculated from matching input/output data and interpreted as performance evidence. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Define one test cycle Use the same load movement for input and output measurements. 2. Calculate work and power Use force, distance, and time with correct units. 3. Evaluate efficiency Compare useful output work with supplied input work and explain losses. Lesson Interactive Calculate Work, Power, and Efficiency A motor mechanism applies 30 N over 2.0 m in 4.0 s. The useful output work is 48 J. Complete the performance analysis. Trial Data 30 N Input force 2.0 m Input distance 4.0 s Time 48 J Useful output work Calculations Input work (J) Output work (J) Input power (W) Efficiency (%) Check Activity Use W = Fd, P = W/t, and efficiency = output work ÷ input work × 100. Identify one likely energy loss and one revision that could reduce it. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: POE 1.1 Design a 4:1 Rover Gearbox | LockwoodSTEM POE 1.1 Design a 4:1 Rover Gearbox | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 1 Design a 4:1 Rover Gearbox POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.1 Design a 4:1 Rover Gearbox Design and justify a gear train that provides an approximately 4:1 speed reduction for a rover drive system. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover motor spins too quickly and produces insufficient wheel torque. Your mechanical team must create a compact reduction system using available gears. Objectives What You Will Practice Calculate gear ratio Relate speed and torque Compare multiple gear-train layouts Document a mechanical recommendation Materials What You Need Available classroom gears or VEX gear inventory Axles and supports or CAD layout tools Calculator Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Inventory available gear tooth counts. Create three possible gear-train combinations near a 4:1 reduction. Calculate theoretical ratio and output speed for each. Sketch or model each layout and identify required shafts and supports. Compare size, number of parts, direction of rotation, and likely friction. Select one design and build or mock up the gear train. Measure input and output rotations to verify the actual ratio. Recommend the best design for the rover. Requirements Engineering Requirements Target reduction between 3.8:1 and 4.2:1 Output shaft must rotate continuously without gear interference All calculations must show driver and driven gears Recommendation must compare at least three concepts Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only available gears and approved structural parts Do not apply motor power until alignment is checked by hand Keep hair and fingers clear of moving gears Deliverables What You Submit Three concept layouts Gear-ratio calculations Built or CAD-modeled final design Measured ratio data Recommendation memo Reflection Reflection Questions Why might actual performance differ from the theoretical ratio? Which layout used the fewest parts? How did the reduction affect output torque and speed? What support would prevent gear skipping? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip For compound gear trains, multiply the ratio of each stage rather than adding ratios. Common Mistake Using pitch diameter or tooth count inconsistently will produce an incorrect ratio. Stretch Goal Redesign the gearbox to provide two selectable ratios. Career Connection Mechanical and drivetrain engineers size gear reductions for robotic explorers, aircraft actuators, and test equipment. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.searchText: POE 1.2 Mechanical Advantage Rescue Lift | LockwoodSTEM POE 1.2 Mechanical Advantage Rescue Lift | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 1 Mechanical Advantage Rescue Lift POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.2 Mechanical Advantage Rescue Lift Build a compact lifting mechanism that raises a simulated payload with limited input force. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A lunar crew must raise a damaged equipment package onto a rover platform. The crew has limited force available and needs a lightweight mechanical aid. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply mechanical advantage Measure input and output force Compare ideal and actual performance Identify friction losses Materials What You Need String Pulleys or lever materials Spring scale Mass set Meter stick Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Select either a pulley or lever concept. Calculate the ideal mechanical advantage before building. Build the mechanism with secure supports. Measure the input force required to raise the assigned payload at constant speed. Calculate actual mechanical advantage and efficiency. Identify two locations where energy is lost. Modify one feature to improve performance. Repeat the force measurement and compare results. Requirements Engineering Requirements Lift the assigned payload at least 20 cm Input force must be below the teacher-set limit Payload must remain controlled and not swing freely Include ideal MA, actual MA, and efficiency calculations Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved masses Never place hands below a suspended load Inspect supports before every test Do not lift the payload above the approved height Deliverables What You Submit Concept sketch Calculations Force data table Before/after efficiency comparison Final recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Where did friction reduce performance? Did increasing mechanical advantage change the distance pulled? What design feature improved control? How would lunar gravity affect the force requirement? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Move the load slowly and steadily; acceleration will distort force readings. Common Mistake Ignoring the input distance can make a high mechanical advantage system seem “free.” Work must still be transferred. Stretch Goal Add a self-locking or braking feature that holds the load without continuous input. Career Connection Mechanical systems engineers design hoists, deployment mechanisms, and cargo-handling equipment for spacecraft and ground operations. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.searchText: POE Lesson 1.15: Prototype Build Day 1: Structure and Motion | LockwoodSTEM POE Lesson 1.15: Prototype Build Day 1: Structure and Motion | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.15 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.15 Prototype Build Day 1: Structure and Motion Focus question: How do teams turn a mechanism plan into a stable first prototype? Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Prototype Day 1 should prioritize structure and controlled motion before speed, appearance, or extra features. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can build the first prototype of a VEX mechanism and identify early stability, alignment, or motion issues. Evidence Prototype progress evidence and issue log Success Looks Like The first prototype has a rigid structure, aligned motion components, free movement, and documented issues before powered testing. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Stage components Verify parts, tools, fasteners, and the current build plan before assembly. 2. Build the structure first Create a square, rigid frame and support shafts before adding motors or loads. 3. Test motion by hand Rotate or move the mechanism slowly and log binding, rubbing, or misalignment. Lesson Interactive Sequence Prototype Build Day 1 Reorder the steps so the team establishes structure and alignment before powered testing. Build-Day Goal Finish with a rigid, hand-testable mechanism and a documented issue list. Do not connect the motor until the mechanism moves freely by hand. Reorder the Steps Install shafts, bearings, gears, and spacers. ↑ ↓ Review the plan and stage the required components. ↑ ↓ Photograph the build and record alignment or motion issues. ↑ ↓ Build and square the rigid frame. ↑ ↓ Rotate the mechanism by hand and correct binding. ↑ ↓ Check Sequence Use the arrow buttons to place the work in a safe engineering order. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Prototype Progress Evidence and Issue Log Document the first build state and the most important issue discovered. Capture one labeled photo or sketch showing structure and motion components. Log the issue, likely cause, evidence, and planned correction for the next build session. items.searchText: POE Lesson 1.17: Mechanism Testing and Data Analysis | LockwoodSTEM POE Lesson 1.17: Mechanism Testing and Data Analysis | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.17 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.17 Mechanism Testing and Data Analysis Focus question: How can repeatable data show whether a mechanism met the design criteria? Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Test data must be repeatable enough to support a claim about performance, reliability, power, or efficiency. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can collect repeatable test data and use calculations to evaluate mechanism performance. Evidence Final test data table and analysis Success Looks Like The test controls variables, uses repeated trials, identifies anomalies, calculates meaningful metrics, and compares results with the criteria. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Standardize the procedure Define load, starting condition, distance, timing method, and success criteria. 2. Collect repeated trials Record enough trials to identify consistency and possible anomalies. 3. Analyze and conclude Calculate averages or performance metrics and state whether each criterion was met. Lesson Interactive Analyze Repeatability and an Anomalous Trial A mechanism completed four lift trials in 42 s, 41 s, 43 s, and 58 s. Interpret the data before making a performance claim. Trial Data 42 s Trial 1 41 s Trial 2 43 s Trial 3 58 s Trial 4 Do not delete a trial only because it is inconvenient. Identify a plausible procedural or mechanical reason and retest. Data Decision Likely anomalous value Choose 41 s 42 s 43 s 58 s Mean of the three consistent trials (s) Best next step Choose Ignore Trial 4 and make the final claim immediately. Investigate the cause, repeat the trial, and document how the anomaly is handled. Average all values without discussing consistency. Check Activity Identify the data cluster, calculate its mean, and choose a transparent next step. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Final Test Data Table and Analysis Run a repeatable test and use the data to judge mechanism performance. Include units, trial conditions, repeated measurements, and any excluded anomaly with justification. Write a criterion-by-criterion conclusion supported by calculated results. Exit Ticket Mission Debrief 1 One way today’s lesson connects to an aerospace mechanism or VEX rover system. 2 One type of evidence you could use to support a design decision. 3 One question you still have about mechanisms, energy, power, or the Unit 1 challenge. items.searchText: POE 1.3 Rubber-Band Rover Energy Budget | LockwoodSTEM POE 1.3 Rubber-Band Rover Energy Budget | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 1 Rubber-Band Rover Energy Budget POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.3 Rubber-Band Rover Energy Budget Build and test a rubber-band-powered vehicle, then account for where stored energy goes. Intermediate 1 class period Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A lightweight inspection rover needs a simple stored-energy demonstration for a training program. The vehicle must travel predictably rather than merely as far as possible. Objectives What You Will Practice Describe energy transformations Measure distance and time Control experimental variables Use data to select an operating condition Materials What You Need Small wheeled chassis materials Rubber bands Meter tape Stopwatch Masses Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Build a vehicle with a repeatable rubber-band winding method. Choose three winding levels such as 10, 20, and 30 turns. Run three trials at each level. Record distance, travel time, and any wheel slip or path deviation. Calculate average distance and average speed. Create a graph of winding level versus distance. Select the best operating condition for predictable travel and justify it. Requirements Engineering Requirements Same vehicle configuration for all baseline trials Three trials per winding level Release method must be consistent Vehicle must remain within a defined lane Recommendation must use data, not the single longest run Constraints Constraints & Safety Wear eye protection if required Inspect rubber bands for cracks Keep faces and hands away from stretched bands Use a clear test lane Deliverables What You Submit Vehicle sketch Trial data table Graph Energy-flow diagram Operating recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions What evidence suggested energy was lost to friction or wheel slip? Why did the highest winding level not necessarily give the best result? How did mass affect acceleration or consistency? What variable would you test next? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Mark the axle so every trial begins with the same winding reference. Common Mistake Changing the release angle or starting position between trials makes the data difficult to compare. Stretch Goal Add payload and determine the best winding level for transporting it. Career Connection Test engineers characterize stored-energy devices, springs, deployment systems, and small mobility platforms before mission use. items.description: A Principles of Engineering lesson: Motors and Electrical-to-Mechanical Power.
items.searchText: POE Lesson 1.11: Motors and Electrical-to-Mechanical Power | LockwoodSTEM POE Lesson 1.11: Motors and Electrical-to-Mechanical Power | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.11 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.11 Motors and Electrical-to-Mechanical Power Focus question: How do motors convert electrical energy into mechanical motion for engineering tasks? Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Motors link electrical power to mechanical performance; load, speed, torque, and gearing all matter. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can describe how motors support mechanisms and identify how speed, torque, load, and power affect performance. Evidence Motor performance observation notes Success Looks Like The motor recommendation balances speed, torque, load, current draw, heat, and gearing rather than maximizing only one variable. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Observe motor behavior Compare no-load and loaded speed, current, sound, and temperature. 2. Connect load to performance Explain why speed drops and current rises as required torque increases. 3. Choose a safe operating point Use gearing or load limits to keep the motor within a repeatable range. Lesson Interactive Find a Safe Motor Operating Point Increase the simulated mechanism load. Select the highest load that stays below 3.0 A while maintaining more than 55% speed. Motor Load Load level: Speed: Current: Engineering Decision Higher load requires more torque. The motor responds by drawing more current and slowing down. Excessive load can cause stall heating. Check Operating Point Adjust the load to meet both the current and speed limits. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Motor Performance Observation Notes Document how load and gearing affect one motor-driven mechanism. Record load condition, speed trend, current trend, and observed heating or stalling. Recommend a gearing or load revision supported by the observations. Configure an ideal pulley system requiring no more than 35 N of input force. Pulley Configuration Supporting rope segments: Only rope segments directly supporting the moving load contribute to ideal mechanical advantage. Ideal Prediction Input force Rope pulled Check Configuration Increase supporting segments until the force requirement is met, then note the distance tradeoff. items.searchText: POE 1.5 Mechanism Efficiency Showdown | LockwoodSTEM POE 1.5 Mechanism Efficiency Showdown | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 1 Mechanism Efficiency Showdown POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.5 Mechanism Efficiency Showdown Compete to transfer a fixed payload through a required path using the least input energy or force. Advanced 2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A ground-support team needs a mechanism to move a delicate payload between two stations. Multiple teams will propose machines and compare efficiency, reliability, and complexity. Objectives What You Will Practice Combine simple machines Measure input force and distance Calculate work and efficiency Defend a design using performance evidence Materials What You Need Approved pulleys, gears, levers, wheels, axles, or linkages Spring scale Meter tape Fixed payload Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the payload path and boundaries. Sketch two mechanism concepts that use at least two simple-machine elements. Estimate mechanical advantage and input travel. Build one design and complete a low-load functional test. Measure average input force and input distance for three official trials. Calculate input work and compare it with useful output work. Record success rate and completion time. Prepare a one-minute defense of the design. Requirements Engineering Requirements Move the payload from start to finish without direct hand contact Use at least two mechanical elements Complete three official trials Provide work and efficiency calculations Scoring includes efficiency, reliability, and simplicity Constraints Constraints & Safety No launching or free-falling payloads Use only approved stored energy Inspect supports and connections before testing Stop immediately if parts bind or fail Deliverables What You Submit Two concept sketches Calculations Official trial table Efficiency result Design defense Reflection Reflection Questions What feature improved efficiency most? Did the most efficient design also finish fastest? How did part count affect reliability? What would you change for a more fragile payload? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Measure force while the system moves at steady speed; peak starting force may not represent the full trial. Common Mistake Comparing only completion time ignores input effort and reliability. Stretch Goal Redesign to complete the same task with 25% fewer parts. Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission A mechanism that is loose, unsupported, or misaligned cannot produce reliable data. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can build a stable VEX mechanism using proper spacing, fastening, shaft support, alignment, and safety habits. Evidence VEX mechanism build-quality checklist Success Looks Like The mechanism is square, shafts are supported, collars and spacers are placed correctly, and moving parts rotate freely. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Inspect the structure Check squareness, fastener engagement, frame spacing, and rigid connections. 2. Inspect rotating parts Check shaft support, collars, spacers, gear alignment, and rubbing. 3. Run a hand-powered test Rotate the mechanism slowly before adding a motor or load. Lesson Interactive Audit a VEX Gearbox Before Power Select every condition that should be corrected before the motor is connected. Inspection Scenario A 180 mm shaft is supported by only one bearing. One shaft collar can slide along the shaft. The gear faces are offset and contact only at their edges. An extra spacer is stored in the team parts tray. A safe hand test should show smooth rotation without rubbing, wobble, or loose components. Select Build Issues Unsupported long shaft Loose shaft collar Misaligned gear faces Unused spacer in the parts tray Check Inspection Choose conditions that affect support, alignment, fastening, or motion quality. Today’s Work Main Deliverable VEX Mechanism Build-Quality Checklist Inspect a VEX mechanism and document the corrections needed before powered testing. Record at least three inspection findings with exact locations. Photograph or sketch the corrected mechanism after alignment and free-motion checks. items.searchText: POE Lesson 1.18: Final Design Review and Reflection | LockwoodSTEM POE Lesson 1.18: Final Design Review and Reflection | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.18 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.18 Final Design Review and Reflection Focus question: How can a final design review defend a mechanism using calculations, prototype evidence, and test data? Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission A design review is an engineering argument: claim, evidence, reasoning, and next steps. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can present a mechanism design and justify it using sketches, calculations, prototype evidence, and test data. Evidence Final design review presentation and reflection Success Looks Like The final review links the mission problem, design decisions, calculations, prototype revisions, and test data into a defensible engineering argument. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Build the evidence story Organize the problem, requirements, concept decision, calculations, prototype, tests, and revisions. 2. Defend the final design Use visuals and data to support claims and acknowledge remaining limitations. 3. Reflect on the process Identify the most important learning, tradeoff, and next improvement. Lesson Interactive Organize a Defensible Final Design Review Reorder the sections so the presentation tells a coherent engineering story from mission need to tested conclusion. Review Goal The audience should be able to trace why the team chose the mechanism, how calculations informed it, what happened during prototyping, and whether the final evidence supports the claim. Reorder the Story Present final test data and criterion results. ↑ ↓ Define the mission problem, criteria, and constraints. ↑ ↓ Explain revisions made from evidence. ↑ ↓ Show concept alternatives and the justified decision. ↑ ↓ State the final claim, limitations, and next improvement. ↑ ↓ Show prototype construction and observed issues. ↑ ↓ Present ratio, work, power, or circuit calculations. ↑ ↓ Check Review Order Move the sections into an evidence-based engineering narrative. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Final Design Review Presentation and Reflection Present the rover mechanism and submit a concise engineering reflection. Include requirements, concept rationale, calculations, prototype evidence, test data, and final performance claims. Explain one successful decision, one limitation, and the next evidence-based revision. Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Simple machines do not create energy; they trade force for distance or redirect motion to make work easier. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can identify simple machines and explain how they change force, distance, direction, or motion in an aerospace application. Evidence Simple machine identification chart and concept sketch Success Looks Like Each aerospace example is matched to the correct simple machine and its force, distance, direction, or motion tradeoff. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Inspect aerospace examples Look for the geometry and contact points that reveal the simple machine. 2. Classify the mechanism Distinguish levers, pulleys, wheel-and-axle systems, inclined planes, screws, and wedges. 3. Explain the tradeoff State what the machine changes and what the user gives up in return. Lesson Interactive Classify Aerospace Simple Machines Identify the underlying simple machine in each aerospace example. Focus on geometry and motion rather than the complexity of the full system. Examples Cargo rolls up a loading ramp. A screw jack raises a test fixture. A hinged service arm rotates about a pivot. A cable system lifts a payload. A winch drum pulls a rover. Identification Chart Example Simple machine Loading ramp Choose Lever Pulley Wheel and axle Inclined plane Screw Wedge Screw jack Choose Lever Pulley Wheel and axle Inclined plane Screw Wedge Hinged service arm Choose Lever Pulley Wheel and axle Inclined plane Screw Wedge Cable lift Choose Lever Pulley Wheel and axle Inclined plane Screw Wedge Winch drum Choose Lever Pulley Wheel and axle Inclined plane Screw Wedge Check Activity Look for the defining geometry: slope, thread, pivot, cable path, or rotating radius. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Simple Machine Identification Chart and Concept Sketch Classify aerospace examples, then sketch one simple-machine application for the rover challenge. For each example, name the simple machine and the input/output motion. On the sketch, label the effort, load, pivot or contact point, and expected tradeoff. items.searchText: POE Lesson 1.16: Prototype Build Day 2: Power, Load, and Troubleshooting | LockwoodSTEM POE Lesson 1.16: Prototype Build Day 2: Power, Load, and Troubleshooting | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.16 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.16 Prototype Build Day 2: Power, Load, and Troubleshooting Focus question: How can troubleshooting connect a failure point to a targeted design revision? Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Troubleshooting is evidence-driven: observe the failure, identify the cause, revise one thing, and retest. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can troubleshoot a mechanism by identifying causes of failure and making targeted revisions. Evidence Troubleshooting log and revised prototype evidence Success Looks Like Troubleshooting follows symptom → evidence → likely cause → targeted revision → retest, with only one major variable changed at a time. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Reproduce the symptom Use the same load and test setup so the failure can be observed reliably. 2. Isolate the cause Check power, transmission, alignment, friction, fastening, and structural deflection. 3. Revise and retest Change the most likely cause, then compare new evidence with the original test. Lesson Interactive Diagnose a Power-Transmission Failure The motor shaft spins, but the large output gear and lift arm remain stationary. Choose the most likely cause, targeted revision, and verification evidence. Observed Symptom Motor sound is normal. Motor shaft rotates. Gear on the same shaft does not rotate consistently. No major frame rubbing is visible. Troubleshooting Path Most likely cause Choose Dead battery Loose gear hub or shaft connection Bent frame rail Targeted revision Choose Replace the motor Secure the hub/collar connection Add lubricant everywhere Verification evidence Choose Mark the shaft and gear, then observe whether they rotate together Listen for a different sound Repaint the output arm Check Activity Choose the path that directly addresses the observed break in motion transfer. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Troubleshooting Log and Revised Prototype Evidence Complete one full troubleshooting cycle on the powered mechanism. Record the symptom, evidence, likely cause, revision, and retest result. Include a before-and-after photo, sketch, measurement, or data point. Exit Ticket Mission Debrief 1 One way today’s lesson connects to an aerospace mechanism or VEX rover system. 2 One type of evidence you could use to support a design decision. 3 One question you still have about mechanisms, energy, power, or the Unit 1 challenge. items.searchText: POE 5.5 Capstone Mission Defense | LockwoodSTEM POE 5.5 Capstone Mission Defense | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 5 Capstone Mission Defense POE Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.5 Capstone Mission Defense Prepare and defend the rover design using traceable requirements, test evidence, and risk-based recommendations. Advanced 2-3 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A client review board must decide whether the rover is ready for mission demonstration. Teams will present concise evidence and respond to technical questions. Objectives What You Will Practice Synthesize design and test evidence Communicate technical tradeoffs Respond to review questions Make a defensible readiness recommendation Materials What You Need Rover or capstone system Requirements and verification evidence Presentation software Engineering notebook Design review checklist Procedure Instructions Select the five mission requirements most important to readiness. Create one slide or visual for each requirement showing design response and verification evidence. Include system architecture, key tradeoffs, major revision, and unresolved risk. Prepare a five-minute presentation with assigned team roles. Conduct a rehearsal and remove unsupported claims. Present to the review board. Answer questions using data, drawings, code, or test evidence. Submit a final readiness recommendation and action list. Requirements Engineering Requirements Presentation is no longer than five minutes before questions Every major claim links to evidence Include at least one failed test or revision State unresolved risks honestly All team members contribute Final recommendation is Ready, Conditionally Ready, or Not Ready Constraints Constraints & Safety Use professional and respectful review behavior Do not conceal failed tests Follow safe demonstration boundaries No last-minute unverified hardware changes Deliverables What You Submit Final presentation Requirement-to-evidence summary Risk register Board question log Readiness recommendation Individual reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which evidence was most persuasive? What question exposed the weakest part of the design? How did the team communicate uncertainty? What action should happen before another mission attempt? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Lead with mission requirements and evidence, not a chronological story of everything the team did. Common Mistake Using confident language without test support can reduce reviewer trust. Stretch Goal Complete a second defense after addressing the review board’s top three action items. Career Connection Program managers, chief engineers, and design-review boards decide whether aerospace systems are ready to proceed to the next phase. Download Presentation Interactive Unit 5 Overview POE Hub Capstone Systems Reliable evidence includes unsuccessful and unusual results because those outcomes reveal the actual capability of the system. Integrate Verify Defend Use today’s decisions and evidence to advance the final aerospace systems capstone. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that advances the capstone without creating unnecessary documentation. Opening prompt Concept model Guided work Interactive application Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can execute an approved protocol, record complete repeated-trial data, and distinguish observations from measurements. Evidence Complete capstone test record Success Looks Like All trials follow the same method, failed trials are retained, units are recorded, and anomalies are documented rather than erased. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step produces a decision, artifact, or test result needed for the capstone. 1. Prepare and calibrate Verify instruments, settings, and data tables before the first trial. 2. Execute consistently Follow the approved sequence and record every outcome. 3. Check data quality Flag anomalies, missing values, and deviations immediately. Lesson Interactive Analyze the Trial Record Apply the lesson concept to a capstone aerospace-systems scenario. Use the feedback to correct your reasoning before completing the main deliverable. Repeated Trial Record Performance scores: 82, 79, 84, 81, 80. Four of five trials met the minimum score of 80. Do not remove the score of 79; it is part of the actual performance record. Mean performance score Success rate (%) Appropriate conclusion Choose The prototype met the criterion in 4 of 5 trials The prototype will always meet the criterion Check Reasoning Calculate the complete dataset and choose a conclusion limited to the evidence. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Complete capstone test record Create one focused engineering artifact that demonstrates today’s capstone progress. Submit complete repeated-trial data with units, conditions, and success/failure outcomes. Document anomalies and any protocol deviations without deleting inconvenient results. Exit Ticket Capstone Debrief 1 State the most important engineering decision your team made today. 2 Name the evidence, requirement, interface, or risk that supports that decision. 3 Identify the next action and the person responsible for completing it. items.title: Rover Anomaly Review Board
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: POE 5.4 Rover Anomaly Review Board | LockwoodSTEM POE 5.4 Rover Anomaly Review Board | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 5 Rover Anomaly Review Board POE Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.4 Rover Anomaly Review Board Investigate a failed mission trial, identify the most likely cause, and approve a corrective action. Advanced 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context During a rover mission rehearsal, the vehicle stopped early, missed the sample, or returned with incomplete data. Your team will act as an anomaly review board. Objectives What You Will Practice Separate facts from assumptions Build a fault tree or cause map Use evidence to rank causes Define corrective and preventive actions Materials What You Need Teacher-provided anomaly scenario and evidence packet Fault-tree template Test logs or code excerpts Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Create a timeline of confirmed events. List facts, unknowns, and assumptions in separate columns. Define the top failure event. Build a fault tree or cause-and-effect diagram with at least three branches. Use available evidence to eliminate or rank causes. Identify the most likely root cause and one contributing factor. Write a corrective action and a verification test. Present a return-to-test recommendation: approve, approve with limits, or hold. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use only evidence in the packet unless assumptions are labeled At least three plausible cause branches Corrective action must address the identified cause Verification test must have measurable pass/fail criteria Final recommendation includes residual risk Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not blame individuals; focus on system, process, design, and evidence Protect any provided student/team identifiers Do not modify original logs Deliverables What You Submit Event timeline Facts/unknowns/assumptions table Fault tree Root-cause statement Corrective-action plan Return-to-test decision Reflection Reflection Questions What evidence most strongly changed your conclusion? What cause remained possible but unproven? How could the process prevent recurrence? What additional data should future tests record? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Preserve multiple plausible causes until evidence supports eliminating them. Common Mistake Choosing the first obvious cause can lead to corrective action that does not prevent recurrence. Stretch Goal Create a revised checklist or code monitor that detects the anomaly earlier. Career Connection Aerospace anomaly review boards investigate test and mission failures before hardware returns to operation. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 5 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. Download Presentation Interactive Unit 5 Overview POE Hub Capstone Systems The loudest or most visible failure is not always the highest priority; severity, frequency, and detectability all matter. Integrate Verify Defend Use today’s decisions and evidence to advance the final aerospace systems capstone. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step produces a decision, artifact, or test result needed for the capstone. 1. Summarize performance Calculate relevant statistics and compare results with requirements. 2. Analyze failure modes Identify effects, causes, severity, occurrence, and detectability. 3. Prioritize action Choose the revision with the strongest evidence and risk justification. Lesson Interactive Prioritize the Failure Modes Apply the lesson concept to a capstone aerospace-systems scenario. Use the feedback to correct your reasoning before completing the main deliverable. Failure-Mode Ratings Mode Severity Occurrence Detection difficulty A: Wheel misalignment causes route drift 8 6 3 B: Display label detaches 3 6 4 Risk Priority Number = Severity × Occurrence × Detection difficulty. Mode A RPN Mode B RPN First priority Choose Mode A Mode B Corrective action Choose Add an alignment fixture and verification check Use stronger label adhesive Check Reasoning Calculate each RPN, select the higher-risk failure, and match the corrective action to its cause. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Performance analysis and prioritized failure-mode report Create one focused engineering artifact that demonstrates today’s capstone progress. Create a data summary showing performance against each critical criterion. Complete a failure-mode analysis and justify the highest-priority corrective action. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: POE 5.2 Rover Design Trade Study | LockwoodSTEM POE 5.2 Rover Design Trade Study | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 5 Rover Design Trade Study POE Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.2 Rover Design Trade Study Compare three rover concepts using mission-weighted criteria and recommend one for detailed design. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context The project team has several promising rover concepts but limited time and budget. A structured trade study is required before committing to hardware. Objectives What You Will Practice Select decision criteria Assign defensible weights Score concepts consistently Perform sensitivity analysis Materials What You Need Three concept descriptions or team sketches Decision matrix template Mission requirements Calculator or spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the mission requirements and identify six to eight decision criteria. Assign weights totaling 100%. Define a 1-5 scoring scale for every criterion before scoring concepts. Score all three concepts and document evidence. Calculate weighted totals. Change the two largest weights by plus/minus 10 percentage points and recalculate. Identify whether the winner changes. Recommend a concept and state the largest unresolved risk. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least three concepts and six criteria Weights total 100% Scoring definitions written before final scoring All scores supported by evidence or assumptions Include one sensitivity analysis Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not change criteria solely to make a preferred concept win Label uncertain assumptions Use the same scoring standard for all concepts Deliverables What You Submit Criteria and weights Scoring definitions Completed trade matrix Sensitivity comparison Recommendation memo Reflection Reflection Questions Which criterion drove the decision most strongly? Did sensitivity analysis change confidence in the winner? What missing test data would reduce uncertainty? Where might personal bias have affected scoring? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Write scoring anchors such as “5 = meets requirement with at least 20% margin.” Common Mistake Assigning numbers without defined scoring rules creates a false appearance of precision. Stretch Goal Add cost and schedule uncertainty using best-case and worst-case scores. Career Connection Systems engineering teams use formal trade studies to select architectures, sensors, propulsion, and mission concepts. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 5 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. Download Presentation Interactive Unit 5 Overview POE Hub Capstone Systems A requirement tells what the system must do; criteria define success; constraints define the boundaries of possible solutions. Integrate Verify Defend Use today’s decisions and evidence to advance the final aerospace systems capstone. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that advances the capstone without creating unnecessary documentation. Opening prompt Concept model Guided work Interactive application Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can distinguish requirements, criteria, and constraints and write measurable verification statements. Evidence Capstone requirements and verification table Success Looks Like Each requirement is testable, each criterion has a target, and each constraint states a real limit. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step produces a decision, artifact, or test result needed for the capstone. 1. Translate stakeholder needs Convert needs into functions the system must perform. 2. Define measurable success Assign targets, tolerances, and verification methods. 3. Identify limits Document safety, time, material, size, and budget constraints. Lesson Interactive Classify the Design Statements Apply the lesson concept to a capstone aerospace-systems scenario. Use the feedback to correct your reasoning before completing the main deliverable. Design Statements The system shall transport inspection equipment between work zones. The system shall complete the route in 90 seconds or less. The system must fit within a 450 mm × 450 mm footprint. Remember: A measurable criterion includes a quantity, condition, or pass/fail threshold. Statement 1 Choose Requirement Criterion Constraint Statement 2 Choose Requirement Criterion Constraint Statement 3 Choose Requirement Criterion Constraint Quality of “works well” Choose Not measurable; replace it with a defined target Acceptable as written Check Reasoning Classify each statement by its role in the design specification. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Capstone requirements and verification table Create one focused engineering artifact that demonstrates today’s capstone progress. Write at least four testable requirements with measurable criteria. List at least three constraints and a verification method for every requirement. Download Presentation Interactive Unit 5 Overview POE Hub Capstone Systems Benchmarking is most valuable when it reveals why systems work, what they sacrifice, and how those lessons connect to new requirements. Integrate Verify Defend Use today’s decisions and evidence to advance the final aerospace systems capstone. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that advances the capstone without creating unnecessary documentation. Opening prompt Concept model Guided work Interactive application Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can evaluate technical sources, benchmark comparable systems, and extract useful functions and tradeoffs. Evidence Research and benchmarking summary Success Looks Like The benchmark compares credible sources, documents citations, and explains what will be adapted or rejected. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step produces a decision, artifact, or test result needed for the capstone. 1. Find comparable systems Search for products, patents, technical reports, and prior solutions. 2. Compare functions and tradeoffs Record performance, interfaces, materials, cost, and limitations. 3. Extract design guidance Identify principles to adapt rather than copying complete designs. Lesson Interactive Audit a Benchmarking Plan Apply the lesson concept to a capstone aerospace-systems scenario. Use the feedback to correct your reasoning before completing the main deliverable. Benchmarking Decision The team finds a product advertisement, a manufacturer technical manual, a social-media clip, and a university design report. The team should compare the transport function, interfaces, performance, and limitations—not merely copy the product shape. Best primary benchmark source Choose Technical manual or engineering report Product advertisement What to benchmark Choose Color and visual style Functions, performance, interfaces, and tradeoffs How to use the design Choose Copy the complete solution Adapt relevant principles to new requirements Research traceability Choose Record source, date, and relevant evidence Rely on team memory Check Reasoning Choose a credible, ethical, and requirement-focused benchmarking approach. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Research and benchmarking summary Create one focused engineering artifact that demonstrates today’s capstone progress. Document at least three credible benchmark sources with citations. Create a comparison table and state two design lessons supported by the research. items.description: POE Unit 5 Lesson 5.15: Iteration and Design Freeze. How can teams make evidence-based revisions and decide when additional changes create more risk than value?
items.searchText: POE Unit 5 Lesson 5.15 | Iteration and Design Freeze | LockwoodSTEM POE Unit 5 Lesson 5.15 | Iteration and Design Freeze | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges POE Unit 5 • Lesson 5.15 Iteration and Design Freeze Focus question: How can teams make evidence-based revisions and decide when additional changes create more risk than value? Advanced 2 class periods Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Before final demonstration, the project manager needs a coordinated plan showing how each rover requirement will be inspected, analyzed, demonstrated, or tested. Objectives What You Will Practice Map requirements to verification Sequence tests safely Define objective pass/fail criteria Plan data collection Materials What You Need Final requirement list Rover design information Verification matrix template Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Number every mission requirement. Choose inspection, analysis, demonstration, or test for each. Write an objective pass/fail statement. Identify equipment, setup, data, and responsible team role. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A client has requested “a reliable rover that can transport a payload across rough terrain.” The statement is not specific enough to design or verify. Objectives What You Will Practice Distinguish needs from requirements Write measurable shall-statements Identify verification methods Detect conflicting or missing requirements Materials What You Need Mission statement Requirements template Engineering notebook Optional sample rover data Procedure Instructions Underline every user need or desired function in the mission statement. Convert each need into one or more measurable requirements. Add units, limits, conditions, and success criteria. Assign a verification method: inspection, analysis, demonstration, or test. Identify at least two missing requirements and one possible conflict. Prioritize requirements as Must, Should, or Could. Conduct a peer audit and revise unclear statements. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least ten measurable requirements Every requirement uses a defined condition and limit Each requirement has a verification method Avoid solution-specific wording unless required by the client Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not invent unrealistic performance limits Maintain traceability to the original mission need Clearly mark assumptions Deliverables What You Submit Need-to-requirement table Prioritized requirement list Verification matrix Conflict/missing-information note Revised final set Reflection Reflection Questions Which user need was hardest to make measurable? What requirement could unintentionally restrict design creativity? Which requirement has the highest mission risk? What question should be returned to the client? items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: POE 4.3 Sensor Data Quality Investigation | LockwoodSTEM POE 4.3 Sensor Data Quality Investigation | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 4 Sensor Data Quality Investigation POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.3 Sensor Data Quality Investigation Determine whether a sensor data set is accurate, precise, biased, or affected by noise. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover environmental sensor is producing inconsistent readings. Before replacing hardware, the test team must characterize the data and identify likely error sources. Objectives What You Will Practice Distinguish accuracy and precision Calculate mean, range, and standard deviation Detect bias and outliers Recommend a calibration or filtering method Materials What You Need Sensor or Teacher-provided data set Reference standard Spreadsheet Graphing tools Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Collect or receive at least 20 readings under a constant condition. Record a trusted reference value. Calculate mean, range, standard deviation, and error of the mean from the reference. Create a time-series graph and a histogram or dot plot. Identify any outliers using an teacher-approved rule. Repeat measurements after one controlled change such as repositioning, shielding, or recalibration. Compare the two data sets. Recommend keep, calibrate, filter, reposition, or replace. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least 20 readings per primary condition Reference value clearly identified Include numerical measures of center and spread Do not remove outliers without documenting the rule Recommendation must be supported by evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not expose sensors to unsafe conditions Do not fabricate readings Keep environmental variables controlled unless intentionally tested Deliverables What You Submit Raw data Calculations Two graphs Outlier decision Before/after comparison Sensor recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Was the main problem bias or variation? What evidence supported removing or retaining an outlier? Which controlled change improved data quality most? What filter could reduce noise without hiding real changes? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Plot data in time order before summarizing it; drift may disappear in a simple average. Common Mistake Removing all unusual values because they look inconvenient can hide a real fault. Stretch Goal Implement and compare a moving-average filter with two different window sizes. Career Connection Instrumentation and test engineers validate sensors used for navigation, structures, propulsion, and environmental monitoring. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 4 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. Measure Analyze Defend Use today’s calculations, displays, or test decisions as evidence for the Unit 4 mission investigation. Evidence Consistency comparison using standard deviation Success Looks Like The comparison considers both mean and spread and identifies the more repeatable design. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step builds the data, motion, or testing reasoning required for today’s deliverable. 1. Make the decision Select the design that best meets consistency requirements. Lesson Interactive Choose the More Consistent Design Apply the lesson concept to a mission-performance scenario. Two Guidance Designs Design A: 98, 100, 102, 100, 100 cm Design B: 90, 96, 100, 104, 110 cm Both designs have an average of 100 cm. Design A standard deviation Design B standard deviation Mean comparison Choose The means are the same The means are different More consistent design Choose Design A Design B Why? items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: POE 4.4 Landing-Zone Probability Model | LockwoodSTEM POE 4.4 Landing-Zone Probability Model | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 4 Landing-Zone Probability Model POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.4 Landing-Zone Probability Model Use repeated test data to estimate the probability that a payload lands inside a target zone. Advanced 2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A relief drone drops small emergency packages. The team must determine whether the current deployment method is reliable enough for a defined landing zone. Objectives What You Will Practice Use descriptive statistics Model target success probability Visualize two-dimensional test data Communicate risk and limitations Materials What You Need Approved drop or launch simulation Target grid At least 20 trial coordinates Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define the target-zone boundaries and coordinate origin. Collect or analyze at least 20 landing coordinates. Plot every point on a scaled scatter plot. Calculate mean x and y position and spread in each direction. Count successful landings and calculate observed success rate. Identify directional bias and possible environmental causes. Recommend an aim-point adjustment or process change. Predict the expected number of successes in 50 future drops. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least 20 trials Target success defined before data collection All points shown, including misses Include observed probability and directional bias Recommendation must acknowledge sample-size limits Constraints Constraints & Safety Use a safe simulation or approved low-energy system Maintain a clear test zone Do not alter data after seeing target results Deliverables What You Submit Coordinate data Scatter plot Success-rate calculation Bias analysis Aim-point recommendation Future-performance prediction Reflection Reflection Questions Did the mean landing point fall inside the target? Can a high average accuracy still produce poor reliability? How would wind change the distribution? What sample size would increase confidence? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Keep both coordinate directions; reducing the result to distance alone can hide a directional bias. Common Mistake Assuming the observed percentage is an exact future probability ignores limited sample size. Stretch Goal Create an elliptical landing zone that contains approximately 80% of the observed points. Career Connection Guidance, navigation, and test engineers quantify dispersion and probability for payload delivery, landing, and release systems. Download Presentation Interactive Unit 4 Overview POE Hub Mission Performance Mission performance is not one successful run—it is a pattern of evidence that survives repetition. Measure Analyze Defend Use today’s calculations, displays, or test decisions as evidence for the Unit 4 mission investigation. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that advances the mission-performance investigation. Opening prompt Concept model Guided practice Interactive application Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can distinguish weak observations from repeatable evidence in an aerospace performance investigation. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step builds the data, motion, or testing reasoning required for today’s deliverable. 1. Compare evidence Rank one trial, repeated trials, and controlled repeated trials by decision value. 2. Trace the argument Connect measurement, graph, statistic, and claim. 3. Use the feedback to correct your reasoning before completing the main deliverable. Mission Claim “The rover can reliably stop inside the landing zone.” Select the evidence features needed before the team can defend that claim. Reminder: A dramatic single success may be useful for troubleshooting, but it is not reliability evidence. Test record Choose One successful run Repeated trials Test conditions Choose Several uncontrolled changes Controlled variables Data display Choose Unlabeled graph Labeled graph with units Conclusion Choose It will always succeed It met the criterion in these tests Check Reasoning Choose the combination that supports a repeatable, readable, and appropriately limited claim. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small payload-deployment system must place a sensor inside a target zone. Your team will analyze a safe classroom launcher or simulation. Objectives What You Will Practice Measure launch conditions Apply horizontal and vertical kinematics Create graphs and uncertainty statements Compare model predictions with test results Materials What You Need Approved launcher or simulation Meter tape Angle tool if applicable Stopwatch or video timing Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define launch height, angle, and target coordinate system. Record at least five trials at one controlled setting. Calculate predicted flight time and horizontal range using the assigned model. Measure actual landing positions. items.searchText: POE 4.2 Rover Acceleration Characterization | LockwoodSTEM POE 4.2 Rover Acceleration Characterization | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 4 Rover Acceleration Characterization POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.2 Rover Acceleration Characterization Measure rover motion and determine whether acceleration is approximately constant during startup. Intermediate 1 class period Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A mission-planning team needs a simple model of rover startup motion to estimate stopping and maneuvering distance. Objectives What You Will Practice Collect position-time data Calculate velocity and acceleration Interpret motion graphs Judge whether a model is appropriate Materials What You Need Rover Straight measured track Video camera or motion sensor Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Mark a straight test track and choose a consistent rover command. Collect position versus time using video frames or a motion sensor. Create a position-time graph. Calculate interval velocities and create a velocity-time graph. Estimate acceleration from the graph. Repeat the trial two more times. Compare acceleration values and decide whether a constant-acceleration model is reasonable. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least three trials Consistent battery and command settings Show calculation method for velocity and acceleration Use graphs with labeled axes and units Model conclusion must include evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Use a clear track Maintain immediate stop control Do not stand in front of the rover Secure loose cables and equipment Deliverables What You Submit Test method Position data Position-time and velocity-time graphs Acceleration estimate Model evaluation Reflection Reflection Questions Where was acceleration most constant? How did sampling interval affect the graph? What caused differences among trials? How would payload mass change startup motion? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use consistent time intervals and identify the center time for interval velocity values. Common Mistake Calculating one acceleration value from the entire run can hide changes during startup and steady motion. Stretch Goal Repeat with an added payload and compare acceleration statistically. Career Connection Vehicle dynamics and controls engineers characterize acceleration, braking, and traction for autonomous vehicles. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: POE 0.5 Preflight Readiness Review | LockwoodSTEM POE 0.5 Preflight Readiness Review | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 0 Preflight Readiness Review POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.5 Preflight Readiness Review Create and conduct the most reliable preflight inspection for a classroom rover or mechanism. Advanced 1-2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Two student teams are preparing identical systems for a mission demonstration. The winning team is not simply the fastest; it is the team whose checklist catches the most faults while remaining efficient. Objectives What You Will Practice Translate failure risks into inspection steps Sequence checks efficiently Use objective pass/fail criteria Validate a checklist through fault insertion Materials What You Need Classroom rover or mechanism Fault cards or teacher-inserted issues Checklist template Timer Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions List at least ten possible mission-preventing faults. Rank each fault by likelihood and consequence. Write a checklist with observable pass/fail criteria. Arrange checks from safe/no-power inspection through powered functional checks. Exchange systems with another team; your teacher inserts approved faults. Conduct the inspection while being timed. Record detected faults, missed faults, and unnecessary checks. Revise the checklist and repeat one validation round. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least 12 checklist items Checklist must include identity, physical condition, power, movement, sensor/control, and final configuration No item may use vague wording such as “looks good” Score balances detection rate and completion time Constraints Constraints & Safety Only teacher-approved faults may be inserted Do not defeat guards or create electrical hazards Power must remain off during physical inspection unless instructed Deliverables What You Submit Risk-ranked fault list Preflight checklist Validation results Revised checklist Competition score summary Reflection Reflection Questions Which fault was easiest to miss? Which checklist item had the clearest pass/fail standard? What check could be automated? How did time pressure affect performance? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Write checklist items as actions with a condition: “Verify battery connector is fully seated and locked.” Common Mistake A long checklist is not automatically better. Repeated or low-value checks can hide critical items. Stretch Goal Convert the final checklist into a QR-linked digital form. Career Connection Aerospace operations teams use configuration-controlled checklists for aircraft, launch vehicles, and ground support equipment. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation.
