items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: POE 0.4 Mission Team Communication Protocol | LockwoodSTEM POE 0.4 Mission Team Communication Protocol | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 0 Mission Team Communication Protocol POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.4 Mission Team Communication Protocol Design and test a concise communication protocol for a multi-station engineering task. Intermediate 1 class period Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover test team must coordinate a driver, sensor observer, data recorder, and safety lead. Miscommunication could damage hardware or invalidate test data. Objectives What You Will Practice Define clear team roles Create standardized callouts Use closed-loop communication Evaluate communication performance Materials What You Need Role cards Simple timed team task Communication log Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Assign four team roles and define each role’s authority. Write standard callouts for ready, start, stop, fault, data confirmed, and reset. Create a rule requiring the receiver to repeat critical commands. Run a baseline task using normal conversation and record errors or delays. Run the task again using the protocol. Compare completion time, errors, and missed information. Revise two parts of the protocol. Requirements Engineering Requirements Every critical command must receive confirmation One person must have stop-work authority Protocol must distinguish normal completion from emergency stop Testing must include before/after evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Use a low-risk teacher-approved task No running or unsafe movement The safety lead may stop the task at any time Deliverables What You Submit Role chart Communication protocol Baseline and final performance table Revision notes Team reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which callout prevented the most confusion? Did the protocol slow the team down or make it faster overall? What information should never be assumed? How could the protocol work in a noisy environment? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use short, unique phrases that cannot be confused with casual conversation. Common Mistake Adding too many callouts can make the system harder to use. Standardize only critical information. Stretch Goal Add a hand-signal or visual backup for two critical commands. Career Connection Flight-test and launch teams use disciplined communication because ambiguous instructions can create serious risk. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.searchText: POE 0.3 Black-Box System Investigation | LockwoodSTEM POE 0.3 Black-Box System Investigation | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 0 Black-Box System Investigation POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.3 Black-Box System Investigation Analyze an unknown input-output system and develop a functional model without opening it. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Mission engineers frequently work with subsystems supplied by another team. They may know the inputs and outputs but not every internal detail. Your team must characterize an unknown classroom system. Objectives What You Will Practice Define system boundaries Identify inputs, processes, outputs, and feedback Plan controlled tests Create and revise a functional model Materials What You Need Teacher-provided black-box device or simulation Approved test inputs Stopwatch or measurement tools Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Observe the system without operating it and define the system boundary. List possible inputs, outputs, energy transfers, and internal processes. Plan at least four controlled tests that change one input at a time. Run the tests and record quantitative and qualitative outputs. Create an initial block diagram. Use evidence to revise the model and predict a new result. Run one confirmation test and evaluate the prediction. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least four controlled tests At least one quantitative output Functional model must show input, process, output, and feedback if present Final prediction must be tested Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not open, alter, overload, or bypass safety limits on the system Use only approved inputs Stop testing if behavior becomes unsafe or inconsistent Deliverables What You Submit Test plan Data table Initial and revised system diagrams Prediction and confirmation result Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which test provided the most useful information? What part of the internal process remains uncertain? How did your model change after testing? What additional sensor would improve the investigation? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Choose tests that isolate one variable rather than changing several conditions at once. Common Mistake Assuming the first explanation is correct can lead to confirmation bias. Actively look for evidence that could disprove it. Stretch Goal Create a fault scenario and explain how the outputs would change. Career Connection Systems engineers use functional models to integrate propulsion, avionics, structures, and controls developed by different teams. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: POE 0.2 Precision Measurement Verification | LockwoodSTEM POE 0.2 Precision Measurement Verification | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 0 Precision Measurement Verification POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.2 Precision Measurement Verification Measure a set of parts, compare repeated readings, and decide whether the measurements are trustworthy. Intermediate 1 class period Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Replacement rover components arrived without complete inspection records. Your team must verify critical dimensions before the parts are released for assembly. Objectives What You Will Practice Use rulers and calipers correctly Evaluate repeatability and measurement variation Record measurements with appropriate precision Make an evidence-based accept/recheck decision Materials What You Need Three to five teacher-selected parts Metric ruler Digital or dial caliper Measurement data sheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Identify the dimensions that are most important to fit or assembly. Measure each critical dimension three times without looking at previous results. Have a partner independently measure the same dimensions. Calculate the range for each set of measurements. Compare your readings with the partner readings and any reference dimension provided. Mark each dimension Accept, Recheck, or Reject and explain why. Write one improvement to the measurement procedure. Requirements Engineering Requirements Record units and instrument used for every dimension Use three repeated measurements per dimension Measurements must be readable and traceable to a labeled feature Decisions must cite numerical evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not force caliper jaws onto a part Use only approved parts Do not treat instrument display resolution as guaranteed accuracy Deliverables What You Submit Labeled part sketch Measurement table Range calculations Accept/recheck/reject decisions Procedure improvement note Reflection Reflection Questions What caused the largest measurement variation? Which instrument was most appropriate for each feature? How would temperature or surface damage affect results? What measurement would you verify first before assembly? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use the same contact points and instrument orientation each time you repeat a measurement. Common Mistake Changing where you measure a feature can create apparent variation that is actually a setup difference. Stretch Goal Design a simple go/no-go gauge concept for one critical dimension. Career Connection Quality engineers and metrology technicians verify incoming components before they enter aircraft or spacecraft assemblies. Beginner 45-60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small aerospace prototyping team is preparing for a rapid repair task. Before work begins, the team needs an independent safety review of tools, PPE, cords, materials, and traffic flow. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize common FabLab and shop hazards Match PPE to the task Communicate corrective actions clearly Apply stop-work authority responsibly Materials What You Need Teacher-provided workstation or safety photo Safety checklist Engineering notebook PPE examples Procedure Instructions Review the assigned workstation without touching anything. Record at least eight observations: safe practices, hazards, or missing controls. Classify each hazard by severity: low, medium, or high. For every hazard, write one corrective action and who should complete it. Create a revised workstation sketch showing safe tool placement, material flow, and walking space. Perform a second inspection after corrections are made. Write a brief go/no-go recommendation for starting work. Requirements Engineering Requirements Identify at least five legitimate hazards or risk controls Include PPE, housekeeping, electrical, cutting/tool, and movement considerations Every hazard must have a specific corrective action Final recommendation must be supported by evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not operate tools during the audit Do not stage unsafe conditions for a photograph Follow your teacher’s directions for handling PPE and equipment Deliverables What You Submit Completed safety audit Annotated workstation sketch Corrective-action table Final go/no-go recommendation Notebook reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which hazard had the highest potential consequence? Which correction was easiest to implement? How can a safe workspace also improve efficiency? When should a student stop work and ask for help? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Separate the probability of an incident from the severity of its outcome when ranking risk. Common Mistake Listing “be careful” is not a corrective action. State what must physically or procedurally change. items.title: Aerospace Material Families and Selection
items.description: POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.10: Aerospace Material Families and Selection. How do engineers select materials when no single material is best in every category?

Download Presentation Interactive Unit 2 Overview POE Hub Structures Mission Material selection is a trade study among properties, processing, cost, environment, safety, and mission priorities. Analyze Test Defend Use this lesson to connect structural reasoning to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that builds toward the aerospace payload support structure challenge. Opening prompt Concept model Guided analysis Interactive practice Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can compare material families using weighted criteria tied to an aerospace structural need. Evidence Material trade study Success Looks Like Criteria weights reflect the mission, scores are evidence-based, and the selected material matches the calculated result. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step builds the structural reasoning needed for the lesson deliverable. 1. Define the mission priorities Choose the properties and constraints that matter for the component. 2. Compare material families Score metals, polymers, composites, or woods using consistent evidence. 3. Defend the selection Use the weighted result and acknowledge one limitation. Lesson Interactive Select a Material for a Lightweight Support Adjust the criterion weights, calculate the weighted totals, and select the strongest mission match. Candidate Material Families Option Low mass Strength Low cost Aluminum 4 4 4 Fiber composite 5 5 1 Steel 2 5 5 Scores use a 1–5 scale. The matrix is a simplified training example; real selection also checks processing, environment, joining, and safety. Mission Weights and Totals Low-mass weight Strength weight Low-cost weight 0 Aluminum 0 Composite 0 Steel Select aluminum Select composite Select steel Check Selection The selected option should match the highest weighted total for the current mission priorities. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Aerospace Material Trade Study Select a material family for one payload-support component. Use at least three weighted criteria and evidence-based scores for three material options. Identify the selected material and one tradeoff or limitation that remains. items.title: Static Equilibrium
items.description: POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.6: Static Equilibrium. What conditions must be satisfied for a loaded structure to remain at rest?

Download Presentation Interactive Unit 2 Overview POE Hub Structures Mission Static equilibrium requires the vector sum of external forces and the sum of moments to equal zero. Analyze Test Defend Use this lesson to connect structural reasoning to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that builds toward the aerospace payload support structure challenge. Opening prompt Concept model Guided analysis Interactive practice Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can use force and moment equilibrium to calculate unknown support reactions. Evidence Equilibrium solution Success Looks Like The support reactions satisfy both force balance and moment balance with correct signs and units. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step builds the structural reasoning needed for the lesson deliverable. 1. Model the structure Create a free body diagram with known loads and unknown reactions. 2. Apply moment equilibrium Choose a pivot that reduces the number of unknowns. 3. Verify force balance Use the calculated reactions to confirm the net force is zero. Lesson Interactive Calculate the Support Reactions A simply supported beam carries a 120 N centered load. Determine the vertical reaction at each support. Loaded Beam 120 N A B The geometry and loading are symmetric. The beam is at rest. Reaction Forces Reaction A (N upward) Reaction B (N upward) Vertical force check: R A + R B − 120 N Check Equilibrium Use symmetry or moment equilibrium, then verify that the vertical force sum equals zero. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Support-Reaction Solution Solve one statically determinate support problem. Show the free body diagram and equations for force and moment equilibrium. Report the support reactions with units and verify both equilibrium conditions. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: POE 2.3 Beam Failure Prediction | LockwoodSTEM POE 2.3 Beam Failure Prediction | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 2 Beam Failure Prediction POE Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.3 Beam Failure Prediction Predict where a beam will fail, test it, and explain the difference between prediction and evidence. Intermediate 1 class period Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover instrument bracket uses a cantilevered support. Before destructive testing, engineers must predict the critical region and expected failure mode. Objectives What You Will Practice Draw free-body diagrams Identify bending moment trends Distinguish stress from deflection Compare prediction with test evidence Materials What You Need Uniform beam samples Clamp or support fixture Incremental masses Ruler Marker Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Measure the beam geometry and mark several observation stations. Draw the beam, support, applied load, and reactions. Predict the region of maximum bending moment and likely failure location. Predict whether the beam will bend elastically, permanently deform, buckle, or fracture. Load the beam in approved increments and record deflection at one location. Stop at your teacher limit or after failure. Compare the observed behavior with the prediction. Write one reason for any mismatch. Requirements Engineering Requirements Complete prediction before testing Use consistent load position Record load and deflection for every increment Identify observed failure mode with evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Wear eye protection Use a shield for brittle samples if directed Keep body parts away from the failure zone Do not exceed approved loads Deliverables What You Submit Free-body diagram Prediction statement Load-deflection table Failure photo or sketch Prediction-versus-result analysis Reflection Reflection Questions Why was the support region critical? When did behavior stop appearing elastic? What measurement uncertainty affected the graph? How would doubling thickness change stiffness? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Mark the beam before testing so you can connect deformation to a specific location. Common Mistake Predicting failure only from where the load is applied ignores the internal bending moment distribution. Stretch Goal Compare two beams with equal mass but different cross-section shapes. Career Connection Structural test engineers compare analytical predictions with physical tests before certifying flight hardware. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. Download Presentation Interactive Unit 2 Overview POE Hub Structures Mission The centroid is the area-weighted average location of a cross-section and serves as a reference for structural analysis. Analyze Test Defend Use this lesson to connect structural reasoning to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that builds toward the aerospace payload support structure challenge. Opening prompt Concept model Guided analysis Interactive practice Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can calculate the centroid of a composite cross-section using component areas and centroid locations. Evidence Composite-area centroid calculation Success Looks Like The section is divided without overlap, component areas are correct, and the weighted averages locate the centroid within the shape. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step builds the structural reasoning needed for the lesson deliverable. 1. Divide the section Break the cross-section into non-overlapping simple shapes. 2. Create the area table Record each area and its centroid coordinates from one datum. 3. Calculate and check Find the weighted average and confirm the result lies within the section. Lesson Interactive Find the Centroid of an L-Section Use the two non-overlapping rectangles and the area-weighted average to locate the composite centroid. Composite Section 20 × 100 60 × 20 x y Shape Area xᵢ yᵢ Vertical 20 × 100 2000 mm² 10 mm 50 mm Horizontal 60 × 20 1200 mm² 50 mm 10 mm Composite Centroid x̄ (mm) ȳ (mm) Reasonableness check Choose The centroid lies inside the material area The centroid lies outside the section Check Centroid Use x̄ = ΣAᵢxᵢ/ΣAᵢ and ȳ = ΣAᵢyᵢ/ΣAᵢ from the lower-left datum. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Composite Centroid Analysis Calculate the centroid of one assigned structural cross-section. items.title: Prototype Build and Load Testing
items.description: POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.17: Prototype Build and Load Testing. How can a team build and test a structural prototype safely while preserving useful evidence?
items.searchText: POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.17 | Prototype Build and Load Testing | LockwoodSTEM POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.17 | Prototype Build and Load Testing | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges POE Unit 2 • Lesson 2.17 Prototype Build and Load Testing Focus question: How can a team build and test a structural prototype safely while preserving useful evidence? Download Presentation Interactive Unit 2 Overview POE Hub Structures Mission A controlled load test increases force gradually, protects people, records deformation and failure behavior, and stops at predetermined limits. Analyze Test Defend Use this lesson to connect structural reasoning to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that builds toward the aerospace payload support structure challenge. Opening prompt Concept model Guided analysis Interactive practice Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can follow a safe build-and-test sequence and capture evidence of structural performance. Evidence Prototype build and load-test record Success Looks Like The prototype matches the plan, the test increases load safely, and observations are connected to load level and location. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step builds the structural reasoning needed for the lesson deliverable. 1. Verify the build Inspect geometry, joints, supports, and critical dimensions before loading. 2. Run a controlled test Apply load in planned increments with a stop rule and safe exclusion zone. 3. Capture evidence Record load, deformation, observations, photos, and failure or stopping condition. Lesson Interactive Sequence a Safe Structural Load Test Put the load-test actions into a safe order that preserves useful evidence. Test Conditions Prototype: Freestanding payload support Planned load increments: 5 N Stop rule: Stop at 25 N, loss of stability, joint separation, or rapid deformation. Testing must protect people and equipment while connecting every observation to a known load level. Reorder the Test Photograph and document final deformation or failure condition ↑ ↓ Stop at the criterion, unsafe deformation, or planned limit ↑ ↓ Increase the load in planned increments while recording data ↑ ↓ Apply a small preload and verify the setup is stable ↑ ↓ Establish the exclusion zone and install shields or restraints ↑ ↓ Inspect geometry, joints, mass, supports, and test equipment ↑ ↓ Check Sequence Inspect first, control the area, stabilize the setup, load gradually, honor the stop rule, and document the final condition. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Prototype Load-Test Record Build and test the payload-support prototype using the approved plan. Document the completed structure, critical dimensions, mass, and pretest inspection. Record each load increment, deformation or observations, maximum verified load, and stopping condition. Exit Ticket Mission Debrief 1 State one structural idea from today in your own words. 2 Name one calculation, measurement, diagram, or observation that could support a design decision. 3 Identify one question or risk to carry into the next structural lesson. items.title: Impact-Protection Lander Structure
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: POE 2.4 Impact-Protection Lander Structure | LockwoodSTEM POE 2.4 Impact-Protection Lander Structure | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 2 Impact-Protection Lander Structure POE Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.4 Impact-Protection Lander Structure Design a lightweight protective structure that limits damage to a payload during a controlled drop. Advanced 2-3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small sensor package must survive a hard landing. Your team will design a structure that manages impact energy without simply surrounding the payload with excessive material. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply energy absorption concepts Design controlled deformation Use iterative drop testing Evaluate protection versus mass Materials What You Need Small payload or raw egg substitute Paper, straws, foam, cardboard, tape, or approved materials Mass scale Drop test area Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Record payload dimensions, mass, and failure risks. Sketch two concepts using crumple zones, suspension, landing legs, or protective frames. Select one concept and define a maximum structure mass. Build the first prototype and photograph it before testing. Conduct a low-height drop, inspect, and revise. Increase to the official height only after passing the lower test. Record damage, orientation, and structural deformation. Calculate total system mass and summarize protection performance. Requirements Engineering Requirements Payload must remain contained Structure must fit within the assigned envelope Mass must remain below the unit limit No loose material may scatter during testing Complete at least two test-and-revision cycles Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only the designated drop zone No throwing or launching Wear eye protection if required Retrieve the device only after the area is clear Deliverables What You Submit Two concept sketches Prototype photos Test log Mass record Damage assessment Final redesign explanation Reflection Reflection Questions Which feature absorbed the most energy? Did the structure protect by staying rigid or deforming? How did landing orientation affect results? What would change for a higher drop speed? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Plan where the structure should deform; accidental deformation may transfer load directly to the payload. Common Mistake Adding soft material everywhere can increase mass without controlling the load path. Stretch Goal Improve survival height by 25% without increasing mass. Career Connection Crashworthiness engineers design landing gear, energy absorbers, seats, and protective structures for aircraft and spacecraft. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. Download Presentation Interactive Unit 2 Overview POE Hub Structures Mission Concept selection is strongest when multiple feasible ideas are compared with weighted criteria and converted into a build-ready plan. Analyze Test Defend Use this lesson to connect structural reasoning to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that builds toward the aerospace payload support structure challenge. Opening prompt Concept model Guided analysis Interactive practice Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can evaluate structural concepts with a weighted decision matrix and create a build plan for the selected concept. Evidence Decision matrix and build plan Success Looks Like Scores are justified with structural reasoning, the selected concept matches the totals, and the plan defines dimensions, materials, joints, and tests. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step builds the structural reasoning needed for the lesson deliverable. 1. Generate distinct concepts Vary geometry, load path, bracing, and connections rather than surface details. 2. Compare with evidence Use weighted criteria and documented scoring rationale. 3. Plan the build Convert the selected concept into dimensions, materials, sequence, and verification steps. Lesson Interactive Select a Structural Concept Use weighted structural criteria to compare three concept directions and choose the highest justified total. Concept Scores Concept Load path Low mass Build reliability A: Braced tower 5 3 4 B: Wide frame 4 2 5 C: Tapered truss 4 5 3 Scores are a training example. A real matrix should include team sketches, estimates, research, and testing risks. Weights and Decision Load-path weight Low-mass weight Reliability weight 0 Concept A 0 Concept B 0 Concept C Choose A Choose B Choose C Check Concept Multiply each score by its weight, sum the totals, and choose the highest justified concept. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Concept Selection Package Select and plan the payload-support concept. Complete a weighted decision matrix for at least three structurally distinct concepts. Create a build plan with dimensions, material quantities, connection details, sequence, and planned tests. Download Presentation Interactive Unit 2 Overview POE Hub Structures Mission A defensible design review connects the mission need, structural decisions, calculations, test data, revisions, limitations, and final claim. Analyze Test Defend Use this lesson to connect structural reasoning to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that builds toward the aerospace payload support structure challenge. Opening prompt Concept model Guided analysis Interactive practice Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can analyze prototype results, prioritize a revision, and present a supported final structural claim. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step builds the structural reasoning needed for the lesson deliverable. 1. Analyze the data Compare load capacity, mass, deformation, and efficiency with the criteria. 2. Prioritize a revision Address the failure location or largest performance gap with a targeted change. 3. Defend the final design Present the problem, decisions, evidence, revision, result, and limitation in a logical order. Lesson Interactive Analyze the Prototype and Build the Design-Review Story Calculate structural efficiency, select the strongest result, and organize the evidence into a defensible final review. Prototype Results Prototype Mass Verified load Max deflection A 120 g 600 N 7 mm B 150 g 900 N 5 mm C 105 g 525 N 11 mm Efficiency A (N/g) Efficiency B (N/g) Efficiency C (N/g) Best overall evidence-based option Choose A B C Organize the Final Review Final performance claim and remaining limitation ↑ ↓ Targeted revision based on the evidence ↑ ↓ Load-test data, deformation, and failure observations ↑ ↓ Prototype geometry, mass, and build evidence ↑ ↓ Load path, calculations, and material reasoning ↑ ↓ Selected structural concept and why it was chosen ↑ ↓ Mission need and measurable criteria ↑ ↓ Check Analysis and Story Calculate load ÷ mass, consider deformation and criteria, then tell the story from need through evidence to claim. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Final Structural Design Review Prepare the final evidence-based review of the payload support structure. Download Presentation Interactive Unit 2 Overview POE Hub Structures Mission Reliable material data comes from controlled variables, consistent procedures, repeated trials, and transparent treatment of anomalies. Analyze Test Defend Use this lesson to connect structural reasoning to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that builds toward the aerospace payload support structure challenge. Opening prompt Concept model Guided analysis Interactive practice Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can evaluate material-test data quality and calculate a defensible summary result. Evidence Materials lab data record Success Looks Like The record includes controlled conditions, repeated measurements, units, anomaly notes, and an appropriate summary statistic. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step builds the structural reasoning needed for the lesson deliverable. 1. Control the procedure Keep specimen geometry, loading rate, and measurement method consistent. 2. Record complete data Capture raw results, units, observations, and trial conditions. 3. Evaluate reliability Calculate summaries, identify anomalies, and decide whether retesting is needed. Lesson Interactive Audit the Materials Test Data Evaluate repeated failure-load results and decide how to handle the anomalous trial. Failure Load Trials 42 N Trial 1 43 N Trial 2 41 N Trial 3 67 N Trial 4 42 N Trial 5 The testing team noted that Trial 4 used a specimen with a visibly thicker connection. Data Decision Likely anomalous trial Choose 67 N 43 N 41 N Mean of the four consistent trials (N) Best next step Choose Document the geometry difference, make a conforming specimen, and repeat the trial Delete Trial 4 without mentioning it Average all trials and make no note Check Data Audit An anomaly should be documented and investigated, not silently hidden. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Materials Test Data Record Complete one organized data record for the assigned material test. Include raw trial data, units, controlled variables, and observations for each specimen. Calculate the required summary and document any anomaly or retest decision. items.description: POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.15: Design Brief: Aerospace Payload Support Structure. How does a clear design brief turn a structural need into measurable engineering work?

Download Presentation Interactive Unit 2 Overview POE Hub Structures Mission A design brief defines the user or mission need, criteria, constraints, deliverables, and evidence required for acceptance. Analyze Test Defend Use this lesson to connect structural reasoning to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that builds toward the aerospace payload support structure challenge. Opening prompt Concept model Guided analysis Interactive practice Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can parse the payload-support design brief into actionable engineering requirements. Evidence Annotated structural design brief Success Looks Like Criteria are measurable, constraints limit solution space, deliverables are identifiable products, and evidence proves performance. Lesson Interactive Explore Cross-Section Bending Stiffness Compare the same 20 mm × 60 mm rectangular member in upright and flat orientations. Section Orientations Upright: b = 20 mm, h = 60 mm Flat: b = 60 mm, h = 20 mm For bending about the horizontal centroidal axis, I = bh³/12. Download Presentation Interactive Unit 2 Overview POE Hub Structures Mission Density connects material volume to mass, while structural efficiency compares useful load capacity with the mass required. Analyze Test Defend Use this lesson to connect structural reasoning to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused sequence that builds toward the aerospace payload support structure challenge. Opening prompt Concept model Guided analysis Interactive practice Evidence check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can calculate mass from density and volume and compare structural load efficiency. Evidence Mass and efficiency calculation Success Looks Like Density, volume, mass, load capacity, and efficiency use consistent units and support a clear comparison. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step builds the structural reasoning needed for the lesson deliverable. 1. Determine material quantity Measure or calculate the component volume. 2. Calculate mass Use density × volume with consistent units. 3. Compare performance Calculate load capacity per unit mass and interpret the result. Lesson Interactive Calculate Mass and Structural Efficiency A polymer lattice has a volume of 120 cm³, density of 1.20 g/cm³, and verified load capacity of 1800 N. Test Article Data 120 cm³ volume 1.20 g/cm³ density 1800 N verified load Structural efficiency in this exercise is load capacity ÷ structural mass. It is useful for comparison but does not replace stiffness, durability, or safety checks. Calculate Mass (g) Efficiency (N/g) Interpretation Choose The structure supports 12.5 N per gram in this verified test condition The material can never fail below 1800 N Check Efficiency Mass = density × volume. Efficiency = verified load ÷ mass. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Structural Efficiency Calculation Calculate and compare the efficiency of one or more structural concepts. Show density, volume, calculated mass, supported load, and units. Calculate load-to-mass efficiency and explain what the result does and does not prove. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: POE 2.2 Wing-Spar Material Trade Study | LockwoodSTEM POE 2.2 Wing-Spar Material Trade Study | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 2 Wing-Spar Material Trade Study POE Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.2 Wing-Spar Material Trade Study Compare candidate materials for a model wing spar and recommend the best option for the mission. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small unmanned aircraft needs a wing spar that is stiff, light, affordable, and manufacturable with available tools. No single material is best in every category. Objectives What You Will Practice Compare material properties Create weighted decision criteria Conduct simple bending tests Defend a materials recommendation Materials What You Need Samples of wood, plastic, aluminum, composite substitute, or approved materials Mass scale Ruler Test fixture Small loads Decision matrix Procedure Instructions Define mission priorities for mass, stiffness, cost, availability, and manufacturability. Measure sample dimensions and mass. Perform a consistent bending test on each material using the same span and load. Record deflection and any permanent damage. Normalize or rank each material for the five criteria. Create a weighted decision matrix. Recommend one material and identify the biggest risk in that choice. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least four candidate materials Same span, support spacing, and test load for every sample Decision matrix must include at least five criteria Recommendation must cite both test data and mission priorities Constraints Constraints & Safety Stay below teacher-approved load limits Wear eye protection during bending tests Do not test brittle materials near faces Handle sharp metal edges carefully Deliverables What You Submit Material property table Bending-test data Weighted decision matrix Mission recommendation Risk statement Reflection Reflection Questions Which criterion most strongly affected the result? Did the stiffest material have the best overall score? How would production quantity change the decision? What missing property would you test next? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Compare materials using equivalent geometry whenever possible; geometry can dominate stiffness. Common Mistake A decision matrix is not objective if weights are chosen after seeing the test results. Stretch Goal Repeat the trade study for a different mission that prioritizes cost or impact resistance. Career Connection Materials and structures engineers select alloys, polymers, composites, and sandwich structures based on mission-specific tradeoffs. Vector Diagram 30° 100 N +x +y Because the angle is measured from +x, the adjacent component uses cosine and the opposite component uses sine. Enter the Components Horizontal component F x (N) Vertical component F y (N) Sign check Choose Both components are positive Horizontal positive, vertical negative Both components are negative Check Components Use Fₓ = F cos θ and Fᵧ = F sin θ with the stated axis directions. Advanced 2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A launch provider is selecting a support frame design. Teams will compete using a scoring formula that rewards high load capacity and low structure mass. Objectives What You Will Practice Optimize structural geometry Use test data to revise a design Calculate an efficiency score Conduct a fair engineering competition Materials What You Need Standardized structural materials Adhesive Mass scale Load-test fixture Official dimension gauge Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the official span, height, and material limits. Sketch three possible structural layouts. Use a quick model or member-count estimate to select one. Build the structure and allow joints to cure. Measure mass and verify dimensions before the official test. Predict failure location and maximum load. Complete the official load test. Calculate the competition score using the provided formula. Document one redesign for a future round. Requirements Engineering Requirements Meet all dimensional limits Use only the issued quantity of material Structure must be free-standing in the fixture Official score uses successful load divided by structure mass No changes after official inspection Constraints Constraints & Safety Follow destructive-test safety boundary Do not stand over the structure Use only approved loading increments Wear eye protection Deliverables What You Submit Three concepts Inspection record Mass and load results Efficiency score Failure analysis Redesign sketch Reflection Reflection Questions Which design choice contributed most to the score? Where did mass fail to contribute useful strength? Did the actual failure match the prediction? How could joint consistency be improved? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Build and inspect one representative joint early; weak joints can dominate the entire structure. Common Mistake Optimizing only for maximum load can produce a heavy structure with a poor efficiency score. Stretch Goal Use the same material allowance to create a second structure with a different geometry. Advanced 2-3 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover design review requires objective evidence of reliability. Each team will complete repeated missions under the same conditions and receive one controlled fault scenario. Objectives What You Will Practice Define reliability metrics Run repeated controlled trials Calculate success rate Respond to a fault without unsafe behavior Materials What You Need Rover and mission course Standard payload Timer Fault scenario cards Data sheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the scoring categories and identify how each will be measured. Complete a preflight inspection. Run three baseline missions and record time, path error, and task success. Receive one teacher-approved fault such as blocked sensor view, shifted target, or low-traction surface. Run two fault-condition missions. Calculate overall success rate and average completion time. Explain how the system detected or failed to detect the fault. Make one approved change and complete a final demonstration. Requirements Engineering Requirements Same code for official baseline trials Complete required mission task and return safely Record every trial, including failures Fault condition must not create unsafe motion Score includes reliability, not only fastest time Constraints Constraints & Safety Emergency stop required Your teacher controls fault setup Do not alter another team’s equipment Keep all observers outside the course Deliverables What You Submit Preflight checklist Five-trial data set Reliability calculations Fault analysis Final demonstration result Reflection Reflection Questions What was the most frequent failure mode? Did the fastest trial represent normal performance? How should reliability be reported with only a few trials? What design change would reduce operator dependence? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use identical start configuration for every official trial to make the comparison fair. Common Mistake Deleting failed trials creates a misleading reliability result. Stretch Goal Complete ten consecutive missions and calculate a larger-sample success rate. items.searchText: POE 3.2 Line-Following Recovery Logic | LockwoodSTEM POE 3.2 Line-Following Recovery Logic | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses POE Unit 3 Line-Following Recovery Logic POE Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.2 Line-Following Recovery Logic Program a rover to follow a path and recover when the line is temporarily lost. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A warehouse-style rover transports equipment through a marked route. Dust or damaged floor markings may interrupt the path, so the rover needs recovery behavior. Objectives What You Will Practice Use feedback control Create state-based logic Test fault recovery Measure path performance Materials What You Need Rover with optical or line sensors Marked course with one intentional gap Programming environment Stopwatch Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Create baseline line-following logic and test it on a continuous path. Define the conditions that indicate the line has been lost. Design a recovery sequence such as stop, search left, search right, and timeout. Add a safe stop if the line cannot be found. Run five trials through a path containing a gap. Record recovery success, completion time, and any departures from the lane. Tune the logic and repeat five official trials. Requirements Engineering Requirements Follow the normal path without manual control Recover from the designated gap Stop safely after the search timeout Complete at least four of five official trials Code must include meaningful comments Constraints Constraints & Safety Use low operating speed during development Maintain a clear test area Provide immediate stop control Do not allow uncontrolled searching outside the boundary Deliverables What You Submit State diagram Commented code Baseline and final results Recovery success rate Tuning explanation Reflection Reflection Questions What event caused the rover to enter recovery mode? Which search pattern worked best? How did timeout length affect safety? What additional sensor could improve recovery? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Draw the control states before writing code: Follow, Lost, Search Left, Search Right, Stop. Common Mistake Adding more nested conditionals without a state plan can make recovery behavior unpredictable. Stretch Goal Add a second fault such as an obstacle that interrupts the path. Career Connection Autonomy engineers design fault-handling states so robotic vehicles remain safe when sensors or navigation references are lost. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context An autonomous service rover must stop at a docking station without striking it or leaving too large a gap. Objectives What You Will Practice Collect sensor calibration data Use conditional logic Evaluate accuracy and repeatability Tune a control threshold Materials What You Need VEX rover or approved mobile platform Distance sensor Programming environment Tape measure Target wall Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Record sensor readings at known distances across the operating range. Create a calibration table and identify any offset or unstable region. Program the rover to approach slowly and stop at the initial threshold. Run five trials from the same start point. Measure final stopping distance for every trial. Adjust speed, threshold, or confirmation logic. Run five final trials and calculate average error and range. Requirements Engineering Requirements Stop inside the teacher-defined target zone Complete five consecutive final trials Use sensor data rather than a fixed travel time Include a controlled low-speed approach Constraints Constraints & Safety Use a clear test lane Install an emergency stop or immediate control method Do not run the rover toward people Keep sensor face unobstructed Deliverables What You Submit Calibration table Program with comments Initial and final trial data Average error and range Tuning reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why did stopping distance vary between trials? How did approach speed affect error? What sensor readings should be ignored? How could the rover detect a missing docking station? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use several consecutive valid readings before declaring that the stop threshold has been reached. Common Mistake Using one sensor reading can make the rover react to noise or a brief reflection. Stretch Goal Add a second phase that aligns the rover after stopping. Observe Isolate Verify Use the lesson activity and interactive to produce evidence for the integrated autonomous mission. Isolate subsystems Test power, devices, wiring, and code separately. 3. Verify the repair Repeat the original test and document the result. Lesson Interactive Debugging record Practice Apply the lesson concept to an aerospace rover or VEX ground-support scenario. Use the feedback to correct reasoning before documenting the main deliverable. Observed Symptom Rover behavior: The program starts, the right motor turns, the left motor does not, and no error message appears. Left: stopped Right: turning Choose the Controlled Debug Path Best first check Choose Confirm left motor connection and configured port Rewrite the entire program Replace every battery immediately Best isolation test Choose Swap the left and right motor ports or run a one-motor test Change motor speed, gearing, and code together Continue the full mission test Evidence of a hardware-side fault Choose The failure follows the motor or cable when ports are swapped The rover looks the same The working motor runs faster Check Debug Plan Start with the smallest test that separates connection, device, and code causes. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves Each step builds the control-systems reasoning needed for today’s deliverable. 1. Set the target Define the desired position, distance, or orientation. 2. Measure error Compare the sensor value with the target. 3. Correct and repeat Command an action that reduces the error without excessive oscillation. Use the feedback to correct reasoning before documenting the main deliverable. Feedback Iteration Target distance (mm) Measured distance (mm) 60 mm Error = measured − target Drive forward Corrective command Predict the Controller Error for the shown values (mm) Correct action Choose Drive forward to reduce distance Drive backward to increase distance Stop even though error is large What makes this closed-loop? Choose The measured distance is repeatedly compared with the target It runs for a fixed time It uses a motor Check Feedback Response The sign and size of error determine the direction and urgency of correction. items.searchText: ADM Unit 3 | Digital Systems and Virtual Integration ADM Unit 3 | Digital Systems and Virtual Integration Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Digital Systems and Virtual Integration ADM Unit 3 Digital Systems and Virtual Integration You will explore digital twins, virtual manufacturing environments, robot kinematics, simulation, collision prevention, conveyor flow, offline programming, and digital twin analysis. 🚀 Engineering Challenge Hub View Lessons Unit Challenge Back to ADM Unit Goal Test before production This unit focuses on how digital systems help engineers simulate, analyze, troubleshoot, and improve manufacturing processes before physical production begins. Unit pathway Lesson Sequence Open each lesson in order and document your work as you move through the unit. Lesson Type Title Focus Open Digital Twin Development, Kinematics & Robot Selection You will learn how digital manufacturing systems are built, represented, and analyzed before physical production begins. Activity 3.1.1 Activity Digital Twin Development Learn what a digital twin is and how virtual models can represent real manufacturing systems. Open Lesson Activity 3.1.2 Activity Virtual World Explore how virtual manufacturing environments can test layouts, workflows, and system behavior. Open Lesson Activity 3.1.3 Activity Modeling Kinematics Investigate how robot motion can be represented and analyzed using kinematics. Open Lesson Activity 3.1.4 Activity The Right Robot for the Job Compare robot options using task requirements, reach, payload, precision, and workspace. Open Lesson Project 3.1.5 Project An Incomplete Facility Analyze a partially developed manufacturing facility and recommend improvements using digital twin and automation concepts. Open Lesson Simulation, Motion Control & Offline Programming You will use digital simulation tools to test robot motion, prevent collisions, control conveyor flow, and program systems virtually. Activity 3.2.1 Activity Simulation Kinematics Use simulation to analyze robot movement, joint motion, and workcell behavior before physical testing. Open Lesson Activity 3.2.2 Activity Don’t Crash! Identify collision risks and use digital tools to prevent unsafe or inefficient robot motion. Open Lesson Activity 3.2.3 Activity Conveyor Flow and Motion Control Study how conveyors, timing, and motion control affect material flow through a manufacturing system. Open Lesson Activity 3.2.4 Activity Offline Programming Explore how robots and automated systems can be programmed virtually before physical operation. Open Lesson Activity 3.2.5 Activity Sorting Silicon Boules Apply sorting logic and digital manufacturing concepts to a semiconductor-style production task. Open Lesson Activity 3.2.6 Activity Digital Twin Analysis Analyze a digital twin to identify problems, evaluate performance, and recommend improvements. Open Lesson Project 3.2.7 Project Circuit Assembly Challenge Use virtual integration, motion control, and process planning to solve a circuit assembly manufacturing challenge. Open Lesson Factory in Motion Challenge Problem You will combine digital systems, virtual integration, motion analysis, and workflow improvement in a final unit challenge. Problem 3.3.1 Problem Factory in Motion Design, simulate, analyze, or improve a virtual manufacturing system that shows how products, robots, conveyors, tools, machines, and workcell layouts interact over time. Open Lesson Essential Questions How can a digital twin represent a real manufacturing system? How do virtual environments reduce risk before production? How can simulation improve safety, motion, timing, and layout? How can digital evidence support process improvement decisions? Learning Targets I can explain the purpose of a digital twin in manufacturing. I can analyze robot motion, kinematics, and workcell layout in a virtual system. I can identify collision risks and process inefficiencies using simulation evidence. I can document digital testing, revisions, and final recommendations. items.title: ADM Unit 4 — Aerospace CNC Manufacturing: From Design Requirements to Machined Prototype
items.description: Design, program, machine, inspect, and defend a non-flight-critical aerospace component prototype.
items.searchText: ADM Unit 4 — Aerospace CNC Manufacturing: From Design Requirements to Machined Prototype | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Aerospace CNC Manufacturing: From Design Requirements to Machined Prototype ADM Unit 4 Aerospace CNC Manufacturing: From Design Requirements to Machined Prototype Analyze an aerospace component, learn how CNC machine code controls motion, develop CAD and CAM files, manufacture a physical prototype, and inspect the result. Engineering Challenge Hub View Lessons Capstone Challenge Back to ADM Unit Goal Plan → Program → Machine → Inspect Transform a verified digital manufacturing plan into an inspected aerospace component prototype. Educational prototype Application Boundary This component is an educational manufacturing prototype. It is not approved for installation on a crewed aircraft, operational aircraft, or flight-critical system. Any real aerospace application would require additional engineering analysis, material certification, process control, inspection, documentation, and regulatory approval. Essential questions What Will Guide the Unit? How do discrete manufacturing steps combine into a controlled aerospace production system? How can a component be made lighter and easier to machine without losing required function? How does G&M code control a CNC mill? How do CAD, CAM, simulation, post-processing, setup, and inspection work together? What evidence is required before a manufactured component can be accepted? Learning targets By the End of the Unit Analyze an aerospace component and its interfaces. Select and justify manufacturing processes. Perform material, tolerance, speed, feed, time, and inspection calculations. Interpret and manually create instructional G&M code. Develop a manufacturable CAD model and technical drawing. Create and verify CAM toolpaths. Complete a supervised CNC setup, dry run, and machining operation. Inspect and defend a physical component using evidence. Unit production toolchain DMC2 Mini + Mach3 + Fusion Workflow Students design the aerospace component in Fusion, create and simulate milling toolpaths in the Fusion Manufacture workspace, post the approved setup with a teacher-validated Mach3Mill post processor, and load the resulting .tap file into Mach3 to operate the DMC2 Mini under direct supervision. CAD: Fusion Design workspace CAM: Fusion Manufacture workspace Post processor: teacher-validated copy of Autodesk Mach3Mill NC output: Mach3-compatible .tap file Machine controller: Mach3 configured for the DMC2 Mini Physical production: teacher-approved setup, toolpath display review, dry run, reduced-speed first cut, inspection, and revision The generic Mach3Mill post is a starting point, not automatic approval. The teacher must validate the post, DMC2 Mini configuration, spindle behavior, units, work offsets, tool changes, and safe start/end behavior before student production. Unit pathway Lesson Sequence Complete the sequence in order. Required teacher approvals separate design, code, CAM, and physical production stages. Lesson Type Title Focus Open Aerospace Manufacturing Planning Analyze the component, establish requirements, compare processes, and prepare for detailed design. Activity 4.1.1 Activity Aerospace Components as Manufactured Systems Trace how raw material, machining, inspection, finishing, and documentation combine to produce an aerospace component. Open Lesson Activity 4.1.2 Activity Aerospace Component Analysis Analyze the function, interfaces, mass, clearances, likely loads, and manufacturing features of an aerospace mounting component. Open Lesson Activity 4.1.3 Activity Design for Aerospace Manufacturability Revise a component concept so it can be machined safely with available stock, tooling, workholding, and inspection equipment. Open Lesson Activity 4.1.4 Activity Aerospace Manufacturing Calculations Use stock, mass, tolerance, cost, spindle-speed, feed-rate, and inspection calculations to support manufacturing decisions. Open Lesson Project 4.1.5 Project Aerospace Component Requirements Review Define the mission need, interfaces, criteria, constraints, process route, material plan, and inspection strategy for the capstone component. Open Lesson CNC Control and Machine Programming Learn the machine coordinate system and understand how G&M code controls motion and machine states. Activity 4.2.1 Activity CNC Mill Anatomy, Safety, and Coordinate Systems Identify CNC mill systems, hazards, machine coordinates, work coordinates, program zero, and safe setup practices. Open Lesson Activity 4.2.2 Activity G&M Code for Aerospace Manufacturing Interpret the structure of a Mach3-compatible CNC program used by the DMC2 Mini and connect each block to machine behavior. Open Lesson Activity 4.2.3 Activity Manual Toolpath Programming Convert a dimensioned two-dimensional aerospace pattern into a manually planned and annotated CNC program. Open Lesson Project 4.2.4 Project Aerospace Toolpath Coding Challenge Write, simulate, revise, and validate manual G&M code for a simplified aerospace mounting plate. Open Lesson CAD, CAM, and Aerospace Component Production Create, verify, manufacture, inspect, and defend the aerospace component prototype. Activity 4.3.1 Activity CAD Design of the Aerospace Component Create a fully constrained, machinable CAD model for the UAV payload sensor mounting bracket. Open Lesson Activity 4.3.2 Activity Aerospace Component Technical Drawing Create an inspection-ready technical drawing with datums, critical dimensions, tolerances, material, and revision information. Open Lesson Activity 4.3.3 Activity CAM Setup and Machining Strategy Create a CAM setup, tool list, operation sequence, and approved cutting parameters for the aerospace component. Open Lesson Activity 4.3.4 Activity Simulation, Post-Processing, and Production Approval Simulate all toolpaths, verify the post-processed code, and complete the production-readiness review. Open Lesson Problem 4.3.5 Problem Aerospace Component CNC Manufacturing Challenge Set up the CNC mill, manufacture the approved component, inspect it, complete a fit test, and defend the manufacturing process. Open Lesson Culminating problem UAV Payload Sensor Mounting Bracket A small unmanned aerial system needs a lighter, manufacturable bracket for an educational sensor or simulated payload. Your team will define requirements, create and verify the digital manufacturing package, machine the approved part, inspect it, and complete an interface fit test. Required component evidence Mission and requirements package CAD model and technical drawing Fusion Manufacture setup and toolpath simulation Fusion-posted Mach3 .tap program CNC production log Dimensional inspection and fit-test results Final manufacturing design review Required component features Assigned airframe interface Payload or sensor interface Cable or connector clearance Exterior contour Weight-reduction feature Tool-compatible radii Approved wall thickness and edge distance Measurable critical dimensions Open Capstone Challenge Certifications and skills Required Readiness Engineering Safety CNC Certification, including the teacher-observed demonstration Fusion CAD Level 1 or teacher-verified equivalent readiness Engineering Drawings Engineering Documentation Design Review Key vocabulary Unit Language manufacturing process design for manufacturability datum interface stock workholding spindle feed rate spindle speed chip load G code M code machine coordinates work coordinates program zero absolute positioning incremental positioning toolpath CAM post processor simulation dry run tolerance dimensional error inspection fit test Interactive tools and printable resources Unit 4 Resource Center Manufacturing Process Router Compare processes using material, geometry, quantity, and tolerance. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: ADM 1.5 Manufacturing Throughput Investigation | LockwoodSTEM ADM 1.5 Manufacturing Throughput Investigation | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Manufacturing Throughput Investigation ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.5 Manufacturing Throughput Investigation Use production data to increase the number of parts processed per hour without reducing quality. Advanced 2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Orion Manufacturing Department: Continuous Improvement Goal: Increase hourly production using verified software improvements. Background Engineering Context Orion Manufacturing expects a surge in demand. The workcell is reliable, but engineers suspect waiting, excessive clearance, and repeated setup motions are limiting output. Teams will compete for the best verified throughput improvement. Objectives What You Will Practice Measure throughput and identify bottlenecks Apply continuous-improvement methods Calculate production-rate improvement Present evidence-based recommendations Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm Cubes or disks Python project Stopwatch Spreadsheet or graph paper Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define one production cycle and the required quality criteria. Run ten baseline cycles and record total time, errors, and idle periods. Create a process map showing robot motion, pickup, transport, placement, and waits. Classify at least three examples of motion, waiting, or over-processing waste. Propose three changes and predict their effect. Implement one change at a time and collect new ten-cycle data. Select the best reliable program and calculate parts per hour. Prepare a short presentation with before/after data and remaining bottlenecks. Requirements Engineering Requirements Improve verified throughput by at least 20% Maintain 100% successful transfers during the final ten-cycle run Use at least two different data displays Document each program change Constraints Constraints & Safety No hardware relocation Robot speed may not exceed approved limits A controlled stop must remain functional Only one variable should be changed between diagnostic trials Deliverables What You Submit Baseline and final Python programs Process map Ten-cycle data tables Before/after graph Parts-per-hour calculation Three-minute presentation Reflection Reflection Questions Which bottleneck limited the original system? Did the fastest trial also have the best reliability? Why should engineers change one variable at a time? What hardware investment would produce the next improvement? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Throughput depends on the slowest repeated step, not simply the maximum robot speed. Common Mistake A single successful fast run is not proof of a reliable production improvement. Stretch Goal Run fifty final cycles and calculate reliability, mean cycle time, and range. Career Connection Continuous improvement and industrial engineers use cycle studies to increase output without buying new equipment. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.title: Design a Stable Pallet Pattern
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: ADM 1.2 Design a Stable Pallet Pattern | LockwoodSTEM ADM 1.2 Design a Stable Pallet Pattern | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Design a Stable Pallet Pattern ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.2 Design a Stable Pallet Pattern Create and program a pallet pattern that stores aerospace components efficiently and remains stable during handling. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Falcon Launch Systems Department: Outbound Logistics Goal: Palletize eight components with high stability and repeatability. Background Engineering Context Falcon Launch Systems ships compact sensor housings in reusable pallets. The existing arrangement leaves unused space and occasionally shifts during transportation. Your team must design a new pattern and program the robot to build it repeatably. Objectives What You Will Practice Plan an efficient pallet layout Translate a layout into robot coordinates Use loops or variables to reduce repeated code Evaluate repeatability and stack stability Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm 8-12 cubes Pallet area Ruler Engineering notebook Python project Procedure Instructions Measure the available pallet area and the dimensions of one cube. Sketch three possible arrangements for eight cubes. Label coordinates or spacing. Create a decision matrix using capacity, stability, robot access, and coding simplicity. Choose one pattern and plan the pickup/drop sequence. Program the first layer and test clearance between placements. Use variables or loops where repeated spacing occurs. Run the complete program five times without manually repositioning cubes. Test stability by gently moving the pallet or performing the approved classroom transport test. Revise spacing or placement order if the stack shifts. Requirements Engineering Requirements Place at least eight cubes Placement error must remain within ±5 mm No cubes may fall during the approved stability test Complete the sequence in under five minutes Return the robot to Home Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only the supplied pallet footprint No manual adjustment after the cycle begins Robot must approach each placement from a safe clearance height Only approved cubes may be stacked Deliverables What You Submit Three labeled pallet concepts Decision matrix Final Python program Five-run reliability log Photo of completed pallet Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why was your selected pattern more stable? How did placement order affect robot access? Which coordinates could be generated from variables? How would fragile parts change your pattern? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip A staggered or interlocking pattern can improve stability without adding packaging. Common Mistake Placing parts too close together can make the magnet or robot wrist contact previously placed parts. Stretch Goal Increase capacity to twelve cubes while keeping the same pallet footprint. Career Connection Automation engineers develop palletizing routines for aerospace, medical, food, and logistics facilities. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.searchText: ADM 1.4 Customer Order Fulfillment Cell | LockwoodSTEM ADM 1.4 Customer Order Fulfillment Cell | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Customer Order Fulfillment Cell ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.4 Customer Order Fulfillment Cell Create a configurable robot program that builds three different customer pallet orders. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications AeroParts Distribution Department: Order Fulfillment Goal: Automate three customer-specific pallet configurations. Background Engineering Context AeroParts Distribution receives small orders with different quantities and arrangements. The current program must be rewritten for every order. Your team must create a flexible program that operators can configure using variables at the beginning of the file. Objectives What You Will Practice Translate order requirements into pallet coordinates Use functions, loops, lists, or variables to create flexible code Verify several production configurations Document an operator-friendly workflow Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm Cubes Three customer order cards Python project Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the three customer order cards and draw each required pallet layout. Identify which pickup and placement actions are common to all orders. Create helper functions for pickup, safe travel, and placement. Create operator variables that select order type or quantity. Program Order A and verify every coordinate. Run Orders B and C by changing only the approved configuration values. Test each order twice and compare the physical pallet to the order card. Add clear comments and an operator instruction block at the top of the program. Requirements Engineering Requirements Correctly complete all three customer orders No code changes outside the configuration section between orders No manual product placement Begin and end at Home Include comments for operator inputs Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only the provided parts and pallet area Maximum cycle time is five minutes per order The robot may carry one part at a time All motions must use safe clearance heights Deliverables What You Submit Three order-layout diagrams Configurable Python program Six-run order verification log Operator quick-start instructions Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which functions made the program easier to adapt? What input error could an operator make? How could input validation improve the system? How would a barcode scanner change the workflow? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Separate values that operators change from the motion logic that should remain protected. Common Mistake Hard-coding every order creates duplicate code and makes later maintenance difficult. Stretch Goal Use a list of coordinates so a new order can be added without changing the pickup/place functions. Career Connection Flexible manufacturing engineers design systems that switch products with minimal downtime or reprogramming. Back to Unit 1 View Code Lesson Focus Stack, test, document Use the example as a starting point, then document how the robot picks, places, stacks, and adjusts height. Lesson Overview In this project, you will apply robotic movement, sequencing, variables, loops, and spatial planning to stack objects accurately and repeatably. The example uses a magnetic end effector to pick up cubes, move them into rows, build additional layers, and adjust placement height. Notes This project extends palletizing by stacking objects in multiple layers. The magnetic end effector must be set before pickup and placement begins. Variables such as z, yPos, and xPos control height and placement locations. Repeated pickup and drop-off patterns are handled with loops. Final submissions should include comments that clearly explain each row, layer, height change, and final placement.
