items.searchText: ADM 1.3 Compare Absolute and Relative Motion | LockwoodSTEM ADM 1.3 Compare Absolute and Relative Motion | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Compare Absolute and Relative Motion ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.3 Compare Absolute and Relative Motion Program the same geometric production path using absolute and relative motion, then recommend the better method. Intermediate 1 class period Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Precision Robotics Inc. Department: Controls Engineering Goal: Select a reusable motion strategy for multiple workcells. Background Engineering Context Precision Robotics is creating reusable code for several similar workcells. Engineers disagree about whether the path should be programmed with absolute coordinates or relative increments. You must test both approaches using the same task. Objectives What You Will Practice Distinguish absolute and relative robot movement Create equivalent programs using two motion strategies Compare readability, editability, and execution Support a programming recommendation with evidence Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm with drawing tool or simulated points Python project Stopwatch Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Choose a rectangular or stepped path with at least eight movements. Sketch the path and label the starting coordinate and all dimensions. Program Version A using absolute move_to() coordinates. Program Version B using move_inc() for repeated or dimension-based moves. Run each version three times and record execution time and positioning success. Change the path width by 20 mm in both programs. Record how many lines or values had to change. Compare code length, readability, reuse, and risk of accumulated error. Write a recommendation for a factory that may move the fixture later. Requirements Engineering Requirements Both programs must complete the same path Use at least eight motion commands Complete three successful trials per version Include comments that identify the coordinate strategy Constraints Constraints & Safety Use identical speed settings for both versions Do not alter the physical workcell between trials Begin from the same Home position Keep the tool above the approved surface Deliverables What You Submit Absolute-motion program Relative-motion program Timing and editability comparison table Annotated path sketch Written recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Which method was easier to understand? Which method was easier to resize? Where could relative error accumulate? When would a hybrid approach be best? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Absolute positions are useful for known fixtures; relative moves are useful for repeated patterns and reusable geometry. Common Mistake A relative program depends on the current position. Starting from the wrong point shifts every later move. Stretch Goal Create a hybrid program that uses absolute coordinates for setup and relative movement for the repeated pattern. Career Connection Robot programmers select coordinate strategies based on fixture stability, product variation, and maintainability. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.searchText: ADM 1.1 Optimize the Pick-and-Place Workcell | LockwoodSTEM ADM 1.1 Optimize the Pick-and-Place Workcell | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Optimize the Pick-and-Place Workcell ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.1 Optimize the Pick-and-Place Workcell Reduce robot cycle time while maintaining 100% successful part transfers. Intermediate 1 class period Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Department: Automated Assembly Goal: Increase output without purchasing a second robot. Background Engineering Context A small aerospace supplier uses a 6-axis robot to move components from an incoming fixture to a pallet. The program works, but the robot travels through several unnecessary positions and pauses longer than needed. Management wants a software-only improvement before purchasing additional equipment. Objectives What You Will Practice Analyze robot motion and identify non-value-added travel Measure and calculate average cycle time Revise movement commands while preserving safety Use test evidence to justify an improvement Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm with magnet end effector Cubes or disks Stopwatch or elapsed-time display Python project Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Load the current pick-and-place program and verify that it completes one full cycle correctly. Run five cycles and record each cycle time. Calculate the average. Sketch the robot path and label every pickup, clearance, travel, and drop-off point. Identify at least three moves, waits, or height changes that may be reduced or combined. Create a copy of the program and make one change at a time. After each change, run five cycles and record accuracy and average time. Select the fastest version that completes ten consecutive transfers without an error. Calculate the percent improvement and summarize the changes that mattered most. Requirements Engineering Requirements Reduce average cycle time by at least 15% Complete ten consecutive transfers with no drops or collisions Begin and end at the approved Home position Keep all movement within the approved work envelope Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not change hardware locations Robot speed may not exceed 100% The magnet must remain the end effector A safety stop must remain available Deliverables What You Submit Original and revised Python programs Robot-path sketch with identified waste Five-trial before/after timing table Percent-improvement calculation Notebook reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which change produced the greatest time savings? What tradeoff did you observe between speed and reliability? Which motion would you redesign if the workcell layout could change? How would one second saved per cycle affect a factory running 8 hours per day? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Optimize path length and unnecessary waits before increasing motor speed. Common Mistake Removing every clearance point may create a collision even when the start and end coordinates are correct. Stretch Goal Achieve a 25% improvement and verify the program for 25 consecutive parts. Career Connection Manufacturing and automation engineers optimize robot motion because small cycle-time savings compound across thousands of parts. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.title: ADM Activity 4.2.3 — Manual Toolpath Programming
items.description: Convert a dimensioned aerospace pattern into a manually planned Mach3-compatible .tap program.
items.searchText: ADM Activity 4.2.3 — Manual Toolpath Programming | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Manual Toolpath Programming ADM Activity 4.2.3 Manual Toolpath Programming Convert a dimensioned aerospace pattern into a manually planned Mach3-compatible .tap program. Back to Unit 4 Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How can a dimensioned toolpath be translated into a safe sequence of CNC instructions? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Establish a program origin and coordinate table. Write an instructional program using safe approach, cutting, retract, and end blocks. Trace and verify every programmed movement before simulation. Manufacturing context Why This Matters Manual programming reveals the machine logic that Fusion later creates automatically. Students will write a short Mach3-compatible milling program, plot the cutter-center path, save it as a teacher-reviewed .tap file, and validate the motion before any machine run. Student task Complete the Manufacturing Sequence 1 Study the dimensioned path, assigned cutter diameter, stock orientation, and teacher-approved program origin. 2 Create a cutter-center coordinate table and identify the active units, G90 or G91 positioning mode, safe Z height, cutting Z depth, and movement order. 3 Write the approved Mach3 safe-start block and confirm the work offset used by the classroom setup. 4 Write G00 rapid moves only above the safe clearance plane and G01 feed moves for controlled cutting motion. 5 Add spindle commands only when the DMC2 Mini Mach3 profile controls the spindle; otherwise annotate the teacher-approved manual spindle step. 6 End with a safe retract, spindle stop when applicable, and M30. 7 Save the reviewed program as a .tap file, trace every block on the grid, and compare the path with the Mach3 toolpath display or classroom visualizer. 8 Revise any wrong units, wrong modal state, unsafe rapid, incorrect depth, unsupported command, or path mismatch. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit The cutter path accounts for the assigned tool and reference point. The tool retracts before rapid travel. The final path matches the dimensioned drawing. Student deliverables What You Submit Toolpath sketch Cutter-center coordinate table Annotated Mach3-compatible program Teacher-reviewed .tap file Line-by-line code trace Path-visualizer or Mach3 toolpath-display evidence Revision note Resources Lesson Resources CNC Coordinate Trainer Open the interactive or printable Unit 4 resource. items.title: ADM Activity 4.3.4 — Simulation, Post-Processing, and Production Approval
items.description: Simulate the Fusion toolpaths, post a Mach3 .tap file, verify it in Mach3, and complete the production-readiness review.
items.searchText: ADM Activity 4.3.4 — Simulation, Post-Processing, and Production Approval | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Simulation, Post-Processing, and Production Approval ADM Activity 4.3.4 Simulation, Post-Processing, and Production Approval Simulate the Fusion toolpaths, post a Mach3 .tap file, verify it in Mach3, and complete the production-readiness review. Back to Unit 4 Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How can a CAM-generated program be verified before it is allowed to control a CNC mill? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Simulate all Fusion operations and inspect tool, holder, stock, workholding, and remaining-material results. Post the approved Fusion setup using the teacher-validated Mach3Mill post processor. Verify the .tap file in Mach3 and complete the production-approval package before machine setup. Manufacturing context Why This Matters Fusion simulation checks the planned stock removal and machine motion before the setup is posted. The approved operations are then post processed with the teacher-validated Mach3Mill post to create a .tap file, which must be independently reviewed in Mach3 before it can control the DMC2 Mini. Student task Complete the Manufacturing Sequence 1 In Fusion Manufacture, select the complete approved setup and run Simulate with the tool, holder, stock, and toolpath visible. 2 Review every operation for collisions, rapid moves, plunges, workholding clearance, remaining stock, gouges, operation order, and final geometry. 3 Correct all Fusion warnings or document why a noncritical warning is acceptable. Regenerate and repeat the full simulation after any change. 4 Open the Fusion Post Library and select the teacher-validated DMC2 Mini copy of the Autodesk Mach3Mill post. Do not select the Mach3 plasma or an unrelated machine post. 5 Post only the approved operations. Confirm the NC program name, units, work offset, tool numbers, manual or automatic tool-change plan, and output folder. Fusion should produce a Mach3-compatible .tap file. 6 Open the .tap file as text and inspect the safe-start block, units, positioning mode, work offset, spindle behavior, feeds, speeds, retracts, depths, unsupported commands, and M30 end. 7 Transfer the approved .tap file using the classroom procedure. In Mach3, load the file and compare the toolpath display, extents, starting point, depth, and program direction with Fusion. 8 Complete the teacher-approved Mach3 verification: correct profile, units, tool, work zero, program line, feed override, spindle procedure, single-block or raised-Z dry run, and emergency-stop readiness. 9 Freeze the approved Fusion version and .tap file. Any later CAD, CAM, post, tool, stock, or setup change requires a new simulation, post, Mach3 review, and teacher approval. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit The post processor matches the classroom CNC controller. The approved code and CAM file are the same version. No machining begins until the teacher records approval. Student deliverables What You Submit Simulation screenshots and report Posted G&M code Code-verification notes CAM verification checklist Production-readiness approval Approved post-processing standard Fusion Mach3Mill Post Use a teacher-validated copy of Autodesk’s generic Mach3Mill milling post as the baseline. Store it in the approved Fusion Post Library location and name the classroom copy so students can distinguish it from unverified generic posts. A post processor translates Fusion toolpaths into controller-specific NC code. It does not prove that the code matches the DMC2 Mini configuration; verification and dry-run approval remain required. Expected output extension: .tap Controller: Mach3 milling profile for the DMC2 Mini Required checks: units, G54/work zero, tool plan, spindle-control method, feeds, retracts, machine limits, and M30 end Never run code from a different post, an older Fusion setup, or an unapproved revision. items.title: ADM Problem 4.3.5 — Aerospace Component CNC Manufacturing Challenge
items.description: Use Fusion and Mach3 to set up the DMC2 Mini, manufacture the approved component, inspect it, complete a fit test, and defend the process.
items.searchText: ADM Problem 4.3.5 — Aerospace Component CNC Manufacturing Challenge | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Aerospace Component CNC Manufacturing Challenge ADM Problem 4.3.5 Aerospace Component CNC Manufacturing Challenge Use Fusion and Mach3 to set up the DMC2 Mini, manufacture the approved component, inspect it, complete a fit test, and defend the process. Back to Unit 4 Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How can a verified digital manufacturing plan be transformed into an accurate, inspected aerospace component prototype? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Complete a supervised CNC setup and dry run. Manufacture and inspect the approved component. Use dimensional and fit evidence to recommend a process or design revision. Manufacturing context Why This Matters This challenge connects the complete classroom workflow: aerospace requirements, Fusion CAD, Fusion Manufacture toolpaths, Mach3Mill post processing, Mach3 verification, supervised DMC2 Mini machining, dimensional inspection, interface fit testing, and process revision. Educational prototype Aerospace Application Boundary This component is an educational manufacturing prototype. It is not approved for installation on a crewed aircraft, operational aircraft, or flight-critical system. Any real aerospace application would require additional engineering analysis, material certification, process control, inspection, documentation, and regulatory approval. Project pathway Milestones 01 Production readiness review 02 Machine setup and dry run 03 Supervised machining 04 Deburring and dimensional inspection 05 Interface fit testing 06 Final manufacturing design review Student task Complete the Manufacturing Sequence 1 Freeze the approved Fusion design version and complete the technical drawing, requirements table, stock plan, inspection plan, and aerospace prototype disclaimer. 2 In Fusion Manufacture, verify the milling setup, stock, WCS orientation, origin, G54 plan, tools, operation order, cutting parameters, heights, boundaries, and workholding clearance. 3 Simulate the complete setup with tool, holder, stock, and toolpath visible. Resolve collisions, gouges, unsafe rapids, excess remaining stock, warnings, and geometry errors. 4 Post the approved setup with the teacher-validated Mach3Mill post and create the final .tap file. Inspect the code and record the matching Fusion file, setup, program, post, and revision. 5 At the DMC2 Mini, complete the teacher-approved machine inspection, reference or startup procedure, tool and stock inspection, workholding, work-zero procedure, file load, Mach3 toolpath-display review, and emergency-stop check. 6 Complete the approved raised-Z dry run, single-block check, or air cut. Confirm extents, direction, depths, clearances, spindle method, feed override, and final safe position. 7 Machine the part under direct supervision. Record pauses, interventions, unusual sounds, vibration, tool condition, program line, and production result. 8 Deburr only with approved tools and inspect every critical feature against the technical drawing using the assigned measurement tool. 9 Complete the airframe-interface, payload-interface, fastener-access, and cable-clearance fit tests using the educational fixture. 10 Analyze dimensional error, tolerance compliance, material use, cycle time, defects, and process problems. Create one evidence-based revision recommendation. 11 Present the final Fusion-to-Mach3 manufacturing package, physical component, inspection evidence, fit-test evidence, safety controls, limitations, and final recommendation. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit The physical part is produced from the approved file and program versions. Inspection includes target, limits, measured value, error, and pass/fail status. The team reports defects and interventions honestly. The final recommendation is supported by manufacturing evidence. items.searchText: ADM Activity 4.3.3 — CAM Setup and Machining Strategy | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 4 CAM Setup and Machining Strategy ADM Activity 4.3.3 CAM Setup and Machining Strategy Create the Fusion Manufacture setup, tool list, operation sequence, and approved cutting parameters for the aerospace component. Back to Unit 4 Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How does CAM convert design geometry into a safe and efficient machining strategy? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Create a Fusion milling setup with approved model, stock, orientation, and work coordinate system. Select classroom tools and create safe, manufacturable Fusion toolpaths in the correct operation order. Document cutting parameters, heights, boundaries, workholding clearance, and estimated machining time. Manufacturing context Why This Matters In the Fusion Manufacture workspace, a setup defines the stock, model orientation, work coordinate system, origin, tools, and operations that will later be posted for Mach3. A correct setup is the bridge between the approved CAD component and the DMC2 Mini. Student task Complete the Manufacturing Sequence 1 Open the approved aerospace component in Fusion and switch from Design to the Manufacture workspace. 2 Create a New Setup for Milling. Select the correct model and define the approved stock using the teacher-provided dimensions or stock mode. 3 Set the setup orientation so Fusion X, Y, and Z match the DMC2 Mini axis directions. Select the approved origin, normally a clearly accessible stock-box point that can be established in Mach3. 4 Confirm the setup work coordinate system and document the Mach3 work offset that will be used, normally the teacher-approved G54 setup. 5 Select only tools from the classroom Fusion tool library and confirm cutter diameter, flute length, overall length, holder, flute count, and tool number. 6 Create the assigned operations in a safe order, such as Face when required, Drilling, 2D Pocket or 2D Adaptive, Engraving when approved, Chamfer when supported, and 2D Contour last. 7 Set approved spindle speed, cutting feed, plunge feed, stepdown, stepover, ramping, stock to leave, compensation type, geometry boundaries, and lead-in/lead-out values. 8 Verify Clearance, Retract, Feed, Top, and Bottom heights for every operation. Check that all rapid motion remains clear of stock, clamps, and fixtures. 9 Generate all toolpaths, review warnings, record the estimated machining time, and save a new Fusion version before simulation. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. items.title: ADM Activity 4.2.1 — CNC Mill Anatomy, Safety, and Coordinate Systems
items.description: Identify CNC mill systems, hazards, machine coordinates, work coordinates, program zero, and safe setup practices.
items.searchText: ADM Activity 4.2.1 — CNC Mill Anatomy, Safety, and Coordinate Systems | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 4 CNC Mill Anatomy, Safety, and Coordinate Systems ADM Activity 4.2.1 CNC Mill Anatomy, Safety, and Coordinate Systems Identify CNC mill systems, hazards, machine coordinates, work coordinates, program zero, and safe setup practices. Back to Unit 4 Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How does a CNC mill translate a digital coordinate system into controlled physical movement? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Identify the DMC2 Mini milling system, Mach3 control interface, axes, spindle, tool, table, workholding, and emergency controls. Distinguish Mach3 machine coordinates from the active work coordinate system used by the Fusion setup. Complete the teacher-approved reference, jogging, zero-setting, program-loading, feed-hold, stop, reset, and dry-run sequence. Manufacturing context Why This Matters The DMC2 Mini is operated through Mach3. Students must understand the physical mill, Mach3 screen controls, machine coordinates, work coordinates, program zero, tool position, workholding, and emergency controls before any code is loaded or motion is enabled. Student task Complete the Manufacturing Sequence 1 Identify the DMC2 Mini frame, spindle, tool holder, cutting tool, table, workholding, X/Y/Z axes, limit or home devices when configured, controller computer, and emergency stop. 2 Open Mach3 and identify the toolpath display, digital readouts, machine-coordinate display, work-coordinate display, jog controls, cycle start, feed hold, stop, reset, single-block mode, feed override, spindle controls, and program window. 3 Complete the teacher-approved startup and machine-reference procedure. Do not use Ref All Home unless the DMC2 Mini has been configured and approved for that procedure. 4 Jog the machine only under direct supervision and record the positive direction of X, Y, and Z on the DMC2 Mini. 5 Explain how the Fusion setup origin becomes the Mach3 work zero, normally through the teacher-approved active work offset such as G54. 6 Practice loading an approved .tap file, reviewing the Mach3 toolpath display, confirming units and program extents, and identifying the stop method without cutting material. 7 Complete a simulated or raised-Z dry run using the teacher-approved speed, spindle, and single-block procedure. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit Axes and origins are labeled from the machine’s actual reference. The work envelope is clear before motion. No student reaches toward a moving spindle or unsecured workpiece. Student deliverables What You Submit CNC mill anatomy diagram Coordinate-system diagram Hazard and control table Completed preflight and safe-state check Coordinate practice results DMC2 Mini control standard Mach3 Operating Boundary Mach3 interprets the NC program and commands the DMC2 Mini axes. Students may not change ports, pins, motor tuning, soft limits, homing, spindle, or machine-profile settings. The active Mach3 profile, machine units, axis directions, work offset, tool, stock, and spindle-control method must match the approved Fusion manufacturing setup. Load only teacher-approved .tap files. Never zero an axis until the teacher-approved work-zero procedure is complete. Use Feed Hold to pause controlled motion and the emergency stop for an immediate hazard. After any reset, verify the machine state, program line, work zero, tool position, and safe restart point before continuing. items.title: ADM Activity 4.2.2 — G&M Code for Aerospace Manufacturing
items.description: Interpret the teacher-approved Mach3 milling command set and connect each block to DMC2 Mini machine behavior.
items.searchText: ADM Activity 4.2.2 — G&M Code for Aerospace Manufacturing | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 4 G&M Code for Aerospace Manufacturing ADM Activity 4.2.2 G&M Code for Aerospace Manufacturing Interpret the teacher-approved Mach3 milling command set and connect each block to DMC2 Mini machine behavior. Back to Unit 4 Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How do G and M codes communicate motion, units, feeds, speeds, and machine states to a CNC device? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Interpret the teacher-approved Mach3 milling command subset used by the DMC2 Mini. Identify modal states, coordinates, feeds, spindle commands, work offsets, and safe start/end behavior. Trace a Mach3 program and compare each block with the intended cutter motion and Fusion setup. Manufacturing context Why This Matters The DMC2 Mini uses Mach3 to interpret the posted NC program. Understanding the Mach3 milling command set allows students to predict motion, identify unsafe code, compare manual instructions with Fusion output, and verify that the machine state matches the manufacturing plan. Student task Complete the Manufacturing Sequence 1 Review the structure of a Mach3 milling program and identify comments, block numbers, G words, M words, X/Y/Z coordinates, F feed, S spindle speed, and program end. 2 Interpret the teacher-approved safe-start states: plane selection, units, cutter compensation canceled, tool-length compensation canceled when not used, canned cycles canceled, absolute positioning, feed-per-minute mode, and the approved work offset. 3 Trace G00 rapid positioning and G01 linear feed motion on a coordinate grid. Add G02/G03 arc motion only after the assigned arc-center or radius method is taught. 4 Compare G90 absolute positioning with G91 incremental positioning and identify the risk of continuing in the wrong modal state. 5 Explain M03 and M05 only in relation to the actual DMC2 Mini spindle configuration. If Mach3 does not control the spindle automatically, the teacher-approved manual spindle procedure replaces automatic spindle commands. 6 Load an approved example into Mach3, examine the toolpath display and program extents, and predict the machine state at the end of each section. 7 Complete the error hunt by locating unsafe retracts, wrong units, wrong positioning mode, unexpected depth, unsupported commands, or missing stop/end behavior. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit Machine-specific commands are verified before use. Every movement is connected to a coordinate and positioning mode. Students distinguish a rapid move from a feed-controlled cutting move. Student deliverables What You Submit Annotated G&M code reference Line-by-line sample program trace Unsafe-code error analysis Short reflection on modal commands Teacher-approved code subset Mach3 Commands Used in This Unit G00 — rapid positioning G01 — linear feed motion G02/G03 — circular interpolation when assigned G17 — XY plane G20/G21 — inch or metric units G40 — cancel cutter compensation G49 — cancel tool-length compensation when the course setup does not use it G54 — approved work coordinate system when configured G80 — cancel canned cycle G90/G91 — absolute or incremental positioning G94 — feed per minute F — feed rate S — commanded spindle speed M03/M05 — spindle start/stop only when configured and teacher-approved M30 — program end and reset Resources Lesson Resources G-Code Path Visualizer Open the interactive or printable Unit 4 resource. items.searchText: ADM 2.2 Automated Packaging Cell | LockwoodSTEM ADM 2.2 Automated Packaging Cell | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 2 Automated Packaging Cell ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.2 Automated Packaging Cell Coordinate conveyors, sensors, and pneumatic gates to move twenty products without a jam. Advanced 2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications AeroPack Systems Department: Packaging Automation Goal: Move twenty parts through packaging without a jam. Background Engineering Context AeroPack Systems packages flight-control components. Parts occasionally arrive too close together, causing collisions at pneumatic routing gates. Your team must redesign the sequence so parts remain spaced and every route completes safely. Objectives What You Will Practice Coordinate conveyor and pneumatic actions Use sensors instead of fixed delays where appropriate Create a state-based production sequence Test and document reliability Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell Entry, transport, and exit conveyors Object or distance sensor Pneumatic cylinders Twenty disks/cubes Python project Procedure Instructions Draw a flowchart from part entry through final destination. Mark every point where a sensor confirmation is needed. Run the existing sequence and record where waiting or collisions occur. Program one-part operation using sensor confirmation before each routing action. Add logic that prevents a second part from entering an occupied zone. Run ten parts, identify failures, and revise. Run a final twenty-part reliability trial. Create a timing diagram showing conveyor and cylinder states for one cycle. Requirements Engineering Requirements Transfer twenty consecutive parts with zero jams Preserve order of arrival Stop conveyors when a routing gate changes position Complete the final trial in under five minutes Constraints Constraints & Safety Conveyor speed may not exceed 70% No manual repositioning during a run Use only approved sensors and cylinders Pneumatic actions must complete before the next part enters the zone Deliverables What You Submit System flowchart Final Python program Timing/state diagram Twenty-part reliability log Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which sensor replaced the most unreliable timer? How did you prevent two parts from occupying one zone? Where could a jam still occur? What should the system do after a detected fault? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Treat each conveyor zone as occupied or clear and do not release a new part until the next zone is confirmed available. Common Mistake Adding long waits may hide a timing problem but reduces throughput and does not guarantee safety. Stretch Goal Add an automatic jam timeout that stops the system and flashes the signal tower. Career Connection Packaging automation engineers integrate conveyors, gates, sensors, and safety logic in high-volume facilities. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: ADM 2.4 Two-Station Manufacturing Handshake | LockwoodSTEM ADM 2.4 Two-Station Manufacturing Handshake | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 2 Two-Station Manufacturing Handshake ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.4 Two-Station Manufacturing Handshake Create a safe request-ready-transfer-confirm handshake between two connected workstations. Advanced 2-3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Orion Robotics Department: Systems Integration Goal: Exchange parts safely between two automated stations. Background Engineering Context Orion Robotics is connecting two manufacturing cells. Station A must never release a part until Station B is ready, and Station B must confirm receipt before Station A begins the next cycle. A failed signal could damage equipment or lose a product. Objectives What You Will Practice Design machine-to-machine communication logic Represent a process with states and flowcharts Program confirmation and timeout behavior Validate communication under normal and fault conditions Equipment What You Need Two connected VEX CTE workcells or a simulated two-station setup Object sensors Conveyors Signal tower Python projects Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define four signals: request, ready, transfer complete, and receipt confirmed. Create a sequence diagram showing which station sends each signal. Program Station B to announce ready only when its receiving zone is clear. Program Station A to wait for ready before releasing a part. Program Station B to confirm receipt after its sensor detects the part. Add a timeout that stops both stations if confirmation does not arrive. Run five normal transfers. Simulate a blocked receiving zone and a missing confirmation; verify safe response. Requirements Engineering Requirements Complete five consecutive normal transfers Never release into an occupied receiving zone Stop safely after a communication timeout Provide visible fault indication on the signal tower Constraints Constraints & Safety No assumptions based only on elapsed time Each transfer requires positive confirmation Stations must start from a documented reset state Fault testing must use approved simulations only Deliverables What You Submit Handshake state/sequence diagram Station A and B code Normal and fault test log Reset procedure Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why are both ready and receipt signals needed? What could happen if one station resets unexpectedly? How did the timeout improve safety? How would a PLC implement this handshake? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Name signals by meaning and state, such as receive_zone_clear, rather than vague names like flag1. Common Mistake A single ready signal is not enough if the sending station never verifies that the product arrived. Stretch Goal Coordinate three stations and include a line-wide stop and reset procedure. Career Connection Controls engineers design handshaking logic between robots, PLCs, conveyors, and inspection machines. Lesson Overview You will use programming logic to make decisions, repeat actions, and control an automated sorting process. This example combines repeated pickup movement, optical sensor input, conditional decisions, and stacked placement locations. Notes This lesson focuses on using loops and conditionals to control an automated sorting process. The loop repeats the pickup, sensing, and placement process for multiple objects. The optical sensor hue value is used to decide which bin or stack location receives the part. zGreen and zRed track stack height so sorted parts can be placed in layers. Final submitted code must include meaningful comments explaining the loop, sensor decision, and placement logic. Back to Unit 2 View Code What You Submit Lesson Focus Pick, place, repeat Use a loop and coordinate offset to repeat a basic workcell movement pattern. Lesson Overview You are introduced to industrial workcells and how a robot can complete a repeatable pick-and-place operation. This example uses a magnetic end effector, a loop, and a coordinate shift to place multiple objects in a simple workcell layout. Notes This lesson introduces a basic industrial workcell movement sequence. The robotic arm uses a magnetic end effector to pick up and place objects. The loop repeats the process so the same task can be performed more than once. The xShift variable changes the placement location for each repeated cycle. Final submitted code must include comments explaining setup, pickup, placement, looping, and coordinate changes. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: ADM 2.1 Machine Vision Quality Inspection | LockwoodSTEM ADM 2.1 Machine Vision Quality Inspection | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 2 Machine Vision Quality Inspection ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.1 Machine Vision Quality Inspection Use an optical sensor to classify parts and reject items that do not meet the color specification. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Department: Quality Assurance Goal: Automatically identify and route production batches. Background Engineering Context An aerospace connector supplier uses color to identify production batches. Parts from the wrong batch must not reach assembly. Your workcell must measure hue, classify each incoming disk, and route it to an accepted or rejected location. Objectives What You Will Practice Collect and interpret optical-sensor data Select threshold values from repeated measurements Use conditional logic for automated decisions Calculate inspection accuracy Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell Optical sensor 6-Axis Arm Red and green disks plus one unknown/test disk Python project Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Turn on the optical sensor light at a consistent power. Collect at least ten hue readings for each known color and record the range. Choose threshold values that separate the two groups. Create an inspection function that returns the detected class. Program the robot to inspect and route each disk. Test a randomized sequence of twenty disks without changing thresholds. Record true color, detected color, and destination. Calculate accuracy and revise thresholds only if the data supports a change. Requirements Engineering Requirements Inspect twenty randomized parts Achieve at least 95% correct classification Send uncertain readings to a reject location Return to a safe position between parts Constraints Constraints & Safety Use one optical sensor Keep lighting and inspection distance consistent Do not identify colors manually during the final run Hardware locations remain fixed Deliverables What You Submit Hue calibration table Python inspection and routing program Twenty-part confusion/accuracy table Threshold justification Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why were repeated readings necessary? Which color had the widest range? How should the system handle an uncertain value? How could ambient light affect production? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use the midpoint between non-overlapping data ranges as a starting threshold, then verify it with randomized tests. Common Mistake Choosing a threshold from one reading often fails when lighting or part position changes. Stretch Goal Add a third color or a confidence band that automatically rejects borderline readings. Career Connection Machine-vision and quality engineers build inspection systems that prevent defective or incorrect parts from reaching customers. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: ADM 2.5 Lean Manufacturing Improvement Project | LockwoodSTEM ADM 2.5 Lean Manufacturing Improvement Project | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 2 Lean Manufacturing Improvement Project ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.5 Lean Manufacturing Improvement Project Identify and remove motion, waiting, transportation, and over-processing waste from a workcell. Advanced 2-3 class periods Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Department: Lean Operations Goal: Reduce waste and improve verified cycle time by 15%. Background Engineering Context Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing meets quality requirements but uses more time and motion than necessary. Your team will complete a Lean observation, collect baseline data, and implement a software improvement supported by evidence. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize common forms of manufacturing waste Create current-state and future-state process maps Measure cycle time and value-added time Implement and verify an improvement Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell Current production program Stopwatch Process-map template or paper Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Observe five cycles without changing the program. List examples of motion, waiting, transportation, defects, and over-processing. Create a current-state process map with times for each step. Mark which steps directly add value for the customer. Select one software change that removes or reduces waste. Predict the expected time savings. Implement the change and run ten verification cycles. Create a future-state map and calculate percent improvement. Prepare a two-minute improvement presentation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Identify at least four examples of waste Implement at least one software improvement Improve average cycle time by at least 15% Maintain product quality and safety Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not remove required inspection or safety actions Change one major variable at a time Use measured data rather than opinion No hardware purchases Deliverables What You Submit Waste observation sheet Current/future process maps Updated code Before/after data and graph Improvement presentation Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which step added the least customer value? Did removing a wait create a new risk? How did the future-state map change? What improvement would require hardware? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Lean improvement removes non-value-added work while protecting quality, safety, and customer requirements. Common Mistake Treating every wait as waste can remove a wait that is actually required for sensor stability or safe motion. Stretch Goal Calculate estimated annual hours saved if the improvement runs 1,000 cycles per week. Career Connection Lean specialists and industrial engineers lead kaizen events that reduce waste and improve flow. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.title: Smart Conveyor Throughput Optimization
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: ADM 2.3 Smart Conveyor Throughput Optimization | LockwoodSTEM ADM 2.3 Smart Conveyor Throughput Optimization | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 2 Smart Conveyor Throughput Optimization ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.3 Smart Conveyor Throughput Optimization Increase conveyor-line throughput while maintaining safe spacing and routing accuracy. Advanced 2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Falcon Manufacturing Department: Production Engineering Goal: Increase verified line throughput by at least 20%. Background Engineering Context Falcon Manufacturing must raise output without purchasing a second line. The conveyors, robot, and routing cylinders are not synchronized, producing idle time in some zones and part bunching in others. Teams will optimize the coordinated process. Objectives What You Will Practice Measure system throughput and spacing Analyze interactions between robot and conveyor timing Use data to optimize a multi-device process Balance speed, accuracy, and reliability Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell Conveyors Sensors Pneumatics 6-Axis Arm if used Thirty parts Stopwatch Spreadsheet Procedure Instructions Run a ten-part baseline trial and record total time, part spacing, and failures. Measure the time required by each major station. Identify the bottleneck station and explain your evidence. Propose at least three software changes. Test one change at a time with ten parts. Choose final conveyor speeds and release logic. Run a thirty-part final trial. Calculate throughput in parts per minute and percent improvement. Requirements Engineering Requirements Increase throughput by at least 20% Maintain zero collisions and correct routing Keep at least the approved minimum spacing between parts Complete thirty final parts without manual intervention Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not move hardware Conveyor speed may not exceed approved classroom limits Safety-stop code must remain active Final settings must be documented Deliverables What You Submit Baseline and final code Station-time study Throughput and spacing data Before/after graph Bottleneck explanation Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which station controlled maximum throughput? Why did increasing one conveyor not always improve the full line? How did reliability influence your final setting? What buffer would help the system? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Optimize the bottleneck first; speeding a non-bottleneck station may only create waiting or jams. Common Mistake Changing conveyor speed, robot speed, and waits simultaneously makes it impossible to identify the useful change. Stretch Goal Develop an adaptive release interval that changes based on downstream sensor status. Career Connection Industrial engineers use line-balancing and bottleneck analysis to improve complete production systems. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.searchText: ADM Unit 2 | Advanced Automation in Manufacturing ADM Unit 2 | Advanced Automation in Manufacturing Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 2 Workcell Safety ADM Activity 2.1.2 Workcell Safety Learn how safety procedures, restricted zones, emergency stops, and safe operating habits protect people and equipment in automated systems. Back to Unit 2 View Code What You Submit Lesson Focus Stop, signal, respond Use event-based programming to stop motion and show a clear visual safety response. Lesson Overview You will learn how safety controls can be built into an automated workcell. This example uses a signal tower button to stop robot motion, display a message, and change tower lights when control has stopped. Notes This lesson focuses on safe workcell behavior and emergency stop logic. The signal tower button is used as an input that triggers a stop response. The control-stopped event changes the signal tower colors to show that the arm has stopped. The repeated movement loop creates motion that can be interrupted by the safety control. Final submitted code must include comments explaining the stop function, event handlers, signal tower behavior, and repeated motion. What You Will Submit What You Submit Engineering notebook entry for Activity 2.1.2 Code or pseudocode with meaningful comments Explanation of how the signal tower button changes system behavior Description of what happens when arm control is stopped Testing notes showing how the stop response was verified Photo, screenshot, or video evidence of the workcell safety behavior Short reflection explaining why emergency stop logic matters in automated manufacturing Code example 2.1.2: Workcell Safety Review the code, copy it when needed, and add comments before submitting your final version. VEXcode Python Example Copy Code Code examples may be incomplete or missing comments. Comments are required for code submissions. def on_signal_tower_pressed(): arm10.set_control_stop(True) brain.screen.clear_screen() brain.screen.set_cursor(1, 1) brain.screen.print("Stop you goofball!") def arm_control_stopped(): # Change colors of tower to show a stop has happened. signal_tower_6.set_color(SignalTower.GREEN, SignalTower.OFF) signal_tower_6.set_color(SignalTower.RED, SignalTower.BLINK) signal_tower_6.pressed(on_signal_tower_pressed) arm10.control_stopped(arm_control_stopped) wait(15, MSEC) while True: arm10.move_to(0, 150, 50) wait(500, MSEC) arm10.move_to(220, 0, 220) wait(500, MSEC) ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.searchText: ADM 3.4 Factory Throughput Simulation | LockwoodSTEM ADM 3.4 Factory Throughput Simulation | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Factory Throughput Simulation ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.4 Factory Throughput Simulation Use a digital twin to balance robot, conveyor, and buffer capacity before changing the physical line. Advanced 2-3 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Nova Factory Systems Department: Industrial Simulation Goal: Select the best production-line configuration virtually. Background Engineering Context Nova Factory Systems is considering three production-line configurations. Building each physically would be costly, so your team must simulate the alternatives and recommend the best design for throughput and reliability. Objectives What You Will Practice Build and compare production scenarios Identify bottlenecks and buffer effects Analyze throughput and utilization data Complete an evidence-based trade study Equipment What You Need Digital twin or factory simulation Three provided layout scenarios Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define the production sequence and output target. Build or load Scenario A with the baseline robot and conveyor settings. Run a simulated production period and record output, idle time, and blocked time. Create Scenario B by changing conveyor speed or buffer capacity. Create Scenario C by changing robot path or station assignment. Run each scenario for the same simulated duration. Calculate throughput, robot utilization, and average work-in-process. Create a weighted decision matrix using output, reliability, complexity, and cost. Recommend one scenario and identify one risk before physical implementation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Compare exactly three scenarios Use identical simulated production duration Report throughput and at least two additional metrics Support recommendation with a decision matrix Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved changes for each scenario Do not change multiple unrecorded variables Simulation assumptions must be listed The recommended scenario must preserve safety Deliverables What You Submit Three simulation configurations Scenario data table Graphs of key metrics Decision matrix Recommendation memo Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which scenario had the highest throughput? Did highest throughput also produce the least work-in-process? What assumption could change the recommendation? Which result should be verified physically first? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Record every simulation assumption; a precise answer from an unrealistic assumption is still unreliable. Common Mistake Comparing scenarios with different run durations or starting inventory produces misleading results. Stretch Goal Perform a sensitivity analysis by changing demand or failure rate. Career Connection Manufacturing simulation engineers test factory layouts and schedules before companies commit capital. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.title: Digital Twin Validation Study
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: ADM 3.1 Digital Twin Validation Study | LockwoodSTEM ADM 3.1 Digital Twin Validation Study | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Digital Twin Validation Study ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.1 Digital Twin Validation Study Compare simulated and physical robot motion and quantify the model error. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications AeroSim Manufacturing Department: Virtual Commissioning Goal: Verify that the digital twin predicts physical performance. Background Engineering Context A new robotic process was developed in a digital twin before the physical cell was available. Before production begins, engineers must verify that simulated positions, paths, and cycle times accurately represent the real workcell. Objectives What You Will Practice Plan a simulation-to-physical validation test Collect comparable position and timing data Calculate error and explain discrepancies Recommend model updates Equipment What You Need Digital twin or simulation environment Physical VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm Measurement tools Stopwatch Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Select five robot target positions distributed through the work envelope. Record each simulated coordinate and predicted travel time. Run the simulated path three times and record cycle time. Transfer the same program to the physical cell after safety review. Measure actual endpoint position or reference alignment at each target. Run three physical trials and record cycle time. Calculate position error and percent timing difference. Identify at least three causes of mismatch and update one model setting. Repeat one test to evaluate the improvement. Requirements Engineering Requirements Validate at least five positions Use three simulation and three physical timing trials Calculate error using a consistent method Document one model correction Constraints Constraints & Safety Use approved speeds during initial physical testing Verify clearance before automatic operation Do not adjust physical hardware during comparison Use the same command sequence in both systems Deliverables What You Submit Validation test plan Simulation and physical data table Error calculations and graph Updated model screenshot Validation conclusion Reflection Reflection Questions Which variable produced the largest mismatch? Why might physical acceleration differ from simulation? What tolerance is acceptable for this process? What additional sensor would improve validation? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Validate the highest-risk positions first: low clearance, long reach, or near workcell boundaries. Common Mistake A simulation that looks correct is not validated until physical measurements are compared. Stretch Goal Create an acceptance limit and automatically flag positions that exceed it. Career Connection Digital manufacturing engineers validate digital twins before deploying high-cost robotic processes. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: ADM 3.2 Offline Programming Deployment | LockwoodSTEM ADM 3.2 Offline Programming Deployment | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Offline Programming Deployment ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.2 Offline Programming Deployment Develop and debug a complete robot task in simulation before its first physical run. Advanced 2-3 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Orbital Components Group Department: Virtual Commissioning Goal: Deploy a new robot task with minimal physical downtime. Background Engineering Context A spacecraft-component line cannot pause while engineers experiment with new code. Your team must program a replacement handling task offline, verify it virtually, and deploy it with minimal physical-cell downtime. Objectives What You Will Practice Develop robot logic in an offline environment Use virtual testing to identify collisions and errors Create a controlled deployment checklist Compare predicted and actual commissioning time Equipment What You Need Simulation/digital twin environment VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm Parts and fixtures Python project Deployment checklist Procedure Instructions Receive the required pickup, inspection, and placement sequence. Measure or verify all fixture coordinates in the virtual model. Write the full program without operating the physical robot. Run at least ten simulated cycles and resolve every collision or fault. Record predicted cycle time and create a risk checklist. Perform a line-by-line safety review before physical deployment. Run the physical system first at reduced speed. Correct only differences that could not be predicted virtually. Record total physical commissioning time and compare it with the predicted plan. Requirements Engineering Requirements Complete ten fault-free simulated cycles before deployment Complete the first physical cycle at reduced speed Achieve five consecutive physical cycles Document every change made after deployment Constraints Constraints & Safety No physical trial-and-error before simulation approval Hardware coordinates must be verified Safety stop must be tested before deployment Use approved reduced speed for first run Deliverables What You Submit Offline Python program Simulation test log Collision/risk checklist Deployment checklist Physical commissioning record Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which issue was discovered only in the physical cell? How much physical downtime did offline programming save? Which model detail was most important? How should future fixtures be documented? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Treat the first physical run as verification, not as the first debugging session. Common Mistake Assuming fixture coordinates are identical between virtual and physical cells can cause immediate collisions. Stretch Goal Deploy a second product variation using only parameter changes. Career Connection Offline robot programmers prepare and validate production code without interrupting active factory lines. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.title: Automated Circuit Assembly Cell
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: ADM 3.5 Automated Circuit Assembly Cell | LockwoodSTEM ADM 3.5 Automated Circuit Assembly Cell | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Automated Circuit Assembly Cell ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.5 Automated Circuit Assembly Cell Design a virtual workcell that transports, positions, and verifies components for circuit assembly. Advanced 3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Satellite Electronics Systems Department: Automation Integration Goal: Simulate a complete component assembly and inspection cell. Background Engineering Context A satellite electronics supplier wants to automate a simplified circuit-board assembly process. The cell must deliver parts in order, avoid collisions, and include a quality-verification step before the product exits. Objectives What You Will Practice Integrate robot, conveyor, and sensor behavior Sequence a multi-step automated assembly Use simulation for system verification Document interfaces and production logic Equipment What You Need Digital twin environment Virtual robot and conveyors Virtual sensors/inspection point Component models Python or simulation logic Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define a three-component assembly sequence. Create a layout showing incoming parts, assembly position, inspection point, and exit. Develop a state or flow diagram for the complete cycle. Program the robot to retrieve and place components in the required order. Add conveyor logic that prevents a new board from entering while assembly is active. Add a simulated inspection decision with pass and reject routes. Run ten simulated boards and record failures and cycle times. Revise the layout or logic until ten consecutive boards pass the system test. Prepare an interface diagram showing signals between devices. Requirements Engineering Requirements Complete ten consecutive simulated assemblies Place all components in the correct order Prevent simultaneous use of an occupied zone Route failed inspection results to reject Provide a documented reset procedure Constraints Constraints & Safety Use the provided virtual equipment set No overlapping robot/conveyor motion in unsafe zones All device interactions require a defined signal or condition Final program must include comments Deliverables What You Submit Workcell layout State/flow diagram Simulation program Ten-board test log Device interface diagram Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which interface was hardest to coordinate? Where was a buffer needed? What physical tolerance would matter most? How would a real camera inspect the assembly? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Define device ownership of each zone so two machines never command the same space at once. Common Mistake Programming each device separately without a shared state model often creates deadlocks or collisions. Stretch Goal Add a rework loop that returns one failed board for a second assembly attempt. Career Connection Systems integrators combine robots, conveyors, sensors, and inspection equipment into complete production cells. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.title: Collision-Free Path Redesign
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: ADM 3.3 Collision-Free Path Redesign | LockwoodSTEM ADM 3.3 Collision-Free Path Redesign | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Collision-Free Path Redesign ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.3 Collision-Free Path Redesign Modify an unsafe robot path so it clears all obstacles while adding the least possible cycle time. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Precision Cell Engineering Department: Robot Safety Goal: Restore safe operation after a fixture change. Background Engineering Context A fixture was added to an existing workcell, creating a collision risk along the original direct path. Engineers need a new path that preserves production speed and maintains a documented safety margin. Objectives What You Will Practice Identify collision zones in a digital model Create safe intermediate waypoints Compare path length and cycle time Verify clearance in simulation and physical operation Equipment What You Need Digital twin Physical workcell if approved Virtual obstacle/fixture Python program Measurement tool Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Run the original path in simulation and capture the collision location. Define a required clearance margin around the obstacle. Create three alternative waypoint paths. Measure or estimate path length for each. Simulate each path and record cycle time and minimum clearance. Select the shortest path that meets the clearance requirement. Verify the selected path at reduced speed on the physical cell. Document final coordinates and the reason each waypoint exists. Requirements Engineering Requirements Zero collisions in ten simulated cycles Maintain the required clearance margin Add no more than 20% to original cycle time Verify one reduced-speed physical cycle Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not remove the obstacle Do not exceed the approved work envelope All waypoint coordinates must be documented Physical verification requires teacher approval Deliverables What You Submit Collision screenshot Three path concepts Clearance/cycle-time comparison Final code Physical verification notes Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why was the shortest geometric path not necessarily the safest? Which waypoint added the most time? How could tool orientation create a collision? What sensor could monitor unexpected obstacles? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Check the entire robot and end effector, not only the tool-center point, when evaluating clearance. Common Mistake A waypoint that clears the tool may still cause an elbow or wrist collision. Stretch Goal Create a reusable safe-travel function for several pickup locations. Career Connection Robot simulation specialists perform collision studies before expensive equipment is installed. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. Lesson Map Back to IED Hub Unit Focus Turn individual parts into an assembly, prototype, drawing package, and final presentation. Assemble Prototype Document Every lesson builds evidence for the final rocket assembly presentation and design package. Unit Overview What Unit 3 Builds You will move from part modeling into assembly relationships, prototype fit evidence, and professional technical drawings. CAD Assemblies You will organize components, place parts, apply relationships, check alignment, and create exploded views. Prototype Evidence You will export, slice, print, assemble, fit-test, and revise a physical rocket prototype. Drawing Package You will create drawing sheets with views, parts lists, balloons, notes, and revision evidence for presentation. Lesson Map Unit 3 Individual Lessons Each lesson has its own presentation and immersive lesson page. Open Lesson PPTX 3.13 Introduction to Technical Drawing Sheets How do drawing sheets communicate part and assembly information? items.description: IED Unit 5: Human-Centered Aerospace Design Capstone lesson hub.
items.searchText: IED Unit 5 | Human-Centered Aerospace Design Capstone | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 5 | Human-Centered Aerospace Design Capstone | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 5 IED Unit 5 Human-Centered Aerospace Design Capstone Unit mission: Design, prototype, test, revise, and present an aerospace solution that responds to real user needs while considering safety, ethics, sustainability, life cycle, and impact. Lesson Map Back to IED Hub Unit Project Complete a human-centered aerospace capstone and final engineering portfolio. Research Prototype Present Every lesson builds evidence for the final portfolio, prototype review, and capstone presentation. Unit Overview What Unit 5 Builds You will connect user research, ethics, sustainability, project management, prototyping, testing, feedback, revision, portfolio evidence, and professional presentation. Human-Centered Research You will define stakeholders, user needs, criteria, constraints, and a design brief before choosing a solution. Prototype + Feedback You will generate concepts, select a final direction, plan fabrication, build, test, collect feedback, and revise. Responsible Communication You will evaluate ethics, safety, sustainability, and life cycle, then assemble a portfolio and final presentation. Lesson Map Unit 5 Individual Lessons Each lesson has its own presentation and immersive lesson page. Lesson Title Focus Question Open 5.1 Human-Centered Aerospace Design Capstone Launch How can engineers design aerospace solutions that meet real user needs while considering safety, ethics, sustainability, and impact? Open Lesson PPTX 5.2 Stakeholder Research and User Needs How can understanding the user help engineers design a better solution? Open Lesson PPTX 5.3 Problem Statement, Criteria, Constraints, and Design Brief How do engineers turn user needs into a clear design problem? Open Lesson PPTX 5.4 Team Norms and Project Management How do engineering teams organize their work so they can complete a complex design project successfully? Open Lesson PPTX 5.5 Concept Generation and Human-Centered Ideation How can engineers generate creative solutions without choosing the first idea too quickly? Open Lesson PPTX 5.6 Decision Matrix and Final Concept Selection How can engineers choose a design concept using evidence instead of personal preference? Open Lesson PPTX 5.7 CAD, Fabrication, and Prototype Planning How do engineers prepare a design for fabrication before building a prototype? Open Lesson PPTX 5.8 CAD Modeling and Prototype Part Development How do engineers turn a fabrication plan into accurate parts that can be built, assembled, and tested? Open Lesson PPTX 5.9 Prototype Build Day 1: Structure and Core Function How do engineers move from a planned design to a physical prototype while documenting changes along the way? Open Lesson PPTX 5.10 Prototype Build Day 2: Integration and Refinement How do engineers refine a prototype so it is ready to be tested by a user or evaluated with data? Open Lesson PPTX 5.11 Testing Protocol and User Feedback Plan How can engineers test whether a prototype solves the user problem? Open Lesson PPTX 5.12 Prototype Testing and User Feedback What evidence shows whether a prototype is successful for the user? Open Lesson PPTX 5.13 Data Analysis and Stakeholder Feedback Review How can engineers combine data and user feedback to decide what should improve? Open Lesson PPTX 5.14 Ethics, Safety, Sustainability, and Life-Cycle Analysis How do engineers make responsible design decisions beyond simply making a prototype work? Open Lesson PPTX 5.15 Final Prototype Revision and Refinement How do engineers use evidence and feedback to make final improvements before presenting a design? Open Lesson PPTX 5.16 Final Engineering Portfolio Workday How can engineers use a portfolio to communicate the complete story of a design project? Open Lesson PPTX 5.17 Final Presentation Preparation and Rehearsal How can engineers present a design solution clearly, honestly, and professionally? Open Lesson PPTX 5.18 Final Capstone Presentations How can engineers communicate the value, evidence, limitations, and future potential of a final design?
