items.title: Object Lines & Hidden Lines
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.3: Object Lines & Hidden Lines. How can a sketch show features that cannot be seen from one view?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.3 | Object Lines & Hidden Lines | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.3 | Object Lines & Hidden Lines | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.3 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.3 Object Lines & Hidden Lines Focus question: How can a sketch show features that cannot be seen from one view? Download Presentation Flight Plan 3D Model + Views Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Use object and hidden lines to make one 2D view complete without unnecessary clutter. Inspect Decide Draw A reader can infer the blocked geometry without seeing the 3D model. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Determine which edges are visible from a selected viewing direction. Represent blocked features with evenly spaced hidden lines. Decide when a hidden line is necessary and when it adds clutter. Success Looks Like The finished view communicates both the visible shape and the necessary hidden geometry. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt When does a feature need to be shown with hidden lines? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters A hidden feature should be shown when it is important to understanding the part and cannot be seen directly in the selected view. Unnecessary hidden lines can make a drawing harder to read. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Object lines show visible edges and outlines. Key Idea 2 Hidden lines show important internal or blocked features. Key Idea 3 Hidden lines should clarify the part rather than fill the view with unnecessary dashes. Interactive Model 3D Object & Hidden Line Explorer Study the part in 3D, switch to standard views, and compare the visible edges and hidden features shown in the orthographic drawings. Loading 3D model… Drag to rotate • Scroll or pinch to zoom • Arrow keys also rotate Calculating dimensions… Standard View Isometric Front Top Right Line Display Shaded Model Object Lines Visible + Hidden Lines Visible/object edge Hidden edge study Viewer Options Auto-rotate model Reset Full Screen Drawing reminder: Hidden lines show important features that are not directly visible from a selected view, such as holes, slots, and interior steps. Use them only when they make the geometry easier to understand. Reference Drawings Front, Top, and Right Orthographic Views Compare each 2D projection with the interactive model. Use the buttons to align the 3D model with the matching standard view. Same Part • Three Views Front View Shows the outer face with hidden features drawn using dashed lines. Show Front in 3D Top View Shows the visible circular holes and rectangular slot from above. Show Top in 3D Right View Shows the side view with hidden features indicated by dashed lines. Show Right in 3D Study prompt: Which features are visible in the top view but hidden in the front and right views? Explain how the dashed lines help reveal the part’s geometry. Lesson Interactive Reveal the Internal Slot The front surface hides a rectangular slot. Turn on only the two dashed lines needed to communicate the hidden sides of the slot without cluttering the view. A B C D Candidate Hidden Lines Toggle Line A Toggle Line B Toggle Line C Toggle Line D Check Hidden Lines A hidden rectangular slot needs two dashed side edges in this view. Your Task Reveal the Features You Cannot See Use the Lesson 1.3 model to create one view that clearly communicates visible and blocked features. Choose the front, top, or right view and list the features directly visible from that direction. Rotate the model to locate holes, slots, or edges hidden behind the visible surfaces. Draw the selected view with strong object lines and evenly spaced hidden lines. Label one hidden-line group with the feature it represents. Quality check: A reader should be able to infer the hidden feature without seeing the 3D model. What You Will Submit Object-Line and Hidden-Line Analysis Submit one clear view and a brief explanation of your line choices. One labeled front, top, or right view containing the required object and hidden lines. A short note explaining why one hidden-line group is necessary. Submission standard: Use uniform dash length and spacing; hidden lines should not look like faint object lines. items.title: Measurement Tools
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.13: Measurement Tools. How do engineers choose the right tool for accurate measurement?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.13 | Measurement Tools | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.13 | Measurement Tools | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.13 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.13 Measurement Tools Focus question: How do engineers choose the right tool for accurate measurement? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Choose and use measurement tools to collect reliable dimensional evidence. Select Measure Record Recorded values include the correct units, precision, and tool choice. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Match an outside, inside, depth, or length measurement to an appropriate tool. Use rulers and calipers with correct alignment and zeroing technique. Record repeated measurements with units and realistic precision. Success Looks Like Another person can understand how each value was measured and how repeatable it was. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why is the most precise tool not automatically the best tool for every measurement? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters Tool choice should match the feature, access, and precision required. A tool that cannot contact the feature correctly may produce a poor result even if its scale is very fine. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Different tools are suited to different measurement types and precision levels. Key Idea 2 A measurement is incomplete without units and an appropriate number of decimal places. Key Idea 3 Repeated trials help reveal technique problems or variation. Lesson Interactive Match the Measurement Tool to the Feature Select the tool whose range, contact surfaces, and precision best match each measurement task. Measurement Task Best Tool Overall length of a 150 mm rocket body section Choose Metric ruler Digital caliper Protractor Tape measure Outside diameter of a 6 mm shaft Choose Metric ruler Digital caliper Protractor Tape measure Angle between a fin edge and the body axis Choose Metric ruler Digital caliper Protractor Tape measure Distance from one side of the classroom to the other Choose Metric ruler Digital caliper Protractor Tape measure Check Tool Choices Do not choose a more precise tool unless its size and measuring surfaces fit the feature. Your Task Select and Verify Measurement Tools Measure assigned rocket or classroom features with the tool best suited to each measurement type. Classify each feature as an outside, inside, depth, thickness, length, or diameter measurement. Select a ruler or caliper and state why it fits the feature. Collect three readings using the same unit and correct technique. Compare the readings and identify the measurement with the greatest variation. Quality check: Report only the precision supported by the selected tool and include units with every value. What You Will Submit Measurement Tool Investigation Submit one data table and one evidence-based conclusion. One measurement table listing the feature, measurement type, tool, unit, and three trials. One short conclusion explaining which tool choice or technique produced the most reliable result. Submission standard: Verify caliper zero before use and do not report unsupported decimal places. items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Measurement Accuracy Competition IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.2 Measurement Accuracy Competition Measure a set of mystery parts as accurately and consistently as possible. Beginner 45 minutes Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Quality inspectors must make fast, repeatable measurements and report them with the correct precision. Objectives What You Will Practice Select appropriate measuring tools Read scales and calipers correctly Record units and precision Analyze measurement variation Materials What You Need 10-15 mystery objects Ruler Dial or digital calipers Measurement data sheet Calculator Procedure Instructions Create a data table with object ID, feature, tool, measurement, and units. Measure each assigned feature once without seeing the reference value. Repeat three selected measurements after a five-minute delay. Calculate the difference between repeated measurements. Compare your results with teacher reference values after all data are submitted. Calculate absolute error for each reference measurement. Identify the tool and feature associated with your largest error. Write a two-step plan for improving measurement reliability. Requirements Engineering Requirements Measure at least ten features Use the most appropriate available tool Record all values with units and realistic precision Repeat at least three measurements Calculate error or variation correctly Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not alter or mark the objects Do not share measurements before the class reveal Use safe caliper pressure on fragile parts Deliverables What You Submit Completed measurement table Repeated-measurement comparison Absolute error calculations Accuracy ranking or score Improvement plan Reflection Reflection Questions When was a ruler sufficient? When were calipers necessary? Did your repeated measurements agree? What caused your largest error? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Close calipers gently. Excess force can compress a part or tilt the jaws. Common Mistake Extra decimal places do not make a measurement accurate. Report only the precision supported by the tool. Stretch Goal Calculate the class mean and range for three measurements and identify possible outliers. Career Connection Quality technicians, machinists, and manufacturing engineers rely on repeatable inspection data to approve parts. items.title: Engineering Change Requests
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.21: Engineering Change Requests. How do engineers document a proposed design change without losing control of the original design?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.21 | Engineering Change Requests | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.21 | Engineering Change Requests | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.21 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.21 Engineering Change Requests Focus question: How do engineers document a proposed design change without losing control of the original design? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Use documented evidence to propose and verify one controlled design change. Define Propose Verify Another engineer can understand what changes, why it changes, and how success will be judged. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Write a clear evidence-based problem statement. Document a proposed change and identify affected parts or records. Create measurable acceptance criteria and a verification method. Success Looks Like The request separates the current design from the proposed revision and includes a testable success condition. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why should an engineering change be documented instead of made directly to the original design? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters A controlled record preserves the current design, explains the reason for the change, identifies affected information, and makes the revision traceable and testable. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 An Engineering Change Request records a proposed revision without erasing the current design. Key Idea 2 The proposal should be supported by observations, measurements, fit issues, or user needs. Key Idea 3 Acceptance criteria define how the team will decide whether the change works. Lesson Interactive Review an Engineering Change Request Complete the four evidence fields for the sample change, then choose the appropriate reviewer decision. Each field needs enough detail for another engineer to act. Problem statement The fin connection loosens after repeated handling. Proposed change Add a small locking feature at the fin-to-body interface. Supporting evidence Two of three team tests showed visible movement at the connection. Verification method Repeat the handling test after the change. ECR Completeness 4/4 complete Reviewer decision Choose Approve immediately Request revision Reject permanently Review question: Does the verification method define a measurable acceptance criterion, or only say that the test will be repeated? Review ECR A complete ECR can still require revision when its success criteria are not measurable. Your Task Develop an Engineering Change Request Identify one evidence-based improvement to the rocket assembly and document it as a controlled proposal. Define the current problem using observations, measurements, fit issues, or user needs. Create a before-and-after sketch showing the proposed change and affected components. Identify impacts on relevant parts, materials, assembly steps, cost, risk, or performance. Write measurable acceptance criteria and a test or inspection method. Quality check: The request must be specific enough for another engineer to implement and verify. What You Will Submit Rocket Engineering Change Request Submit one controlled change document and one decision summary. One completed ECR containing the problem, proposed change, reason, affected items, and a labeled before-and-after sketch. One verification and recommendation summary stating the acceptance criteria and whether the team recommends approval, revision, or rejection. Submission standard: Preserve the original design record and identify which documents would need a later revision. items.title: Why Documentation Matters
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.12: Why Documentation Matters. Why is a design not finished when the sketch or model is finished?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.12 | Why Documentation Matters | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.12 | Why Documentation Matters | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.12 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.12 Why Documentation Matters Focus question: Why is a design not finished when the sketch or model is finished? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Test whether another person can use technical information without verbal help. Draft Test Revise The revised document resolves the specific confusion observed during the test. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Explain why engineering documentation must stand on its own. Observe how another person interprets a drawing or instruction set. Revise unclear information using evidence from the test. Success Looks Like A partner can complete the assigned action using the revised document without coaching. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How can an engineer know whether documentation is actually clear? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters The document must be tested by someone who did not create it. Their errors, pauses, and questions reveal missing or ambiguous information. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Documentation preserves what a design is and how work was completed. Key Idea 2 A usable document must make sense to someone who was not present. Key Idea 3 Testing and revision improve clarity more reliably than assuming the instructions are clear. Lesson Interactive Documentation Stress Test Choose the instruction that another team could execute without asking a follow-up question, then identify the main ambiguity in the weaker document. Document A “Put the small connector back into the body and tighten it until it looks right.” Choose Document A Document B “Insert Item 4 into the aft end of Item 2 with the keyed tab facing the marked reference line. Turn the retaining ring clockwise until hand-tight, then confirm the tab remains aligned.” Choose Document B Main ambiguity in the weaker document Choose Part identity, orientation, and stopping condition A spelling error No color coding Run Stress Test Strong documentation names the part, reference direction, action, and verification condition. Your Task Test Whether Documentation Can Stand Alone Create a short drawing-and-instruction set for a simple assembly or arrangement, then test it with a partner. Prepare an initial document without asking the partner for help. Remain silent while the partner attempts to follow it. Record each hesitation, incorrect action, or request for information. Revise the document to resolve the observed problems. Quality check: The revision must directly address the ambiguity revealed by the test. What You Will Submit Documentation Test and Revision Submit one before-and-after package and one feedback summary. The original and revised versions of the drawing or instruction set, kept together for comparison. A short tester-feedback summary naming the most important revision and why it was needed. Submission standard: Do not erase the original version; it is evidence of the improvement process. items.title: Centerlines & Symmetry
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.4: Centerlines & Symmetry. How do engineers show the center of a feature or object in a technical sketch?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.4 | Centerlines & Symmetry | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.4 | Centerlines & Symmetry | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.4 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.4 Centerlines & Symmetry Focus question: How do engineers show the center of a feature or object in a technical sketch? Download Presentation Flight Plan 3D Model + Views Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Mark circular centers and axes of symmetry with standard centerline patterns. Locate Mark Verify The center or axis is unambiguous in every view where it is needed. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Recognize the long-short pattern used for centerlines. Locate the exact center of a circular feature. Distinguish feature symmetry from symmetry of the entire part. Success Looks Like Centerlines cross at the true center and identify a real axis or symmetrical feature. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why is the outline of a circle not enough to communicate its exact center? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters The outline shows the feature size and shape, but a centerline identifies the precise center or axis used to locate and align the feature. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Centerlines identify centers, axes, and symmetrical features. Key Idea 2 A centerline uses a repeating long-short pattern that differs from a hidden line. Key Idea 3 The entire part may be asymmetrical even when one feature is symmetrical. Interactive Model 3D Centerline & Symmetry Explorer Rotate the part, move to standard views, and compare the circular feature, hidden geometry, and centerlines shown in the three orthographic views. Loading 3D model… Drag to rotate • Scroll or pinch to zoom • Arrow keys also rotate Calculating dimensions… Standard View Isometric Front Top Right Line Display Shaded Model Object Lines Visible + Hidden Lines Visible/object edge Hidden edge study Viewer Options Auto-rotate model Reset Full Screen Drawing reminder: Centerlines identify the center of circular features and axes of symmetry. They help engineers communicate alignment, feature location, and repeated geometry clearly. Reference Drawings Front, Top, and Right Orthographic Views Compare each 2D projection with the interactive model. Use the buttons to align the 3D model with the matching standard view. Same Part • Three Views Front View Shows the front profile with hidden geometry and centerline information. Show Front in 3D Top View Shows the circular feature from above with centerlines marking its center. Show Top in 3D Right View Shows the side profile with hidden geometry and centerline information. Show Right in 3D Study prompt: Which view shows the circular feature directly, and how do the centerlines help identify its exact location? Compare that with the views where the same feature is hidden. Lesson Interactive Place the Center and Identify Symmetry Click the exact center of the circular feature, then identify the symmetry shown by the circle in this view. Symmetry of the circular feature in this view Choose Horizontal only Vertical only Horizontal and vertical No symmetry Tip: Centerlines pass through the true center and extend slightly beyond the circular feature. Check Placement Place the marker where the horizontal and vertical diameters intersect. Your Task Locate Centers and Symmetry Use the Lesson 1.4 model and views to identify the circular feature and the axis that passes through it. Find the view where the circular feature appears directly and mark its exact center. Add crossing centerlines using the correct long-short pattern. Check another view and show the same feature axis where it is useful. State whether the whole part, the circular feature, or both are symmetrical. Quality check: Centerlines must cross at the true feature center and must not be confused with hidden lines. What You Will Submit Centerline and Symmetry Study Submit evidence that connects the centerline pattern to a real feature or axis. One corrected drawing showing the circular center and the related axis in one or two views. One sentence identifying whether the symmetry applies to the feature, the whole part, or both. Submission standard: Extend centerlines only far enough beyond the feature to remain clear and readable. items.title: Top, Front & Right Side Views
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.8: Top, Front & Right Side Views. How do engineers keep multiple views of the same object organized and accurate?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.8 | Top, Front & Right Side Views | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.8 | Top, Front & Right Side Views | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.8 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.8 Top, Front & Right Side Views Focus question: How do engineers keep multiple views of the same object organized and accurate? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Read and complete standard views by matching shared widths, heights, depths, and features. Trace Transfer Verify Every edge in the completed view is supported by information from the two given views. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Identify the information contributed by the front, top, and right views. Transfer feature locations between views using projection lines. Reconstruct a missing view without inventing unsupported geometry. Success Looks Like The completed view matches the shape and feature locations shown by the source views. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How can two orthographic views provide enough evidence to construct a third view? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters Each source view contributes different information. Shared heights, widths, depths, and feature locations can be transferred to determine the missing projection. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 The front, top, and right views describe the same object from different directions. Key Idea 2 Projection lines transfer feature positions between related views. Key Idea 3 A missing view must be derived from the existing geometry rather than guessed. Lesson Interactive Choose the Missing Right-Side View The two given drawings describe one object. Use them together to decide which candidate completes the orthographic set as the right-side view. Given Views Front View Top View Transfer rule: The right-side view must keep the same heights as the front view and the same depths/features implied by the top view. Candidate Right Views View A View B View C Check Right View Look for agreement in overall height, feature placement, and the location of the circular feature. Your Task Complete the Missing Standard View Use two provided orthographic views to infer and construct the missing front, top, or right view. Identify which heights, widths, depths, and feature positions come from each source view. Use light projection lines and a miter transfer when needed. Construct the missing view lightly and compare each edge with the source views. Darken the final object and hidden lines only after the geometry is consistent. Quality check: Every edge in the completed view must be supported by information from at least one source view. What You Will Submit Missing-View Reconstruction Submit the completed set and a short explanation of your reasoning. One three-view set with the missing view completed and projection evidence still visible. One brief feature trace explaining how a specific edge or opening was transferred through the views. Submission standard: Base every line on the source views and keep enough projection evidence to show how the missing view was constructed. items.title: Tolerances
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.14: Tolerances. Why do engineers allow some variation in measurements, but not too much?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.14 | Tolerances | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.14 | Tolerances | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.14 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.14 Tolerances Focus question: Why do engineers allow some variation in measurements, but not too much? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Use allowable variation to decide whether measured parts are acceptable for assembly. Calculate Compare Judge Every pass-or-fail decision is supported by numerical limits and functional reasoning. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Distinguish nominal size from an acceptable size range. Calculate upper and lower limits from a stated tolerance. Classify measured samples and explain a possible functional consequence. Success Looks Like The inspection decision follows calculated limits rather than visual judgment. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why can two parts have slightly different measurements and still both be acceptable? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters Manufacturing cannot produce every feature at one exact value. A tolerance defines the range that still allows the part to perform its intended function. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Nominal size is the target value for a feature. Key Idea 2 Tolerance defines the allowed variation around the target. Key Idea 3 A measurement is acceptable only when it falls within the calculated limits. Lesson Interactive Tolerance Decision Calculator Enter a nominal size, bilateral tolerance, and measured value. The tool calculates the acceptable limits; you decide whether the sample passes. Nominal size (mm) ± tolerance (mm) Measured size (mm) Your decision Choose Pass Undersized Oversized Calculated Limits Lower Limit 19.850 mm Upper Limit 20.150 mm Calculated Status Oversized Check Decision A part passes only when the measurement is within both limits, including the endpoints. Your Task Determine Whether Parts Meet Tolerance Use stated nominal sizes and tolerances to evaluate sample measurements. Calculate the upper and lower acceptable limits for each assigned feature. Compare each sample with the limits and classify it as acceptable, undersized, or oversized. Explain one possible assembly consequence of an out-of-range sample. Recommend a reasonable tolerance for one additional feature and justify the choice. Quality check: Every classification must be supported by shown calculations and units. What You Will Submit Tolerance and Inspection Analysis Submit one completed analysis and one short engineering recommendation. One table showing limit calculations and pass, undersized, or oversized decisions for the samples. One paragraph explaining a functional consequence and justifying a tolerance for one additional feature. Submission standard: Include units and plus/minus notation; a nominal value alone is not an inspection limit. items.title: Final Rocket Assembly Proposal Presentation
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.22: Final Rocket Assembly Proposal Presentation. How can a team justify a proposed rocket assembly improvement using engineering evidence?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.22 | Final Rocket Assembly Proposal Presentation | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.22 | Final Rocket Assembly Proposal Presentation | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.22 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.22 Final Rocket Assembly Proposal Presentation Focus question: How can a team justify a proposed rocket assembly improvement using engineering evidence? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Present an evidence-based rocket improvement proposal using coordinated technical documents. Synthesize Present Defend Every major claim is supported by a drawing, measurement, analysis, or documented observation. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Organize the problem, evidence, proposed change, and verification plan into a clear presentation. Select technical visuals that directly support the proposal. Share speaking roles and respond to questions using evidence. Success Looks Like The audience can understand the current design, proposed improvement, expected benefit, and method of verification. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt What makes an engineering presentation persuasive rather than merely polished? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters The presentation connects a specific claim to credible evidence and explains how the proposed change will be implemented and tested. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 A design proposal connects the current assembly, evidence, and recommended change. Key Idea 2 Technical visuals should support the argument rather than decorate the slides. Key Idea 3 A professional team can explain limitations and answer questions honestly. Lesson Interactive Match Claims to Technical Evidence Plan a defensible final proposal by pairing each claim with the document that provides the strongest direct evidence. Presentation Claim Strongest Evidence “The revised feature fits within the required size range.” Choose Measurement/tolerance record Exploded view ECR BOM “The audience can understand how the rocket parts connect.” Choose Measurement/tolerance record Exploded view ECR BOM “The proposed improvement addresses a documented problem.” Choose Measurement/tolerance record Exploded view ECR BOM “The final package accounts for every component and quantity.” Choose Measurement/tolerance record Exploded view ECR BOM Best opening for the final proposal Choose State the observed engineering problem and why it matters Begin with acknowledgments and save the problem for the end Read every BOM row aloud before explaining the proposal Check Evidence Plan Strong presentations establish the problem, present the change, and support each major claim with direct evidence. Your Task Present and Defend the Rocket Improvement Proposal Assemble the strongest evidence from the unit into a professional team proposal. Organize the presentation around the current problem, evidence, proposed change, expected benefit, and verification plan. Select the drawings, measurements, BOM information, assembly evidence, and ECR details that directly support the argument. Assign meaningful speaking responsibilities to every team member. Rehearse within the time limit and prepare responses to likely questions about feasibility, risk, and evidence. Quality check: Every major claim must be supported by a relevant technical document or documented observation. What You Will Submit Final Rocket Assembly Proposal Submit one coordinated team package and one individual reflection. One team presentation with the final ECR and the supporting technical evidence needed to justify the proposal. One individual reflection identifying the strongest evidence used and one improvement for future technical presentations. Submission standard: Remove information that does not help explain or justify the proposed change. items.title: Adhesives & Fasteners
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.15: Adhesives & Fasteners. How do engineers decide the best way to connect parts together?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.15 | Adhesives & Fasteners | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.15 | Adhesives & Fasteners | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.15 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.15 Adhesives & Fasteners Focus question: How do engineers decide the best way to connect parts together? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Choose a joining method based on material, strength, access, and removability needs. Compare Select Justify The recommendation is supported by the actual requirements of the connection. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Distinguish permanent, removable, and adjustable connection methods. Compare adhesives and fasteners using relevant design criteria. Predict a possible connection failure and propose a prevention step. Success Looks Like The selected method fits the materials, access, loading, and future service needs of the joint. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why might the strongest adhesive still be the wrong choice for a connection? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters The joint may need to be inspected, repaired, or disassembled. Material compatibility, access, cure time, mass, and serviceability can matter as much as maximum strength. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Connection methods may be permanent, removable, adjustable, or temporary. Key Idea 2 Adhesives and fasteners perform differently depending on materials and joint conditions. Key Idea 3 A good selection balances strength with access, assembly, inspection, and repair needs. Lesson Interactive Connection Method Trade Study Select the requirements for an example rocket access-panel joint. The tool recommends a connection method based on the chosen criteria. Joint requirements Must be removable for inspection Must survive repeated service Must resist vibration Mass must be minimized Joint carries only a low load Current Recommendation Structural epoxy Best for a permanent bond. A real selection must also consider material compatibility, available edge distance, environment, and manufacturing access. Evaluate Recommendation Choose at least two requirements so the recommendation is based on engineering criteria. Your Task Select a Connection Method for the Rocket Evaluate one connection between two rocket components and recommend an appropriate adhesive or fastener. Identify the materials, expected direction of force, available access, and whether the joint must be removable. Compare at least three joining options in a simple criteria table. Sketch the selected joint and show the fastener location or adhesive area. Identify one likely failure mode and a step that would reduce the risk. Quality check: The recommendation must connect each important joint requirement to evidence from the comparison. What You Will Submit Adhesive and Fastener Decision Submit one comparison package and one recommendation. One criteria table paired with a labeled sketch of the selected joint. One paragraph justifying the choice and explaining one failure-prevention step. Submission standard: Do not choose a permanent joint without considering future inspection or disassembly needs. items.title: Documenting the Rocket Assembly
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.17: Documenting the Rocket Assembly. What information does someone need to understand or recreate the rocket assembly?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.17 | Documenting the Rocket Assembly | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.17 | Documenting the Rocket Assembly | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.17 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.17 Documenting the Rocket Assembly Focus question: What information does someone need to understand or recreate the rocket assembly? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Create a consistent component record another person can use to identify and inspect the rocket assembly. Name Label Record Part names, item numbers, and connection descriptions remain consistent throughout the record. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Assign a clear name and item number to each major component. Create an annotated assembly sketch showing component location and orientation. Record identifying features and connection information consistently. Success Looks Like Another person can match every listed component to its position in the physical assembly. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why can inconsistent part names create errors in an engineering record? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters If the same component is called by different names, readers may count it twice, select the wrong part, or misunderstand which connection is being described. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 A component record uses standardized names and item numbers. Key Idea 2 Annotated sketches connect written information to the physical assembly. Key Idea 3 Consistent terminology allows another person to identify and inspect the same parts. Lesson Interactive Find the Component-Record Inconsistencies The master record should use one item number, one standardized name, and one verified quantity for each component. Flag the two inconsistent rows. Flag Item Standard Name Quantity Observation 1 Nose Cone 1 Forward exterior part 1 Rocket Tip 1 Forward exterior part 3 Fin 3 Equally spaced around aft body 4 Retaining Screw 1 Two screws observed during disassembly Check Record Look for duplicate identities, inconsistent names, and quantities that conflict with physical evidence. Your Task Create the Rocket Assembly Record Convert the team’s observations into a consistent master record of the rocket components. Assign one permanent item number and standardized name to each major component. Create an annotated assembly sketch showing component position and orientation. Record identifying features that distinguish similar parts. Add concise notes describing how adjacent components connect or align. Quality check: Every reference to a component must use the same name and item number. What You Will Submit Rocket Assembly Documentation Record Submit one master record and one matching visual. One master component record with item numbers, standardized names, quantities, and identifying features. One annotated assembly sketch using the same item numbers and showing orientation and connections. Submission standard: Keep names and item numbers consistent across the component record and the annotated assembly sketch. Objectives What You Will Practice Measure real objects accurately Create multiview and isometric sketches Apply dimensioning conventions Estimate functional tolerances Materials What You Need Approved hand tool Ruler and calipers Graph and isometric paper Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Select an approved tool such as an Allen wrench, screwdriver, small wrench, or pliers. Identify the primary functional features and measurement datums. Measure overall dimensions, thicknesses, diameters, and feature locations. items.title: Isometric Circles, Arcs, and Shading
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.6: Isometric Circles, Arcs, and Shading. How can engineers show curved features and surface depth in an isometric sketch?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.6 | Isometric Circles, Arcs, and Shading | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.6 | Isometric Circles, Arcs, and Shading | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.6 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.6 Isometric Circles, Arcs, and Shading Focus question: How can engineers show curved features and surface depth in an isometric sketch? Download Presentation Flight Plan 3D Models Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Represent curved forms as ellipses and arcs, then use consistent shading to show depth. Construct Curve Shade Curved features align with their surfaces and the shading follows one clear light direction. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Represent isometric circles as ellipses on the correct face. Connect arcs and straight edges with smooth, believable transitions. Use light, medium, and dark values consistently to communicate surface direction. Success Looks Like The curved geometry looks attached to the part and the shading strengthens rather than hides the form. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why does a circular feature usually look like an ellipse in an isometric sketch? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters The circular feature is viewed on an angled face, so its apparent shape is compressed into an ellipse while still representing a true circle on the part. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Circles usually appear as ellipses in isometric view. Key Idea 2 Curved features must be placed on the correct isometric face. Key Idea 3 Consistent values help the viewer distinguish surface direction and depth. Interactive Models 3D Isometric Sketch Study Models Use these models to study curved features, arcs, and shading. Rotate each part to see how circles and rounded forms appear from different angles in an isometric sketch. Model A Curved Feature Study Inspect the part and identify where circles would appear as ellipses in an isometric sketch. Notice how the curved surfaces transition into flat faces. Rotate • Zoom • Compare Loading 3D model… Drag to rotate • Scroll or pinch to zoom • Arrow keys also rotate Calculating dimensions… Standard View Isometric Front Top Right Line Display Shaded Model Object Lines Visible + Hidden Lines Visible/object edge Hidden edge study Viewer Options Auto-rotate model Reset Full Screen Sketch reminder: In an isometric sketch, circular features typically appear as ellipses. Use light shading to show which faces turn away from the viewer. Study prompt: Rotate the model to an isometric view and describe where you would draw ellipses or arcs if you were sketching it by hand. Model B Surface Depth and Shading Study Inspect the second part to see how curved and flat surfaces combine. Use the shaded view to think about how you would add value and contrast in a hand sketch. Form • Curves • Shading Loading 3D model… Drag to rotate • Scroll or pinch to zoom • Arrow keys also rotate Calculating dimensions… Standard View Isometric Front Top Right Line Display Shaded Model Object Lines Visible + Hidden Lines Visible/object edge Hidden edge study Viewer Options Auto-rotate model Reset Full Screen Sketch reminder: Shading should support the form, not hide it. Keep object edges crisp and use darker values on faces that receive less light. Study prompt: Choose a front, top, or right view, then return to isometric. Explain which surfaces would be darkest, medium, and lightest if you shaded this part by hand. Lesson Interactive Ellipse and Shading Laboratory Change the viewing angle to see a circular top appear more or less flattened, then choose which side should be darkest for the selected light direction. Light Viewing angle: 48° Light direction From the left From the right Which side should be darkest? Left side Right side Top ellipse Light Medium Dark Check Shading The surface facing away from the light should receive the darkest value. Your Task Sketch Curves and Show Surface Depth Choose one of the two Lesson 1.6 models and create an isometric study of its curved and flat surfaces. Rotate both models and select the one with the most useful curved-feature challenge. Block in the overall form and construct circles as ellipses on the correct faces. Refine the transitions where curved surfaces meet straight edges. Choose one light direction and apply light, medium, and dark values consistently. Quality check: Ellipses must align with their surfaces, and the shading must follow the stated light direction. What You Will Submit Curved Isometric and Shading Study Submit one completed model study and one concise explanation. One refined isometric sketch showing the curved construction and three-value shading. A light-direction arrow and one sentence explaining how a circle appears in isometric view. Submission standard: Keep object edges readable and use shading to support the geometry rather than cover it. items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Peer Design Review of the Rocket IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.4 Peer Design Review of the Rocket Conduct a professional, evidence-based review of another team’s rocket design and recommend prioritized improvements. Intermediate 45-60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineering teams use formal reviews to identify risk before spending time and money on fabrication. Objectives What You Will Practice Use criteria to evaluate a design Separate observations from opinions Identify design risk Give actionable technical feedback Materials What You Need Another team’s rocket sketches or model Design review form Engineering notebook Ruler or calipers if permitted Procedure Instructions Review the project criteria and constraints before seeing the design. Inspect the design silently for three minutes and record only observations. Ask the design team three clarifying questions. Evaluate fit, stability, manufacturability, assembly, documentation, and safety. Identify two strengths supported by evidence. Identify three risks and rate each as low, medium, or high. Write one specific recommendation for each risk. Meet with the team for five minutes and explain the highest-priority recommendation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use respectful, technical language Support every rating with observed evidence Identify at least two strengths and three risks Make recommendations specific enough to act on Prioritize the recommendations Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not redesign the project for the team Do not change or handle a model without permission Keep feedback focused on criteria and constraints Deliverables What You Submit Completed design review form Risk-priority table Three recommendations Brief feedback summary signed by both teams Reflection Reflection Questions Which risk was most likely to affect performance? How did the team’s explanation change your evaluation? Which recommendation could be completed fastest? What feedback would help your own design? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use the pattern “I observed..., which may cause..., so I recommend...” for clear feedback. Common Mistake “I do not like it” is not engineering feedback. Tie comments to requirements, evidence, or risk. Stretch Goal Review the revised design later and document whether each high-priority risk was reduced. Career Connection Design review engineers and project teams use preliminary and critical design reviews to find issues before production or flight. items.title: Rocket Assembly Reverse Engineering
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.11: Rocket Assembly Reverse Engineering. How can engineers learn from an existing rocket assembly by carefully taking it apart?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.11 | Rocket Assembly Reverse Engineering | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.11 | Rocket Assembly Reverse Engineering | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.11 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.11 Rocket Assembly Reverse Engineering Focus question: How can engineers learn from an existing rocket assembly by carefully taking it apart? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Disassemble an existing rocket carefully to discover its parts, order, and connections. Observe Disassemble Reassemble The rocket can be returned to its original condition using the recorded sequence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Use a controlled sequence to examine an existing assembly. Identify parts, orientation, and connection methods during disassembly. Verify that the assembly can be rebuilt without relying on memory. Success Looks Like The disassembly record preserves the order and orientation needed for successful reassembly. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt What information could be lost if a rocket is taken apart too quickly? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters Part order, orientation, small hardware, and connection details can be lost. A controlled process preserves evidence before each component is moved. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Reverse engineering studies an existing product to understand its parts and relationships. Key Idea 2 Careful disassembly protects components and preserves the original order. Key Idea 3 Reassembly is the final check that the observations were complete. Lesson Interactive Plan a Documented Disassembly Reorder the steps so the team protects evidence, preserves orientation, and finishes with a record that can support reassembly. Remove interior components one at a time and record their orientation. ↑ ↓ Photograph or sketch the fully assembled rocket from multiple directions. ↑ ↓ Compare the final component record with the physical parts and confirm reassembly. ↑ ↓ Establish part labels, front/reference direction, and a parts tray. ↑ ↓ Remove exterior or easily accessible parts and record hardware immediately. ↑ ↓ Why order matters Evidence of the assembled condition must exist before anything changes. Every removed part needs a stable name and orientation reference. The record must be checked against the actual parts. Check Sequence Use the arrow buttons to place documentation before removal and verification at the end. Your Task Reverse Engineer the Rocket Assembly Carefully disassemble the assigned rocket to discover its components and the order in which they fit together. Record the intact rocket with a labeled overview sketch or photo before removing parts. Remove one component at a time and record its temporary name, orientation, and connection method. Keep small parts organized in the order removed. Reassemble the rocket and note any step that was difficult to reconstruct. Quality check: The record must support successful reassembly without depending on memory or verbal instructions. What You Will Submit Rocket Reverse-Engineering Record Submit one sequence record and one component summary. One numbered disassembly record with labeled sketches or photos showing part order and orientation. One preliminary component list that includes quantities and a reassembly confirmation. Submission standard: Focus on observation, order, orientation, connection evidence, and successful reassembly. items.title: Isometric Sketching
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.5: Isometric Sketching. How can engineers show a 3D object clearly on a flat page?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.5 | Isometric Sketching | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.5 | Isometric Sketching | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.5 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.5 Isometric Sketching Focus question: How can engineers show a 3D object clearly on a flat page? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Build a proportional 3D-looking sketch using isometric axes and light construction lines. Orient Block Refine The finished sketch follows consistent isometric directions and retains evidence of the construction process. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Establish the vertical and angled axes used in isometric sketching. Use light construction lines to block the object’s overall form. Darken only the final visible edges after checking proportion and alignment. Success Looks Like Parallel edges follow the same isometric direction and the object fits within its construction box. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why should an isometric sketch begin with light construction lines? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters Light construction lines make it possible to test proportion and placement before committing to dark final edges. They support revision without confusing the final object. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Isometric sketches show width, height, and depth at the same time. Key Idea 2 Edges follow one vertical and two consistent angled directions. Key Idea 3 Light construction lines establish proportion before final object lines are darkened. Lesson Interactive Explore the Three Isometric Axes Adjust the width, depth, and height of the box. Watch how each dimension follows one of the three isometric axes while parallel edges remain parallel. Width: 5 Depth: 4 Height: 4 Which axis changes when only height changes? Choose Left 30° axis Right 30° axis Vertical axis Check Axis Move one slider at a time and observe which family of parallel edges changes. Your Task Construct a Clean Isometric Sketch Create an isometric sketch from a provided object or block diagram using the box-in method. Draw the vertical axis and two angled isometric directions lightly. Block in the object’s overall length, width, and height as a transparent box. Locate steps, cuts, or openings by referencing the nearest faces. Darken the final visible edges and erase only the construction lines that interfere with readability. Quality check: The finished object must remain aligned to the isometric axes and fit within the original construction box. What You Will Submit Isometric Construction Drawing Submit one sketch that shows both the construction process and the refined result. One isometric sketch with light construction evidence and clearly darkened final edges. One brief self-check naming an alignment or proportion corrected during the process. Submission standard: Focus on accurate proportion, isometric-axis alignment, and clear contrast between construction and final lines. items.title: Rocket Bill of Materials
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.19: Rocket Bill of Materials. How do engineers keep track of every part needed to build an assembly?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.19 | Rocket Bill of Materials | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.19 | Rocket Bill of Materials | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.19 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.19 Rocket Bill of Materials Focus question: How do engineers keep track of every part needed to build an assembly? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Build a verified part list that matches both the physical rocket and its exploded view. List Count Verify Every item number and quantity corresponds to a real component in one complete assembly. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Explain the purpose and structure of a Bill of Materials. Create one row for each unique component and record the correct quantity. Verify the list against the physical assembly and exploded view. Success Looks Like Every exploded-view item has one matching BOM row and the quantities describe one complete rocket. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why should repeated identical parts appear in one BOM row rather than several separate rows? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters A BOM lists each unique item once and uses the quantity field to show how many are required. This makes counting, ordering, and checking more reliable. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 A Bill of Materials is a structured list of the unique parts in an assembly. Key Idea 2 Item numbers connect the BOM to the exploded view. Key Idea 3 Quantities must be verified against the physical assembly rather than guessed. Lesson Interactive Verify an Exploded View Against a BOM Compare the item balloons and physical counts with the sample BOM. Select the two errors that must be corrected. Exploded-View Evidence Item 1 — Nose Cone — quantity 1 Item 2 — Fin — quantity 3 Item 3 — Body Tube — quantity 1 Item 4 — Retaining Screw — quantity 2 Which BOM issues are present? Item 4 is missing from the BOM. Item 2 is listed with quantity 2 instead of 3. “Nose Cone” should be replaced with “Pointy Part.” Unknown material information makes the entire BOM invalid. Check BOM Every balloon must have one matching row, and quantities must agree with the physical assembly. Your Task Build and Verify the Rocket Bill of Materials Use the physical rocket and exploded view to create a complete parts list. Transfer each exploded-view item number into a separate BOM row. Record the quantity, standardized part name, description, and material when known. Count repeated components carefully for one complete assembly. Cross-check every row against both the exploded view and the physical rocket. Quality check: Every ballooned component must have one BOM entry, and every BOM entry must represent a real component. What You Will Submit Verified Rocket Bill of Materials Submit one verified table and one checking note. One completed BOM with item number, quantity, part name, description, and known material information. One verification note identifying how the physical assembly and exploded view were used to confirm the list. Submission standard: Flag unknown information instead of guessing, and use one row per unique item. items.title: Rocket Assembly Notes
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.20: Rocket Assembly Notes. How do engineers write reassembly instructions that another team can follow?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.20 | Rocket Assembly Notes | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.20 | Rocket Assembly Notes | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.20 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.20 Rocket Assembly Notes Focus question: How do engineers write reassembly instructions that another team can follow? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Write and test step-by-step instructions another team can follow correctly. Sequence Test Revise The final instructions guide a successful reassembly without verbal coaching. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Write ordered assembly steps using clear action verbs and consistent item names. Add orientation cues, cautions, and completion checks where needed. Use peer-test evidence to revise unclear instructions. Success Looks Like A different team can follow the sequence and verify each completed step. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt What makes an assembly instruction more useful than “put the parts together”? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters A useful instruction names the part, action, direction, connection, and completion check. It removes the need to guess what happens next. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Assembly notes communicate sequence, orientation, connection, and cautions. Key Idea 2 One clear action per numbered step reduces skipped or combined operations. Key Idea 3 Testing reveals where readers need additional detail or verification cues. Lesson Interactive Build a Testable Reassembly Sequence Put the instructions in executable order, then choose where the most important alignment checkpoint belongs. Secure the connection using the specified fastener and torque/hand-tight instruction. ↑ ↓ Inspect parts and confirm item numbers, orientation marks, and mating surfaces. ↑ ↓ Verify alignment, retention, and free movement or fit after assembly. ↑ ↓ Insert the mating component while maintaining the reference orientation. ↑ ↓ Align the keyed tab, centerline, or reference marks before insertion. ↑ ↓ Best point for an alignment quality checkpoint Choose Before inspecting the parts After alignment and before fully securing Only after the complete assembly is finished Check Instructions A good sequence verifies identity and orientation before connection, then checks quality before and after securing. Your Task Write Reassembly Instructions Another Team Can Follow Transform the assembly record into a clear reassembly sequence and test it with another team. List the required tools, materials, and components before Step 1. Write numbered steps using one action per step and the established item names or numbers. Add orientation cues, cautions, and completion checks where mistakes are likely. Have another team perform a dry run, then revise the unclear steps. Quality check: The instructions must be executable in order and include checks before any irreversible action. What You Will Submit Tested Rocket Reassembly Instructions Submit one revised instruction set and one testing note. One final tools list and numbered reassembly sequence with orientation and quality checks. One peer-test note naming the confusion observed and the revision made to correct it. Submission standard: Avoid vague verbs; name the part, action, direction, connection, and completion condition. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Create Picture-Only Assembly Instructions IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.3 Create Picture-Only Assembly Instructions Disassemble an approved object and create picture-only instructions that another student can use to reassemble it. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context An international customer needs assembly instructions that can be understood without translating text. Objectives What You Will Practice Create exploded and sequential technical visuals Identify assembly order Communicate safety and orientation visually Test instructions with a user Materials What You Need Approved object with 5-15 components Phone or camera Sketching tools Page-layout software or paper Parts tray Procedure Instructions Select and photograph the assembled object. Disassemble it carefully while recording the order and orientation of every part. Create a numbered parts layout photograph or exploded sketch. Plan 6-12 assembly steps. Create one image for each step using arrows, highlights, and orientation symbols; do not use explanatory sentences. Add visual warnings where a user could reverse, force, or damage a part. Give the instructions and mixed parts to another student. Observe without speaking, record confusion points, and revise at least two images. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use no explanatory sentences in the assembly steps Include all parts exactly once Show orientation and movement clearly Include at least one visual safety or caution symbol Allow a test user to complete assembly without verbal coaching Constraints Constraints & Safety Object must be teacher-approved No powered or spring-loaded device may be opened without permission Keep all parts contained and return the object to working condition Deliverables What You Submit Parts layout or exploded view 6-12 picture-only steps User-test observation notes Two documented revisions Final instruction sheet Reflection Reflection Questions Where did the test user hesitate? Which visual symbol worked best? How did you show depth or orientation? What would you change for a younger user? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Keep the camera angle consistent unless a new view is necessary to reveal a hidden feature. Common Mistake A beautiful image may still be unclear. Every image must answer: what moves, where, and in which orientation? Stretch Goal Redesign the instructions to fit on one double-sided sheet while remaining usable. Career Connection Technical illustrators and manufacturing engineers create assembly and service instructions for global users. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.title: Orthographic Projection
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.7: Orthographic Projection. Why do engineers use multiple 2D views instead of only one 3D sketch?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.7 | Orthographic Projection | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.7 | Orthographic Projection | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.7 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.7 Orthographic Projection Focus question: Why do engineers use multiple 2D views instead of only one 3D sketch? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Translate a 3D object into aligned front, top, and right projections. Select Project Align All three views describe the same object with matching feature locations and proportions. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Explain how orthographic projection represents a 3D object with flat views. Choose a front view that communicates the characteristic shape clearly. Use projection lines to align corresponding features across views. Success Looks Like Shared edges and features align across the front, top, and right views. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why is one flat view often not enough to describe a three-dimensional object? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters A single view can hide depth or overlapping features. Multiple aligned views reveal different sides while describing one consistent object. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Orthographic projection represents a 3D object with multiple flat views. Key Idea 2 Each view shows only two directions of the object at a time. Key Idea 3 Alignment between views allows the reader to connect the same feature across projections. Lesson Interactive Use the 3D Part to Identify the Top View Study the interactive 3D model, then select the orthographic drawing that shows the part from above. If you need help, use the standard-view buttons to check the model from the top, front, or right side. 3D Part Reference Loading 3D model… Drag to rotate • Scroll or pinch to zoom • Use the view buttons to test a projection Calculating dimensions… Standard View Isometric Front Top Right Line Display Shaded Model Object Lines Visible + Hidden Lines Viewer Options Auto-rotate model Reset Full Screen Projection hint: A top view shows width and depth. It does not show the object’s height changes as a tall profile. Which drawing is the top view? View A View B View C Check Top View Use the model and the three drawings together. The top view is the one you would see looking straight down from above. Your Task Translate One Object into Three Projections Start with a provided isometric object and create a coordinated front, top, and right orthographic set. Select the front view that shows the object’s characteristic shape clearly. Draw the front view and use light projection lines to transfer feature positions. Construct the top and right views in the correct arrangement. Check that steps, holes, and corresponding edges align across all three views. Quality check: The views must describe one consistent object; no feature may shift position or change shape between projections. What You Will Submit Three-View Orthographic Set Submit one coordinated drawing set and one short design-reading note. One labeled and aligned front, top, and right orthographic set with light projection evidence. One sentence explaining why the selected front view is the clearest choice. Submission standard: Focus on projection, alignment, consistent geometry, and even spacing between the three views. items.title: Rocket Exploded View
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.18: Rocket Exploded View. How can engineers show rocket parts separated without losing how they fit together?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.18 | Rocket Exploded View | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.18 | Rocket Exploded View | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.18 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.18 Rocket Exploded View Focus question: How can engineers show rocket parts separated without losing how they fit together? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Separate components visually while preserving orientation, alignment, and assembly relationships. Arrange Align Reference A reader can mentally return every component to its assembled position. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Explain how an exploded view communicates part relationships. Separate components along clear assembly axes without changing orientation. Use item balloons and direction cues to identify and reconnect parts. Success Looks Like The separated parts remain aligned and their assembly order is clear. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why should parts remain in their assembled orientation in an exploded view? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters Orientation communicates how surfaces, holes, and interfaces fit together. Rotating parts only to fill the page can hide the true assembly relationship. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 An exploded view separates parts so each component can be seen. Key Idea 2 Alignment preserves the relationship between separated components. Key Idea 3 Item balloons and assembly-direction cues help readers identify and reconnect parts. Lesson Interactive Arrange an Example Exploded View Reorder the example training-rocket components from forward to aft. The exercise uses a generic assembly so it does not replace your physical rocket observations. Fin can / aft body ↑ ↓ Nose cone ↑ ↓ Motor mount / aft retainer ↑ ↓ Main body tube ↑ ↓ Body coupler ↑ ↓ Exploded-view rules Keep components on a shared assembly axis. Preserve the orientation used in the assembled product. Separate parts enough to read interfaces without implying false motion. Check Forward-to-Aft Order Arrange the example from the nose at the top/front to the motor mount at the aft end. Your Task Draw a Functional Rocket Exploded View Create an exploded drawing using the component names and item numbers established in Lesson 1.17. Choose a primary assembly axis and place the main components in their assembled orientation. Separate parts with enough spacing to see interfaces while preserving alignment. Add item balloons that match the established component numbers. Use direction arrows or brief notes where insertion direction is not obvious. Quality check: A reader must be able to mentally reassemble the rocket by following the alignments and item references. What You Will Submit Rocket Exploded-View Drawing Submit one exploded drawing and one concise assembly note. One complete exploded view with correct orientation, spacing, alignment, and item balloons. One short assembly-order or interface note for the connection most likely to be misunderstood. Submission standard: Preserve part orientation and use the established item numbers consistently throughout the drawing.
