items.title: Line Conventions
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.2: Line Conventions. How do different types of lines help engineers communicate clearly?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.2 | Line Conventions | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.2 | Line Conventions | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.2 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.2 Line Conventions Focus question: How do different types of lines help engineers communicate clearly? Download Presentation 3D Model + Views Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Distinguish solid visible-edge lines from dashed hidden-feature lines. Compare Classify Apply A reader can tell which edges are visible and which features are blocked from view. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Explain why engineering drawings use standardized line patterns. Identify visible edges and hidden features in a selected view. Use consistent solid and dashed line patterns in a drawing. Success Looks Like The line pattern alone clearly distinguishes visible edges from hidden features. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why might a dashed line communicate something different from a solid line? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters Engineering line patterns act like a visual code. A solid line can show an edge that is directly visible, while a dashed line can show an important feature hidden behind a surface. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Line conventions are standardized visual signals used in technical drawings. Key Idea 2 Solid object lines show edges that are directly visible from the selected view. Key Idea 3 Dashed hidden lines show important features that are blocked by another surface. Interactive Activity Use the model and the three orthographic views together. Rotate the part, choose a standard view, and compare the visible edges. Interactive Model 3D Line Convention Explorer Rotate the part, move to standard views, and compare how visible and hidden edges communicate its shape. Loading 3D model… Drag to rotate • Scroll or pinch to zoom • Arrow keys also rotate Calculating dimensions… Standard View Isometric Front Top Right Line Display Shaded Model Object Lines Visible + Hidden Lines Visible/object edge Hidden edge study Viewer Options Auto-rotate model Reset Full Screen Drawing reminder: In a formal orthographic drawing, visible edges use solid object lines and hidden edges use short, evenly spaced dashes. This viewer is a study aid—not a substitute for a correctly projected technical drawing. Reference Drawings Front, Top, and Right Orthographic Views Compare each 2D projection with the interactive model. Use the buttons to align the 3D model with the matching standard view. Same Part • Three Views Front View Shows the stepped L-shaped profile. Show Front in 3D Top View Shows the rectangular footprint and visible step edge. Show Top in 3D Right View Shows the side profile from the right. Show Right in 3D Study prompt: Identify which edges remain visible in all three views and which features appear differently when the viewing direction changes. Lesson Interactive Classify Visible and Hidden Edges For each example, decide whether the line should be a solid object line or a dashed hidden line. This activity intentionally does not use centerlines or construction lines, which are introduced later. Feature in the Selected View Line Sample Your Classification Outside edge directly facing the viewer Choose Object line Hidden line Side of a slot blocked by the front surface Choose Object line Hidden line Top corner visible from the chosen direction Choose Object line Hidden line Back edge of an internal recess Choose Object line Hidden line Check Classifications Ask one question for each edge: can the viewer see it directly from this direction? Your Task Compare Visible and Hidden Edges Use the Lesson 1.2 model and reference views to study how the same part changes when viewed from different directions. Focus only on visible object lines and dashed hidden lines. Choose one standard view and compare it with the 3D model. Trace or redraw the view using solid lines for visible edges and dashed lines for hidden features. Create a two-item key labeling the object-line and hidden-line patterns. Quality check: Every line should match a real edge or feature in the selected view, and the two patterns must be easy to distinguish. What You Will Submit Visible-and-Hidden-Line Study Submit a focused comparison using only the line conventions introduced in this lesson. One labeled standard-view drawing using correct object and hidden lines. A two-sentence note identifying one visible edge and one hidden feature in the drawing. Submission standard: Use only the solid and dashed line patterns practiced in this lesson, and keep each pattern consistent. items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Engineering Drawing Makeover IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.5 Engineering Drawing Makeover Revise a weak engineering drawing so it communicates the part clearly and can be used for fabrication or inspection. Intermediate 60 minutes Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A manufacturing technician returned a drawing because it was incomplete, cluttered, and difficult to inspect. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize missing drawing information Apply dimensioning standards Improve layout and readability Add appropriate notes and tolerances Materials What You Need Teacher-provided weak drawing or prior student drawing Drafting tools or CAD drawing workspace Drawing checklist Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Audit the drawing for missing views, dimensions, units, scale, title block information, notes, and tolerances. Mark at least eight issues directly on a copy. Choose the minimum set of views needed to define the part. Rearrange the views for alignment and readable spacing. Add or correct dimensions, avoiding duplication. Add centerlines, hidden lines, hole notes, and detail views where needed. Complete the title block and add general tolerances. Use the checklist to perform a final self-inspection. Requirements Engineering Requirements Correct at least eight identified issues Use consistent units and dimension style Include a complete title block Include enough views to define the part Use tolerances only where they support function or inspection Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not change the part geometry unless the drawing reveals an impossible feature Keep the final drawing on one sheet Follow the class drawing standard Deliverables What You Submit Annotated original drawing Revised drawing Completed drawing checklist Short explanation of the three most important corrections Reflection Reflection Questions Which missing item created the greatest manufacturing risk? How did you decide which views to keep? Where did you use a tolerance and why? How could an inspector use your revised drawing? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Every dimension should have a purpose: location, size, or relationship. Common Mistake Adding more dimensions can create conflicts. Avoid dimensioning the same feature in multiple places. Stretch Goal Exchange drawings with a partner and perform a blind completeness audit. Career Connection Mechanical designers and documentation specialists maintain drawings throughout a product’s life cycle. items.title: Rocket Assembly Systems
items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.16: Rocket Assembly Systems. How do multiple rocket parts work together as one assembly?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.16 | Rocket Assembly Systems | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.16 | Rocket Assembly Systems | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.16 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.16 Rocket Assembly Systems Focus question: How do multiple rocket parts work together as one assembly? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Explain how rocket parts and functional groups work together as one system. Group Connect Trace The map shows real interactions rather than only a list of component locations. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Distinguish an individual part, a subassembly, and the complete assembly. Group rocket components by function and identify their interfaces. Trace how a change or failure in one component can affect the larger system. Success Looks Like Arrows and labels explain how forces, alignment, or function move between components. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why can a small problem in one component affect the performance of the entire rocket? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters Components depend on one another for alignment, support, connection, and function. A change at one interface can create effects elsewhere in the assembly. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 A part is one component; a subassembly is a connected group of parts. Key Idea 2 Interfaces describe where components touch, connect, align, or transfer force. Key Idea 3 System behavior depends on interactions, not only on the quality of individual parts. Lesson Interactive Trace a Rocket System Failure Select a component and a compatible failure mode. The interactive builds a local-to-system cause-and-effect chain. Component Fin Nose cone Body coupler Motor mount Failure mode Loose Misaligned Cracked Shifted Validate Chain A strong system explanation traces a physical relationship from the component to the overall assembly. Your Task Map the Rocket as an Interacting System Analyze the rocket as a set of connected functional groups rather than unrelated pieces. Group the major components by function, such as structure, stability, connection, or recovery. Create a map showing components and their physical or functional interfaces. Label what each connection transfers or controls. Trace one cause-and-effect chain showing how a loose, missing, or changed component affects the assembly. Quality check: Every connection on the map must describe a real relationship such as alignment, support, force transfer, or motion. What You Will Submit Rocket Assembly System Map Submit one visual system model and one cause-and-effect explanation. One labeled system map grouping components and naming the relationships between them. One written cause-and-effect chain explaining how a component problem could influence the larger assembly. Submission standard: Use arrows with relationship labels; do not submit only a list of parts. Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Combine isometric, orthographic, line-convention, and dimensioning skills in one bracket drawing. Interpret Integrate Check Every view and dimension describes the same bracket geometry and design intent. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Interpret the form and mounting features of an aerospace-style bracket. Create coordinated isometric and orthographic sketches of the same part. Add the critical dimensions needed to define the bracket. Success Looks Like The drawing package communicates the bracket’s form, mounting features, and required sizes consistently. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt What information would another engineer need before turning a bracket idea into CAD? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters The engineer needs a clear overall form, coordinated views, mounting-feature locations, and critical sizes. The drawings must agree with one another. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 A bracket supports, connects, or aligns other components. Key Idea 2 An isometric sketch communicates overall form while orthographic views show precise feature placement. Key Idea 3 Critical dimensions define the bracket envelope and mounting features. Lesson Interactive Match the Correct Front View of the Bracket Use the isometric bracket sketch as your reference. Imagine looking straight at the face with the semicircular cutout, then select the front view that matches the same geometry. Reference Bracket Sketch Front-view note: In this activity, the front view is the face that shows the semicircular cutout. Use that face to orient the sketch before you choose. Which drawing is the correct front view? View A View B View C Check Front View Look for the bracket’s three easiest-to-track features: the semicircular cutout, the tall wall, and the diagonal gusset. Your Task Create an Aerospace Bracket Sketch Package Develop a compact technical sketch package for a provided or assigned aerospace-style bracket. Identify the bracket’s supporting surfaces, mounting holes, and major steps or bends. Create a clear isometric sketch showing the overall form. Create aligned front, top, and right views with the required line conventions. Add the critical overall and feature dimensions needed to define the bracket. Quality check: The isometric sketch, orthographic views, and dimensions must all describe the same part. What You Will Submit Aerospace Bracket Drawing Package Submit one coordinated drawing sheet and one short design-intent note. One sheet containing the isometric sketch, aligned orthographic views, and critical dimensions. A two-sentence note explaining what the bracket connects, supports, or aligns. Submission standard: Use consistent feature names and geometry throughout the entire sheet. items.description: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.9: Dimensioning Basics. How do engineers show the size of an object clearly in a drawing?
items.searchText: IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.9 | Dimensioning Basics | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.9 | Dimensioning Basics | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.9 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.9 Dimensioning Basics Focus question: How do engineers show the size of an object clearly in a drawing? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Add size and location information so a drawing can guide fabrication or inspection. Identify Place Audit All required sizes and feature locations are stated once without clutter or duplication. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Identify the dimensions needed to define overall size and feature location. Use dimension lines, extension lines, arrowheads, and symbols correctly. Audit a drawing for missing, duplicated, or ambiguous dimensions. Success Looks Like Another person can determine the required sizes without measuring the drawing itself. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt Why is a perfectly drawn shape still incomplete without dimensions? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters The views communicate shape, but dimensions communicate the required size and feature locations. Without them, a fabricator would have to guess or scale the picture. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Views communicate shape; dimensions communicate size and location. Key Idea 2 Dimension lines, extension lines, arrows, symbols, and values work together. Key Idea 3 Good dimensioning is complete without repeating the same information. Lesson Interactive Audit a Dimensioned Drawing Inspect the sample drawing and identify all three problems that would make manufacturing or inspection less reliable. 100 mm 100 mm Ø20 60 Select all dimensioning problems. The hole size is shown, but its center location is missing. The 100 mm overall width is stated twice. The diameter dimension is placed inside the object and competes with geometry. The drawing needs different colors for every dimension. Check Audit A complete drawing states every required size and location once, without relying on scale. Your Task Dimension a Part for Manufacturing Add a complete but nonredundant set of dimensions to a provided technical drawing. Identify the overall sizes and the information needed to locate each feature. Place extension and dimension lines outside the object whenever possible. Use diameter and radius symbols correctly for circular and curved features. Audit the drawing for missing, duplicated, crossed, or ambiguous dimensions. Quality check: Every required size and location must be stated once, and no information should depend on scaling the drawing. What You Will Submit Fully Dimensioned Technical Drawing Submit one completed drawing and one audit note. One technical drawing with complete, correctly placed overall and feature dimensions. One short audit note identifying a missing or duplicate dimension that was corrected. Submission standard: Use one unit system consistently and do not place a dimension value on an object line. Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Use quick sketches to capture and communicate an idea before refining it. Observe Explore Explain A classmate can identify the object, its purpose, and its important features from the sketch. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets Explain why engineers sketch before committing time to a final design. Create several quick sketches that explore an object or idea. Add labels that clarify shape, function, and questions. Success Looks Like A classmate can understand the selected idea without a verbal explanation. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt What can a sketch communicate faster than a paragraph? Think first, then be ready to share a short response that connects the question to engineering communication. Reveal: why this matters A sketch can show shape, arrangement, relationships, and possible changes at a glance. Engineers use it to think and communicate before a design is finalized. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Engineering sketches are thinking tools, not art assignments. Key Idea 2 Quick sketches make it easier to compare more than one idea. Key Idea 3 Labels and notes explain what the drawing alone may not show. Lesson Interactive Build a Sketch That Communicates A useful engineering sketch does more than resemble an object. Select the annotations that would help another student understand the purpose, geometry, and use of this example bracket. 1 2 3 4 Select exactly three useful annotations. 1 — Mounting hole: secures the bracket to the frame. 2 — Support face: contacts the attached component. 3 — Load direction: force acts downward on this face. 4 — Make this corner bright yellow because it looks better. Check Annotations Choose the notes that communicate engineering information rather than decoration. Your Task Create a Sketch That Explains an Idea Choose a simple classroom object or rocket-related component. Explore how a sketch can communicate its shape, purpose, and important features before the idea is finalized. Create two or three small thumbnail sketches showing different viewpoints or arrangements. Select the clearest idea and redraw it at a larger scale. Add at least three labels describing important features, function, or unanswered questions. Quality check: The refined sketch should be understandable to a classmate without additional explanation. What You Will Submit Sketch Communication Entry Submit one organized notebook entry showing both exploration and refinement. One notebook page containing the thumbnail sketches and one labeled refined sketch. A two- or three-sentence reflection explaining why the refined sketch communicates the idea best. Submission standard: Keep the thumbnails visible as evidence of the thinking process. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 5 Aerospace Product Life-Cycle Analysis IED Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.4 Aerospace Product Life-Cycle Analysis Map the life cycle of an aerospace-related product and recommend two realistic improvements. Advanced 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A product can meet its immediate performance goal while creating hidden environmental or social impacts during material extraction, manufacturing, use, maintenance, or disposal. Objectives What You Will Practice Use life-cycle thinking Identify impacts across product stages Distinguish evidence from assumptions Recommend feasible design changes Materials What You Need Research access Life-cycle map template Engineering notebook At least three credible sources Procedure Instructions Choose an approved product such as a drone battery, aircraft seat component, composite panel, satellite enclosure, or rocket packaging. Define the product function and expected service life. Map raw materials, processing, manufacturing, transportation, use, maintenance, and end-of-life. For each stage, identify energy, material, waste, emissions, safety, or labor considerations. Mark the three stages with the greatest likely impact and support the choice with evidence. Generate four improvement ideas. Evaluate ideas for impact reduction, technical feasibility, cost, and possible unintended consequences. Recommend two improvements and identify how success would be measured. Requirements Engineering Requirements Include every major life-cycle stage Use at least three credible sources Identify at least three impact categories Recommend two feasible improvements Include one unintended consequence or tradeoff Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not claim precise environmental numbers without a valid source Keep the scope clear and manageable Use respectful language when discussing labor or community impacts Deliverables What You Submit Life-cycle map Source list Impact hotspot analysis Four improvement ideas Two recommendations with metrics Tradeoff statement Reflection Reflection Questions Which life-cycle stage was easiest to overlook? Which recommendation had the best impact-to-feasibility balance? What assumption most affected your analysis? How could product life be extended? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Define the system boundary. State what is included and excluded from the analysis. Common Mistake “Recyclable” does not guarantee recycling will occur. Consider collection, separation, contamination, and market demand. Stretch Goal Compare a reusable and single-use version of the same product. Career Connection Sustainability, materials, supply-chain, and systems engineers evaluate product impacts beyond initial manufacture. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 5 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 5 Mission Focus You can analyze test data and stakeholder feedback to identify the most important revision priorities. Analyze Prioritize Decide Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: Revision priorities are based on combined evidence and do not overvalue one isolated comment or trial. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Combine Data and Stakeholder Feedback. Learning Targets Summarize test data and user feedback. Identify patterns, strengths, weaknesses, and conflicts in the evidence. Select revision priorities based on evidence. Success Looks Like You can analyze test data and stakeholder feedback to identify the most important revision priorities. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How can engineers combine data and user feedback to decide what should improve? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Combine Data and Stakeholder Feedback. Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: Revision priorities are based on combined evidence and do not overvalue one isolated comment or trial. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Data and feedback should be reviewed together. Key Idea 2 Revision priorities should focus on the most important user need or performance issue. Key Idea 3 A good design conclusion names both strengths and limitations. Your Task Combine Data and Stakeholder Feedback Analyze quantitative results and qualitative feedback together to identify strengths, weaknesses, and revision priorities. Organize the performance data and feedback themes. Calculate or graph the required test results. Compare the evidence with each design criterion and user need. Rank the most important revision opportunities. Quality check: Revision priorities are based on combined evidence and do not overvalue one isolated comment or trial. Lesson Interactive Combine Data and Stakeholder Feedback Use quantitative results and repeated user comments to identify the revision that addresses the strongest evidence. Evidence summary Reliability: 19 successful cycles out of 20 — target ≥ 18/20 Setup time: 35 s mean — target ≤ 20 s Comfort: 3 of 5 users rated the grip comfortable — target ≥ 4/5 Repeated comment: “The handle is hard to grasp with gloves.” Which metric most clearly misses its target? Choose Reliability Setup time Number of total cycles What is the repeated feedback theme? Choose Grip and glove usability Appearance Noise Which revision should be prioritized? Choose Change the color Redesign the handle interface Replace the motor Set Revision Priority Find the metric that misses its target and connect it to the repeated stakeholder comment. What You Will Submit Evidence Review One analysis summary containing results, feedback themes, and prioritized revisions. Submission standard: Revision priorities are based on combined evidence and do not overvalue one isolated comment or trial. items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 5 Engineering Portfolio Showcase IED Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.5 Engineering Portfolio Showcase Transform your strongest project into a concise portfolio case study that demonstrates process, evidence, revision, and communication. Advanced 2-3 class periods Creative Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context An engineering portfolio should show how you think, not only display a final object. Objectives What You Will Practice Curate technical evidence Explain a design process clearly Improve visual and written communication Reflect on growth and tradeoffs Materials What You Need One completed IED project Original notebook and files CAD/screenshots/photos Presentation or page-layout software Portfolio checklist Procedure Instructions Select a project with enough evidence to show at least one meaningful revision. Write a 40-60 word project overview including the problem, user or client, and final outcome. Choose 6-10 artifacts that show problem definition, concepts, CAD, build, test, and revision. Improve one weak artifact, such as a sketch, drawing, photograph, graph, or CAD view. Create a before/after or problem/revision comparison. Write three short captions that explain decisions rather than merely name images. Create a one-page case study or 3-5 slide presentation. Deliver a two-minute presentation and use feedback to make one final revision. Requirements Engineering Requirements Show the problem, process, evidence, revision, and result Use only your own work or clearly identify team contributions Include at least one quantitative result Include one honest limitation or unresolved issue Use consistent visual hierarchy and readable text Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not include private student information Do not claim sole credit for team work Keep the final case study to one page or five slides Use high-quality, appropriately cropped images Deliverables What You Submit Project overview 6-10 curated artifacts One improved artifact Before/after comparison Final case study or slides Two-minute presentation Final reflection Reflection Reflection Questions What does the portfolio reveal about your engineering process? Which artifact provides the strongest evidence? What did you remove and why? How would you describe your growth this year? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Every image needs a job. Include it only if it supports a decision, test, revision, or result. Common Mistake A portfolio made only of polished final images hides the engineering process that employers and programs want to see. Stretch Goal Create a second version tailored to an internship, college program, or competition audience. Career Connection Engineers use portfolios and technical presentations to communicate capability, design thinking, and project impact. Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 5 Mission Focus You can use a decision matrix to compare concepts and justify a final concept selection. Score Compare Select Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The selected concept is supported by the matrix and the justification acknowledges weak evidence or risk. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Select the Capstone Concept with Evidence. Learning Targets Use design criteria to compare multiple concepts. Score concepts using a decision matrix. Justify the selected concept with evidence and tradeoffs. Success Looks Like You can use a decision matrix to compare concepts and justify a final concept selection. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How can engineers choose a design concept using evidence instead of personal preference? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Select the Capstone Concept with Evidence. Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: The selected concept is supported by the matrix and the justification acknowledges weak evidence or risk. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 A decision matrix makes concept selection more transparent. Key Idea 2 Scores should connect to criteria, not popularity. Key Idea 3 The best concept is the one that best fits the defined problem and constraints. Your Task Select the Capstone Concept with Evidence Use weighted criteria and research evidence to compare the concepts and choose a defensible direction. Confirm that the matrix criteria match the design brief. Set and justify criterion weights. Score each concept using known evidence. Select the concept and document uncertainty or needed proof. Quality check: The selected concept is supported by the matrix and the justification acknowledges weak evidence or risk. Lesson Interactive Select a Concept with a Weighted Decision Matrix Weights represent criterion importance. Calculate each concept’s weighted total, then select the highest-scoring concept. Concept Usability ×4 Reliability ×3 Sustainability ×2 Weighted total A: Quarter-turn cam 3 4 5 — B: Captive sliding pin 5 3 4 — C: Magnetic latch 4 5 2 — Select Concept A Select Concept B Select Concept C Calculate and Check Multiply each rating by its weight, add the products, and use the total—not personal preference. What You Will Submit Concept Selection Evidence A completed decision matrix. A short evidence-based selection justification. Submission standard: The selected concept is supported by the matrix and the justification acknowledges weak evidence or risk. Background Engineering Context Engineering projects often begin with incomplete client statements such as “make this easier” or “we need a better holder.” Objectives What You Will Practice Ask effective stakeholder questions Separate needs from proposed solutions Write measurable requirements Present and justify a concept Materials What You Need Client interview form Engineering notebook Sketching tools Decision matrix template Presentation materials Procedure Instructions Pair with a classmate and assign client and designer roles. items.description: IED Unit 5 Lesson 5.14: Ethics, Safety, Sustainability, and Life-Cycle Analysis. How do engineers make responsible design decisions beyond simply making a prototype work?
items.searchText: IED Unit 5 Lesson 5.14 | Ethics, Safety, Sustainability, and Life-Cycle Analysis | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 5 Lesson 5.14 | Ethics, Safety, Sustainability, and Life-Cycle Analysis | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 5 Lesson 5.14 IED Unit 5 • Lesson 5.14 Ethics, Safety, Sustainability, and Life-Cycle Analysis Focus question: How do engineers make responsible design decisions beyond simply making a prototype work? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 5 Mission Focus You can evaluate a design using ethical, safety, sustainability, and life-cycle considerations. Evaluate Question Improve Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The analysis addresses project-specific impacts and goes beyond a generic statement that the design is safe or sustainable. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Evaluate Responsible Design Impacts. Learning Targets Identify ethical and safety considerations connected to the design. Consider sustainability, materials, life cycle, and impact. Recommend a responsible improvement or limitation statement. Success Looks Like You can evaluate a design using ethical, safety, sustainability, and life-cycle considerations. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How do engineers make responsible design decisions beyond simply making a prototype work? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Evaluate Responsible Design Impacts. Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: The analysis addresses project-specific impacts and goes beyond a generic statement that the design is safe or sustainable. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 A working design is not automatically a responsible design. Key Idea 2 Engineers consider who benefits, who may be affected, and what happens over the product life cycle. Key Idea 3 Responsible design decisions should be stated clearly in the final documentation. Your Task Evaluate Responsible Design Impacts Examine the current design for ethical, safety, sustainability, life-cycle, accessibility, and broader stakeholder effects. Identify hazards and who could be affected. Review materials, energy, waste, repair, and end-of-life considerations. Consider accessibility, fairness, privacy, or unintended consequences relevant to the project. Record one required responsibility-driven change or justified decision. Quality check: The analysis addresses project-specific impacts and goes beyond a generic statement that the design is safe or sustainable. Lesson Interactive Review Ethics, Safety, Sustainability, and Life Cycle Select the actions that make the design more responsible across use, maintenance, communication, and end of life. Select every responsible action Add a guard around the pinch point Disclose that the prototype was not tested in rain Use replaceable wear components instead of sealing the assembly Label separable materials for end-of-life recovery Hide failed test data to strengthen the presentation Which issue has the highest immediate priority? Choose Color preference A foreseeable user injury risk Packaging appearance Responsible engineering: a working prototype is not automatically safe, ethical, sustainable, or ready for deployment. Check Responsibility Review Consider the complete product life cycle and communicate limitations honestly. What You Will Submit Responsible Design Review One completed ethics, safety, sustainability, and life-cycle analysis. One responsibility-driven design decision or revision. Submission standard: The analysis addresses project-specific impacts and goes beyond a generic statement that the design is safe or sustainable. Your Task Generate Human-Centered Design Concepts Create multiple distinct ideas that respond to the defined user needs without evaluating them too early. Lesson Interactive Create a Diverse Concept Set Select three concepts that solve the same need using genuinely different operating principles—not just different colors or surface styling. Select three meaningfully different concepts A rotating quarter-turn cam with a large lever The same cam with a blue lever A sliding captive pin with a spring return The sliding pin with a rounded corner A magnetic latch with a mechanical safety catch Which ideation rule supports creativity? Choose Reject weak ideas immediately Defer judgment until many ideas exist Stop after the first workable concept Ideation goal: increase the number and variety of possible solutions before comparing them. Check Concept Set Look for different mechanisms or physical principles, not cosmetic variations. What You Will Submit Concept Generation Set At least three annotated concept sketches or equivalent concept descriptions. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Final revisions should come from evidence, not last-minute guesses. Key Idea 2 A refinement can improve function, usability, safety, clarity, or documentation. Key Idea 3 Every final change should be traceable to a test result, feedback comment, or criterion. Your Task Complete the Final Evidence-Based Revision Implement the highest-value feasible improvements from testing, feedback, and responsible-design analysis. Select revisions using evidence and project constraints. Update the design files, prototype, or user interaction. Document what changed and why. Perform a focused verification check on the revised feature. Quality check: Each final change has a documented source and the verification evidence supports the claimed improvement. Lesson Interactive Approve the Final Prototype Revision Choose the smallest testable change that directly addresses the strongest evidence without introducing unnecessary project risk. Evidence Mean task time meets the target. Only 3 of 5 users rate the grip comfortable. Four users mention difficulty grasping the handle while wearing gloves. The mechanism itself operates reliably. Choose the final change Replace the reliable motor with a higher-speed model. Increase handle diameter and add a glove-friendly texture. Restart the entire project with a different mechanism. How should the change be controlled? Choose Change the prototype without updating records Document the revision, update the model, and verify the affected criterion Approve Revision Late-stage revisions should be evidence-based, limited in scope, documented, and verified. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A precision rocket component must be shipped to a test site. The package must protect the part while minimizing material and waste. Objectives What You Will Practice Balance protection and material use Apply life-cycle thinking Design packaging around a product Use test evidence to revise a solution Materials What You Need Provided rocket component or surrogate Corrugated cardboard, paperboard, paper, or approved recycled material Scale Ruler Drop-test area Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Measure the component and identify surfaces that must be protected. Define shipping hazards such as drop, vibration, abrasion, and moisture. Set criteria for protection, package size, mass, material type, and recyclability. Sketch three packaging concepts using minimal material. Select and build one concept. Record package mass and external dimensions. Perform three approved drop tests from increasing heights. Inspect the part and package, revise one feature, and retest. Requirements Engineering Requirements Prevent visible damage in three approved drop tests Use at least 70% recyclable or reusable material by mass Use no loose plastic foam Keep package volume below the teacher-set limit Allow the component to be removed without damage Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved drop heights and test area No hazardous or messy filler Component must be returned in original condition Adhesive use must be measured or documented Deliverables What You Submit Hazard and criteria list Three concept sketches Material and mass record Final package Drop-test results Sustainability justification Revision notes Reflection Reflection Questions Which hazard controlled the design? Where was material unnecessary? How did protection compete with sustainability? What would change for repeated shipping? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Protect the component by controlling movement and distributing impact, not just by adding more material. Common Mistake A package made from recyclable material is not sustainable if it uses far more material than necessary. Stretch Goal Design a reusable package that completes ten shipping cycles. Career Connection Packaging, logistics, and aerospace quality engineers protect expensive parts while controlling mass, cost, contamination, and waste. Your Task Present and Defend the Capstone Solution Deliver the final presentation, demonstrate the design when appropriate, and answer questions with honest evidence and limitations. State the user need and design criteria. Explain the selected solution and prototype. Present testing, feedback, and responsible-design evidence. Lesson Interactive Check Whether a Final Claim Is Defensible Select the evidence that belongs in a professional final presentation and choose the strongest way to answer an audience question. Evidence needed to defend the final design A specific claim tied to criteria Quantitative test results Stakeholder or user feedback A limitation or condition not yet tested A statement that the team is confident An advisor asks, “Will this work outdoors in rain?” The prototype was not tested in rain. What is the best response? Choose Yes, it should work because the design is strong. That question is outside the project. Rain performance has not been verified. We would add water-exposure testing before claiming outdoor readiness. Professional communication: credibility increases when engineers distinguish tested evidence from assumptions and future work. Check Final Defense Support claims with data and feedback, and state limitations honestly. What You Will Submit Final Capstone Submission The final presentation and engineering portfolio. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 5 Redesign for Limited Hand Strength IED Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.1 Redesign for Limited Hand Strength Redesign an approved classroom product to reduce required grip force or improve control without removing its core function. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A user can understand a classroom product but has difficulty gripping, twisting, or pressing it because of limited hand strength. Objectives What You Will Practice Identify user needs through empathy and evidence Translate needs into measurable requirements Generate accessible concepts Evaluate a human-centered prototype Materials What You Need Approved classroom product User-needs interview sheet Sketching materials Cardboard, foam, clay, or other prototype materials Force gauge if available Procedure Instructions Select a product with a grip, cap, button, lever, or control. Create a respectful user profile based on limited hand strength; do not simulate a disability in an unsafe way. Observe the product and identify at least three barriers. Convert barriers into measurable requirements such as diameter, force, reach, or texture. Sketch three concepts and collect feedback from a peer acting as a reviewer. Build a low-fidelity prototype of the selected concept. Run a usability test using the same task for the original and redesign. Document feedback and make one revision. Requirements Engineering Requirements Address at least two identified user barriers Include at least three measurable requirements Preserve the product’s core function Avoid a design that creates a new safety hazard Collect and respond to user feedback Constraints Constraints & Safety Use respectful, person-centered language Do not ask a student to imitate pain or injury Prototype materials must be safe and reversible Do not permanently modify school property Deliverables What You Submit User profile and needs Barrier observations Three concept sketches Requirements list Prototype Original/redesign usability comparison Revision summary Reflection Reflection Questions Which user need was hardest to convert into a requirement? What feedback changed your design? Did improving accessibility help other users too? What would require additional real-user testing? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Ask what task is difficult and why. Avoid assuming the solution before understanding the user. Common Mistake Making a handle larger is not automatically accessible; reach, force, texture, feedback, and context all matter. Stretch Goal Redesign the product for one additional user need without reducing the first improvement. Career Connection Human factors and accessibility engineers design controls, tools, interiors, and equipment for a wide range of users. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 5 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. Stakeholder statement Evidence type “My fingers hurt after opening the latch several times.” Choose Pain point Context Goal Preference “I usually operate it outside while wearing thick gloves.” Choose Pain point Context Goal Preference “I need to finish the inspection in under two minutes.” Choose Pain point Context Goal Preference “I would rather feel a click than rely only on a light.” Choose Pain point Context Goal Preference Which follow-up question is strongest? Check Research Notes Use open questions to learn about real experiences rather than confirm a solution idea. What You Will Submit Stakeholder Research Summary One stakeholder map or research summary. Lesson Interactive Resolve Prototype Integration Problems Match each interface problem to a corrective action, then identify the issue that must be handled first. Integration issue Best corrective action A wire flexes sharply where it enters the moving housing. Choose Add strain relief and reroute the wire Increase mechanical clearance Relocate the access panel The linkage rubs the frame near the end of travel. Choose Add strain relief and reroute the wire Increase mechanical clearance Relocate the access panel Which issue should be prioritized first? Choose A visible layer line A user-accessible pinch point A mismatched color Check Integration Plan Correct the cause of each interface problem and prioritize user safety before appearance. items.title: Turn Class Data into an Engineering Decision
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 4 Turn Class Data into an Engineering Decision IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.4 Turn Class Data into an Engineering Decision Analyze a class data set, create appropriate visualizations, and make an evidence-based engineering recommendation. Intermediate 60 minutes Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineers must convert raw measurements into a clear conclusion that supports a design decision. Objectives What You Will Practice Organize and clean data Select appropriate graph types Use descriptive statistics Connect evidence to a decision Materials What You Need Class data set Spreadsheet software Calculator Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Import or enter the data and check units, labels, blanks, and obvious entry errors. State the engineering question the data should answer. Calculate mean, median, range, and one additional useful statistic. Create at least two graph types and choose the one that communicates the result best. Identify any outlier and decide whether to keep, correct, or investigate it. Compare at least two groups or conditions. Write a claim supported by two specific pieces of evidence. Make one recommendation and state one limitation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use a data set with at least 15 values Label all axes and units Calculate at least four statistics Create at least two candidate graphs Support the recommendation with numerical evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not delete outliers without explanation Use graph scales that do not exaggerate differences Protect student names or private information Conclusions must stay within the available data Deliverables What You Submit Clean data table Statistic calculations Two candidate graphs Final selected graph Claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph Recommendation and limitation Reflection Reflection Questions Which graph communicated the data best? How did the mean and median differ? What did the outlier change? What additional data would strengthen the recommendation? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Start with the decision question, not the graph type. Common Mistake A visually dramatic graph can still be misleading if the scale or labels are inappropriate. Stretch Goal Create a dashboard with a filter or comparison control. items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 4 Build a Simple Electromechanical Device IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.5 Build a Simple Electromechanical Device Design and build a simple electromechanical device such as an alarm, fan, indicator, mini conveyor, or launcher with a safe, defined function. Advanced 2-3 class periods Creative Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small aerospace support task needs a device that senses or receives an input and produces a mechanical or visual output. Objectives What You Will Practice Create a system block diagram Build a basic electrical circuit Integrate electrical and mechanical components Test and revise a device Materials What You Need Low-voltage power source Switch or approved sensor Motor, buzzer, LED, or actuator Wires and breadboard as appropriate Approved mechanical materials Multimeter Procedure Instructions Choose an approved task and write a one-sentence function statement. Create an input-process-output block diagram. Draw a circuit diagram and label voltage, components, and polarity. Create a mechanical sketch showing how the output does useful work. Build and inspect the electrical circuit before connecting the mechanical load. Test one subsystem at a time. Run at least five full-system trials and record success, current, speed, or another performance measure. Revise one feature and repeat the test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use only teacher-approved low-voltage components Include a user-controlled stop or power-disconnect method Show both circuit and mechanical diagrams Complete five repeated trials Document one revision Constraints Constraints & Safety No connection to wall power No projectiles, exposed blades, or unsafe pinch points Keep current within component ratings Power must be disconnected before rewiring Deliverables What You Submit Function statement System block diagram Circuit diagram Mechanical sketch Working device or demonstration Five-trial test table Revision reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which subsystem caused the most problems? How did electrical limits affect mechanical performance? What safety feature was most important? How would you make the device more reliable? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Test the electrical output before attaching a mechanical load. This isolates faults. Common Mistake Randomly changing wiring and mechanics at the same time makes troubleshooting much harder. Stretch Goal Add an automatic sensor input or a second operating mode. Your Task Build the Structure and Core Mechanism Construct the prototype frame and main mechanical relationship while documenting deviations from the approved plan. items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 4 Friction Surface Investigation IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.2 Friction Surface Investigation Compare friction for three surface materials and recommend the best tray liner. Beginner 60-90 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A payload tray slides during rover motion. The team needs evidence about which surface pairing provides the most resistance to sliding. Objectives What You Will Practice Design a controlled friction test Measure force or critical angle Collect repeated data Use averages to make a recommendation Materials What You Need Small test block Wood, plastic, foam, or other approved surfaces Spring scale or adjustable ramp Protractor Ruler Data sheet Procedure Instructions Choose either a pull-force method or incline-angle method. Define the independent, dependent, and controlled variables. Prepare three surfaces with equal test area. Run at least five trials per surface using the same block and load. Record force or critical angle for every trial. Calculate mean and range for each surface. Create a graph and identify any outlier. Recommend a liner and explain one limitation of the test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Test at least three surfaces Complete five trials per surface Keep block mass and contact area constant Calculate mean and range Create one labeled graph Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved surfaces Do not exceed spring-scale capacity Keep hands clear of a moving block Recommendation is based on dry classroom conditions Deliverables What You Submit Test plan and variables Raw data table Mean/range calculations Graph Material recommendation Test limitation Reflection Reflection Questions Which surface had the most consistent data? What variable was hardest to control? How could dust or moisture affect the result? Would the best high-friction material always be best for a moving mechanism? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Mark a consistent starting position and pull direction for every trial. Common Mistake Do not base a conclusion on the single highest measurement; use repeated data. Stretch Goal Repeat the chosen surface with two different loads and compare the effect. Career Connection Tribology and mechanical engineers study friction, wear, and lubrication in vehicles, machines, and aerospace mechanisms. Background Engineering Context A rover motor spins too quickly and does not provide enough output torque for a wheel or lifting mechanism. Objectives What You Will Practice Calculate gear ratios Design single- or multi-stage systems Connect ratio to speed and torque Build or model a mechanism Materials What You Need Gear sets or CAD gear models Axles and supports Calculator Tachometer or rotation-count method Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the required input and desired approximate 5:1 reduction. Create three possible gear-train layouts and calculate each overall ratio. Select a design based on ratio accuracy, part count, size, and direction of rotation. Build or model the selected train. Mark input and output gears. Rotate the input a known number of turns and count output turns. Compare measured and calculated ratio. Explain the expected effect on output speed and ideal torque. Requirements Engineering Requirements Target an overall reduction between 4.8:1 and 5.2:1 Show calculations for three concepts Support and align every axle Demonstrate rotation without gear skipping Compare calculated and measured ratio Constraints Constraints & Safety Use available gears only Do not force mismatched gears Ignore friction only when labeling the result as ideal Mechanism must fit within the assigned footprint Deliverables What You Submit Three gear-train sketches Ratio calculations Selection justification Built or CAD mechanism Measured ratio data Speed/torque explanation Reflection Reflection Questions Why might measured rotation differ from the calculation? Common Mistake Counting gear teeth only within one stage will not give the total ratio of a compound system. Stretch Goal Add a selectable second ratio for high speed and high torque. Advanced 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small inspection drone needs a replacement arm. The material must be light, stiff enough, manufacturable, and affordable. Objectives What You Will Practice Use material properties in a trade study Distinguish strength, stiffness, density, and toughness Apply weighted decision criteria Defend an engineering recommendation Materials What You Need Candidate material data sheets Decision matrix template Calculator or spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the mission profile, arm dimensions, expected load, and available manufacturing processes. Compare aluminum, PLA, ABS, nylon, and carbon-fiber composite using density, stiffness, strength, toughness, cost, and manufacturability. Choose weighting factors that total 100%. Normalize or score each material consistently. Complete the weighted decision matrix. Perform one simple mass comparison using equal part volume. Identify one property not captured well by the numerical matrix. Write a recommendation with one risk and one verification test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Compare at least five candidate materials Use at least six criteria Explain all weighting choices Include one quantitative mass comparison Identify a verification test before flight use Constraints Constraints & Safety Use provided or credible property data Do not treat all composites as identical Recommendation applies only to the stated mission and geometry No physical load testing beyond approved classroom limits Deliverables What You Submit Material-property comparison table Weighted decision matrix Mass calculation Recommendation memo Risk and test plan Reflection Reflection Questions Which criterion controlled the result? How would a crash-resistance requirement change the choice? Why might the lightest material not be best? What data would you verify with a supplier? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Strength and stiffness are different. A material may resist breaking but still bend too much. Common Mistake A decision matrix does not replace judgment. Poor data or arbitrary weights can produce a misleading winner. Stretch Goal Recalculate the matrix for a cold-weather mission or a low-cost training drone. Career Connection Materials and aerospace engineers select materials by balancing performance, environment, manufacturing, cost, and risk. items.title: Motion Graphs and System Behavior
items.description: IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.8: Motion Graphs and System Behavior. How can graphs help engineers understand system behavior over time?
items.searchText: IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.8 | Motion Graphs and System Behavior | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.8 | Motion Graphs and System Behavior | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.8 IED Unit 4 • Lesson 4.8 Motion Graphs and System Behavior Focus question: How can graphs help engineers understand system behavior over time? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 4 Mission Focus You can interpret a motion or performance graph and connect it to a system behavior claim. Graph Interpret Connect Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The graph uses correct scales and the written interpretation matches the plotted evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Represent System Behavior with Motion Graphs. Learning Targets Identify what a motion or performance graph shows over time. Use graph patterns to describe speed, change, delay, or inconsistency. Connect graph evidence to a system behavior conclusion. Success Looks Like You can interpret a motion or performance graph and connect it to a system behavior claim. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How can graphs help engineers understand system behavior over time? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Represent System Behavior with Motion Graphs. Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: The graph uses correct scales and the written interpretation matches the plotted evidence. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Graphs make system behavior easier to compare and communicate. Key Idea 2 Patterns over time can reveal delays, spikes, slowdowns, or inconsistent performance. Key Idea 3 A graph should support a specific engineering claim. Your Task Represent System Behavior with Motion Graphs Convert position, speed, force, or another measured behavior into a graph that reveals how the system changes over time. Identify the variables and units for both axes. Organize the measurements in time order. Create a properly labeled graph. Describe one meaningful trend, peak, plateau, or irregularity. Quality check: The graph uses correct scales and the written interpretation matches the plotted evidence. Lesson Interactive Interpret a Position–Time Graph Match graph shape to the behavior of a moving mechanism. Candidate Graphs Graph A Graph B Graph C Meaning of the selected graph Choose Position increases at constant speed Object remains stopped Object moves out and returns Check Graph Interpretation A straight position–time line with constant positive slope represents constant speed away from the starting point. What You Will Submit Motion Behavior Graph One labeled motion graph. A brief interpretation of the most important pattern. Submission standard: The graph uses correct scales and the written interpretation matches the plotted evidence. items.title: Material Testing Lab
items.description: IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.3: Material Testing Lab. How can engineers test materials before choosing them for a prototype?
items.searchText: IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.3 | Material Testing Lab | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.3 | Material Testing Lab | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.3 IED Unit 4 • Lesson 4.3 Material Testing Lab Focus question: How can engineers test materials before choosing them for a prototype? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 4 Mission Focus You can run a simple material test, record observations, and connect results to a design decision. Test Measure Evaluate Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The procedure is applied consistently enough that the samples can be compared fairly. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Run a Controlled Material Test. Learning Targets Set up a fair material comparison using consistent procedures. Record observations, measurements, and test conditions clearly. Use test results to support a material recommendation. Success Looks Like You can run a simple material test, record observations, and connect results to a design decision. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How can engineers test materials before choosing them for a prototype? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Run a Controlled Material Test. Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: The procedure is applied consistently enough that the samples can be compared fairly. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Testing turns a material preference into evidence. Key Idea 2 Fair tests control variables so results can be compared. Key Idea 3 Test notes should include setup, measurements, observations, and conclusions. Your Task Run a Controlled Material Test Collect comparable evidence from material samples using the assigned test method. Identify the independent, dependent, and controlled variables. Measure and record each sample consistently. Repeat trials when required and note unusual results. Photograph or describe the observed failure or deformation. Quality check: The procedure is applied consistently enough that the samples can be compared fairly. Lesson Interactive Interpret a Load–Deflection Test Use measured load and deflection to calculate stiffness and compare material samples. Sample Test Applied load (N) Deflection (mm) Calculated stiffness — Sample Load Deflection A 50 N 3.5 mm B 50 N 2.0 mm C 50 N 5.0 mm Which sample is stiffest? Choose Sample A Sample B Sample C Relationship: stiffness = load ÷ deflection. Check Test Conclusion Calculate the stiffness value, then identify the sample that deflects the least under the same load. What You Will Submit Material Test Data A completed material-test data table. One labeled photo or observation of sample behavior. Submission standard: The procedure is applied consistently enough that the samples can be compared fairly. Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 4 Mission Focus You can model prototype components and record evidence that parts fit and move as intended. Model Inspect Revise Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The modeled components fit the approved layout and can be fabricated with available tools and materials. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Model and Check Prototype Components. Learning Targets Create or revise CAD components needed for the prototype. Check fit, clearance, and movement between modeled parts. Record CAD evidence before physical construction. Success Looks Like You can model prototype components and record evidence that parts fit and move as intended. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How do engineers model and check parts before building? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Model and Check Prototype Components. Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: The modeled components fit the approved layout and can be fabricated with available tools and materials. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 CAD models should be checked against the function they must support. Key Idea 2 Fit and motion issues are easier to fix before fabrication. Key Idea 3 Model screenshots and notes help explain why parts are ready or need revision. Your Task Model and Check Prototype Components Develop the required CAD components and evaluate fit, motion space, and manufacturability before construction. Model the assigned components from the approved layout. Use parameters or dimensions to control critical geometry. Assemble or position the parts for a fit check. Revise any interference or impractical feature. Quality check: The modeled components fit the approved layout and can be fabricated with available tools and materials. Lesson Interactive Verify CAD Components, Fit, and Motion Use model parameters to check whether the assembly is ready for prototyping. Pin clearance Clearance: 0.10 mm Motion limit Travel: 90° Model status: Revise model How should moving parts be organized? Choose Separate components One merged body Sketches only Target: 0.30 mm clearance and 70° travel. Check CAD Model A usable motion model needs separate components, realistic fit clearance, and a defined motion limit. What You Will Submit Prototype CAD Check The saved component or assembly CAD files. One annotated fit or motion-clearance screenshot. Submission standard: The modeled components fit the approved layout and can be fabricated with available tools and materials. items.description: IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.17: Testing Protocol Development. How do engineers design fair tests to evaluate whether a prototype works?
items.searchText: IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.17 | Testing Protocol Development | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.17 | Testing Protocol Development | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.17 IED Unit 4 • Lesson 4.17 Testing Protocol Development Focus question: How do engineers design fair tests to evaluate whether a prototype works? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 4 Mission Focus You can write a testing protocol that identifies variables, criteria, procedures, and data to collect. Define Control Plan Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The protocol changes one intended condition at a time and produces evidence tied to a criterion. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Write a Fair Prototype Testing Protocol. Learning Targets Identify the test goal and success criteria. Define variables, constants, and repeated trials. Plan how results will be recorded and compared. Success Looks Like You can write a testing protocol that identifies variables, criteria, procedures, and data to collect. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How do engineers design fair tests to evaluate whether a prototype works? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Write a Fair Prototype Testing Protocol. Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: The protocol changes one intended condition at a time and produces evidence tied to a criterion. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 A fair test is planned before data collection begins. Key Idea 2 Test protocols help teams avoid changing too many variables at once. Key Idea 3 The data table should match the decision the team needs to make. Your Task Write a Fair Prototype Testing Protocol Create a repeatable method for measuring whether the prototype meets the Unit 4 performance criteria. State the test question and success criterion. Identify variables, units, equipment, and trial count. Write ordered steps that another team could repeat. Create the data table before testing begins. Quality check: The protocol changes one intended condition at a time and produces evidence tied to a criterion. Lesson Interactive Develop a Valid Testing Protocol Choose the steps and variables needed for a fair, repeatable performance test. Select all valid protocol features Repeat at least five trials Keep the panel load constant Measure deployment time consistently Record values with units Change voltage and load together Record only the best trial Independent variable Choose Supply voltage Deployment time Trial number only Dependent variable Choose Deployment time Supply voltage Team name Check Protocol A test protocol controls other conditions, repeats trials, identifies variables, and records measurements consistently. What You Will Submit Prototype Test Protocol One approved testing protocol with a prepared data table. Submission standard: The protocol changes one intended condition at a time and produces evidence tied to a criterion. items.title: Concept Generation and Decision Matrix
items.description: IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.11: Concept Generation and Decision Matrix. How can engineers choose a mechanism concept using evidence and criteria?
items.searchText: IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.11 | Concept Generation and Decision Matrix | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.11 | Concept Generation and Decision Matrix | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.11 IED Unit 4 • Lesson 4.11 Concept Generation and Decision Matrix Focus question: How can engineers choose a mechanism concept using evidence and criteria? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 4 Mission Focus You can generate mechanism concepts and use a decision matrix to support a concept selection. Generate Score Select Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The selected concept follows the matrix evidence and is not chosen before alternatives are compared. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Generate and Select a Mechanism Concept. Learning Targets Generate multiple possible concepts before choosing one. Use criteria to compare mechanism options fairly. Explain how decision matrix results support the selected concept. Success Looks Like You can generate mechanism concepts and use a decision matrix to support a concept selection. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How can engineers choose a mechanism concept using evidence and criteria? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Generate and Select a Mechanism Concept. Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: The selected concept follows the matrix evidence and is not chosen before alternatives are compared. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Concept generation prevents teams from locking into the first idea too soon. Key Idea 2 A decision matrix turns criteria into a more transparent comparison. Key Idea 3 Scores should be explained with evidence, not used as magic answers. Your Task Generate and Select a Mechanism Concept Develop multiple system concepts and use a decision matrix to choose one based on evidence and challenge criteria. Create at least three meaningfully different concepts. Label the proposed mechanism and expected input/output. Establish weighted criteria using prior lesson evidence. Score the concepts and justify the selected direction. Quality check: The selected concept follows the matrix evidence and is not chosen before alternatives are compared. Lesson Interactive Use a Weighted Decision Matrix Calculate weighted concept scores instead of choosing a favorite concept. Weights and Ratings Criterion Weight Concept A Concept B Concept C Performance 5 4 3 5 Low mass 3 2 5 3 Low cost 2 4 3 2 Weighted total — — — Recommended concept Choose Concept A Concept B Concept C Calculate Weighted Scores Check Decision Multiply each rating by its criterion weight, add the products, and select the highest total. What You Will Submit Concept Selection Package Three labeled concept sketches. A completed decision matrix with a selection justification. Submission standard: The selected concept follows the matrix evidence and is not chosen before alternatives are compared.
