items.title: Engineering Notebook & Documentation Basics
items.description: A Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on engineering notebook & documentation basics.
items.searchText: IED Lesson 0.5: Engineering Notebook & Documentation Basics | LockwoodSTEM IED Lesson 0.5: Engineering Notebook & Documentation Basics | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.5 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.5 Engineering Notebook & Documentation Basics Focus Question: What makes engineering documentation useful? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Make thinking visible Improve notebook evidence so another person can trace what happened, why it changed, and what supports the decision. Label Record Explain Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Turn rough notes into clear, dated, labeled, evidence-based documentation. Learning Targets Explain what strong engineering documentation looks like. Improve the Lesson 0.4 paper-airplane worksheet. Connect documentation quality to engineering decisions and communication. Success Looks Like… Another person can understand your design, test, and revision without asking you to fill in missing details. Core habit: Document enough information for someone else to follow the work later. Opening prompt Weak vs. strong Documentation standard Revision workshop Peer check File work Exit Opening Prompt Could another person understand your work? Good documentation is written for the future reader—not only for the person who completed the activity. Quick class share: What information would be missing from the note “It worked”? Reveal the documentation standard Strong documentation makes engineering thinking visible. It is clear, dated, labeled, evidence-based, and detailed enough to support a review or repeat the work. Compare Weak vs. Strong Documentation More words do not automatically create better evidence. Weak Evidence Undated or unlabeled notes Missing sketches or measurements Vague claims such as “it worked” No explanation of changes Hard for another person to follow Strong Evidence Dated, labeled, and organized Sketches show important features Data and observations are specific Decisions are explained with evidence Another person can understand the work Documentation Standard Use five checks throughout the course These checks apply to notebook pages, photos, screenshots, data tables, and design-review evidence. Clear Another person can understand what happened. Dated The work can be traced over time. Labeled Sketches, tables, and images have meaning. Evidence-Based Claims connect to data or observations. Review-Ready There is enough detail to explain a decision. Revision Workshop Improve the Lesson 0.4 artifact Use the documentation standard to strengthen the paper-airplane worksheet. Review the evidence Check the date and page number. Verify that sketches and versions are labeled. Confirm that both distances are recorded. Replace vague statements with specific observations. Explain why the revision was chosen. Upgrade a weak note Weak: “We fixed the wing and it worked better.” Stronger: “Version 1 curved left. We corrected the uneven left-wing fold. Version 2 traveled 12 ft farther and followed a straighter path.” Quick Check Which note is review-ready? Vote before opening the answer. 1 “Changed it because it was bad.” 2 “After Version 1 curved left, we leveled the wing tips. Version 2 traveled straighter.” Reveal the stronger note Best answer: 2 It identifies the observation, the change, and the result. The reader can follow the reasoning. Mission Debrief What You Submit Improve the existing artifact rather than creating disconnected new work. Revised Documentation Artifact The improved Lesson 0.4 worksheet with clear labels, data, page number, and revision explanation. Next Mission Lesson 0.6 Problem Definition, Criteria & Constraints Open Lesson 0.6 Resources Lesson 0.5 Resources Use only the files and references that support today’s work. PowerPoint Lesson 0.5 Student Presentation Google Slides-friendly 16:9 lesson deck with question slides followed by separate answer-reveal slides. items.title: Engineering Notebook Excellence Audit
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Engineering Notebook Excellence Audit IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.4 Engineering Notebook Excellence Audit Upgrade one incomplete or weak notebook entry into a professional engineering record. Beginner 30-45 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineering notebooks are legal and technical records of design work. A clear notebook allows another person to understand what happened, reproduce a test, and trace why decisions were made. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize the features of strong engineering documentation Improve clarity and organization Add missing technical evidence Reflect on design decisions Materials What You Need Engineering notebook One previous notebook entry Ruler Pen or pencil Colored pencil or highlighter Procedure Instructions Choose a previous entry that is incomplete, difficult to follow, or missing evidence. Use a checklist to identify missing date, title, purpose, sketches, measurements, labels, results, and reflection. Create a revised version on a new page without erasing the original record. Add at least one labeled sketch or diagram. Add a table, measurement, calculation, or test result that supports the work. Write a short reflection describing what happened, what changed, and what should happen next. Ask a classmate to read the revised page for 60 seconds and explain the work back to you. Make one final improvement based on that feedback. Requirements Engineering Requirements Keep the original entry unchanged Include a date and descriptive title Use complete labels and units Include at least one visual and one quantitative piece of evidence End with a next-step statement Constraints Constraints & Safety No copied text from another student Revised page must fit on one notebook spread Use permanent notebook practices established in class Deliverables What You Submit Completed notebook audit checklist Original page reference Revised notebook entry Peer feedback note Three improvement rules you will use in future entries Reflection Reflection Questions What information was missing from the original entry? Could another student reproduce the work from your revised page? Which change improved clarity the most? How will better documentation help during a design review? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use headings and white space to guide the reader. More writing is not always clearer writing. Common Mistake Decorating a page is not the same as documenting evidence. Prioritize technical content over appearance. Stretch Goal Create a one-page “excellent notebook entry” guide for a new IED student. Career Connection Engineers use notebooks, test logs, and change records to communicate across teams and support patents, safety reviews, and manufacturing decisions. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.title: Engineering Failure Investigation
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Engineering Failure Investigation IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.5 Engineering Failure Investigation Investigate a major engineering failure and identify how design-process improvements could have reduced the risk. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineering failures are rarely caused by a single bad decision. They often involve technical limits, communication problems, testing gaps, and pressure from schedules or cost. Objectives What You Will Practice Distinguish immediate causes from root causes Connect evidence to design-process decisions Identify ethical and communication factors Develop prevention recommendations Materials What You Need Internet research access Engineering notebook Presentation or document software At least two credible sources Procedure Instructions Choose an approved case such as Challenger, Columbia, Mars Climate Orbiter, Tacoma Narrows Bridge, Hyatt Regency walkway, or another teacher-approved failure. Create a short timeline of at least five events before the failure. Identify the system or component that failed first. Use a five-whys analysis to identify at least one technical root cause and one organizational root cause. Find evidence of a warning, test result, or concern that was missed or misunderstood. Map the failure to stages of the engineering design process. Develop three specific prevention actions involving design, testing, communication, or decision-making. Present the investigation in a one-page visual brief or three-minute presentation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use at least two credible sources Separate facts from your own conclusions Include both technical and human/organizational factors Provide three actionable prevention recommendations Cite sources in a consistent format Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not use graphic images Do not copy a prewritten case summary Keep the final product to one page or three minutes Use respectful language when discussing injuries or loss of life Deliverables What You Submit Timeline Five-whys root cause analysis Engineering design process map Three prevention actions Source list One-page brief or short presentation Reflection Reflection Questions Which warning sign was most important? Where could better testing have changed the outcome? How did communication influence the failure? What responsibility does an engineer have when a safety concern is ignored? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Ask “What allowed this condition to exist?” instead of stopping at “Which part broke?” Common Mistake A root cause is not simply the last event before failure. Look for deeper design, process, and communication conditions. Stretch Goal Compare two failures and identify one recurring pattern in engineering decision-making. Career Connection Safety, reliability, systems, and quality engineers study failures to prevent recurrence and improve standards. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.title: Reverse Engineer a Classroom Object
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Reverse Engineer a Classroom Object IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.2 Reverse Engineer a Classroom Object Analyze a classroom object and create an engineering record that explains its parts, materials, assembly, and likely manufacturing methods. Beginner 45-60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineers often study an existing product before they redesign it. Reverse engineering begins with careful observation, component identification, and reasoned predictions about how a product works. Objectives What You Will Practice Practice technical observation Identify product components and functions Connect materials to manufacturing processes Create an exploded concept sketch Materials What You Need One approved classroom object Engineering notebook Ruler Colored pencils or fine-tip pens Optional magnifier Procedure Instructions Select an object with at least four visible parts, such as a stapler, tape dispenser, scissors, hole punch, or marker. Create a clean isometric sketch of the complete object. Number every visible component and create a matching parts list. For each component, record its function and likely material. Predict how each part was manufactured: molding, stamping, extrusion, machining, forming, or another process. Create an exploded sketch showing the likely assembly order. Identify one design feature that improves safety, comfort, durability, or ease of assembly. Propose one redesign and explain the problem it solves. Requirements Engineering Requirements Identify at least four components Use labels and leader lines correctly Include a material and process prediction for every component Show a logical exploded assembly order Support predictions with visible evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not disassemble sealed, sharp, powered, or school-owned equipment without permission Complete all sketches by hand Do not use an internet image as the primary drawing Deliverables What You Submit Complete-object isometric sketch Numbered parts list Material and manufacturing table Exploded sketch Redesign annotation and explanation Reflection Reflection Questions Which component was hardest to understand? What visible clues helped identify the manufacturing process? Which material choice appeared most important? How would your redesign affect manufacturing cost? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Look for seams, draft angles, fasteners, surface textures, and repeated shapes. These are clues about manufacturing. Common Mistake Do not confuse a component function with its material. “Spring” is a component; “spring steel” is a material choice. Stretch Goal Compare your object with a competing version and identify three design differences. Career Connection Product design and manufacturing engineers routinely analyze competitor products to understand performance, cost, and assembly decisions. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.searchText: IED Lesson 0.4: Engineering Design Process | LockwoodSTEM IED Lesson 0.4: Engineering Design Process | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.4 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.4 Engineering Design Process Focus Question: How do engineers use testing and revision to improve a design? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Run a complete design cycle Use a paper-airplane challenge to define, build, test, compare, and revise a design with measurable evidence. Design Test Revise Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Complete a fast, measurable design cycle and create the first numbered notebook artifact. Learning Targets Describe the engineering design process as a flexible cycle. Apply the cycle to a paper-airplane distance challenge. Use test evidence to revise a design. Success Looks Like… You can explain what changed between Version 1 and Version 2 and support the change with test data. Core habit: A revision needs a reason, and the reason should come from evidence. Opening prompt Design cycle Challenge briefing Version 1 Version 2 Compare evidence Exit Opening Prompt Is the first design supposed to be the best? Engineers use early versions to create evidence—not to prove they were right immediately. Quick class share: Why might a first prototype be useful even when it does not perform well? Reveal the design-process idea The design process is a flexible cycle. Engineers define, generate, develop, construct, test, evaluate, revise, and communicate—often moving backward and forward as evidence changes. Design Cycle A flexible process—not a rigid checklist Different projects may repeat or combine stages. 1 Define Clarify the goal, criteria, and constraints. 2 Generate Create multiple possible solutions. 3 Develop Select and plan a promising approach. 4 Construct + Test Build a prototype and collect evidence. 5 Evaluate + Revise Compare results and improve the design. 6 Present Communicate the design and next steps. Design Sprint Paper Airplane Distance Challenge Complete one fast cycle with measurable evidence. Version 1 Create one individual concept sketch. Choose one team Version 1 concept. Build with one sheet of paper. Complete one official distance test. Record the distance to first ground contact. Version 2 Study Version 1 evidence. Choose one deliberate revision. Build with one new sheet of paper. Complete one official distance test. Compare the two results. Measurement: Record distance from the launch line to the first ground contact in feet and inches. Decision Challenge Which revision is evidence-based? Vote before revealing the answer. Version 1 curves sharply left and lands after 18 ft. Which Version 2 decision is strongest? A Change several folds at once because more change is better. B Adjust the uneven wing fold, keep other features the same, and retest. C Decorate the airplane so it looks faster. D Build a completely different airplane without recording Version 1. Reveal the evidence-based revision Best answer: B The observed left curve points to an asymmetry. Changing one likely cause makes the next test easier to interpret. Strong revision: observed problem → targeted change → new test. Evidence Check Leave with a complete design-process artifact Your worksheet becomes the first numbered notebook document. 1 Individual concept sketch is complete. 2 Version 1 and Version 2 distances are recorded. 3 The revision is described clearly. 4 The decision is supported by evidence. 5 The worksheet is numbered and added to the Table of Contents. Mission Debrief What You Submit Submit the evidence from the full design cycle. Design Process Evidence Paper Airplane Design Process Worksheet The completed paper-airplane design-process worksheet including both test versions and the revision conclusion. items.title: Rocket Launch Pad Design Challenge Launch
items.description: A Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on rocket launch pad design challenge launch.
items.searchText: IED Lesson 0.7: Rocket Launch Pad Design Challenge Launch | LockwoodSTEM IED Lesson 0.7: Rocket Launch Pad Design Challenge Launch | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.7 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.7 Rocket Launch Pad Design Challenge Launch Focus Question: How can a launch pad design support a rocket safely and effectively? View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Launch the first full challenge Use the brief, criteria, constraints, research, and individual ideas to create one evidence-based team concept. Define Sketch Combine Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Move from a design brief to individual concepts and one shared team direction. Learning Targets Understand the Rocket Launch Pad Design Challenge brief. Identify the problem, criteria, and constraints before brainstorming. Create an individual concept before combining ideas into one team concept. Success Looks Like… The team concept combines useful features from multiple individual ideas and addresses the challenge requirements. Core habit: Generate individually first, then combine features rather than simply choosing one person’s idea. Opening prompt Challenge brief Launch-pad examples Define requirements Individual sketch Combine concepts Exit Opening Prompt What does a launch pad need to do? Look past appearance and identify functions: support, stability, access, alignment, protection, and organization. Quick class share: Name one launch-pad feature and explain the need it serves. Reveal the challenge mindset Research is useful when you connect a feature to its function. Do not copy a real launch pad at full complexity. Adapt useful ideas to the classroom challenge. Challenge Brief Design and build a launch pad The first complete Unit 0 challenge begins here. Design Challenge Your team will create a launch pad that: Fits and supports the provided 3D-printed rocket Stands on its own Includes research-informed launch-pad features Uses only approved classroom materials Is justified through sketches, documentation, testing, and presentation Visual Research Observe structure and function Use the image to identify support, access, stability, and ground-system features. Use real systems for inspiration—not for direct copying. Identify the function of each feature before adapting an idea. Image: NASA/Aubrey Gemignani, public domain via Wikimedia Commons Requirements Keep the design target visible Every concept should be checked against the same requirements. Fit + Support The provided rocket must sit securely. Stability The pad must stand without tipping or collapsing. Realistic Features Include features connected to launch-pad functions. Materials Use approved classroom materials; no custom 3D-printed parts. Documentation Use sketches, notes, tests, and explanations. Concept Workflow Individual ideas → shared team concept Every student contributes before the team combines features. 1 Define Review the problem, criteria, and constraints. → 2 Brainstorm Each student creates one individual concept sketch. → 3 Combine Blend useful features from multiple ideas into one team concept. Scenario Response How should the team choose a direction? Vote before opening the answer. Four students have different launch-pad concepts. One student wants the team to use only their sketch because it looks the most complete. A Use the most complete sketch without discussion. B Vote immediately and discard the other ideas. C Share all sketches, identify useful features, and combine them into one team concept. D Ask the teacher to choose the design. Reveal the strongest team process Best answer: C The team should combine useful features from multiple concepts. This increases participation and creates a design that can be justified against criteria and constraints. Mission Debrief What You Submit Move from individual thinking to a documented shared concept. Launch Pad Concept Evidence One individual concept sketch from each student. One labeled team concept with a short criteria-and-constraints explanation. Next Mission Lesson 0.8 Launch Pad Build Plan Open Lesson 0.8 Resources Lesson 0.7 Resources Use only the files and references that support today’s work. items.title: Final Documentation & Design Review
items.description: A Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on final documentation & design review.
items.searchText: IED Lesson 0.11: Final Documentation & Design Review | LockwoodSTEM IED Lesson 0.11: Final Documentation & Design Review | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.11 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.11 Final Documentation & Design Review Focus Question: How do engineers communicate and defend a final design? View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Defend the final design Organize process evidence and explain how testing, revisions, criteria, and constraints shaped the finished prototype. Show Support Defend Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Prepare a concise design review that shows the process—not only the finished object. Learning Targets Prepare final documentation for the launch-pad prototype. Explain how the design changed from concept to final version. Justify how the final prototype meets criteria and constraints. Success Looks Like… Every important design claim is supported by a sketch, photo, test result, observation, or documented decision. Core habit: Use evidence language to explain what changed, why it changed, and how the final design performs. Opening prompt Evidence audit Organize process Final documentation Prepare explanation Peer check Exit Opening Prompt What makes a final design believable? A finished prototype is not enough; the team must show how evidence shaped it. Quick class share: What would you need to see before accepting a team’s claim that its design meets the requirements? Reveal the design-review purpose A design review explains and defends the final design with evidence. It shows the path from problem definition to testing, revision, and final performance. Visual Communication Use diagrams to make structure understandable Labels and views help an audience inspect the design claim. A design review needs visuals that make structure and relationships understandable—not only a verbal description. Image: NASA/KSC, public domain via Wikimedia Commons Evidence Set Show the process and support the claims Select evidence that helps the audience understand decisions. Show the Process Problem definition Initial concepts Build plan Prototype construction Testing and improvement Final design Use Evidence Labeled sketches Materials and dimensions Photos Test results Observations Design explanations Review Preparation Organize the story before presenting The review should be concise, ordered, and evidence-based. Check that the prototype is finished and stable. Organize evidence from Lessons 0.7–0.10. Create or update a final labeled sketch. Summarize the most important test results. Explain one major improvement. Show how the final design meets criteria and constraints. Evidence Language Use sentence frames to defend decisions Specific language helps connect claims to proof. Our launch pad meets the stability criterion because… The provided rocket is supported by… Our most important test result was… After testing, we changed… because… The evidence that supports this decision is… With more time, the next improvement would be… Scenario Response The prototype is finished, but the reasoning is missing Choose the strongest next step before opening the answer. A team plans to show only the finished prototype because the changes seem obvious. A Present the prototype without process evidence. B Say the changes are obvious and skip the explanation. C Add the original problem, test results, revisions, and final justification. D Focus only on decoration and presentation style. Reveal the strongest review plan Best answer: C The audience needs evidence showing how the team reached the final design. A review should make the reasoning inspectable. Mission Debrief What You Submit Create the final evidence package for the launch-pad challenge. Final Launch Pad Review One final design-review artifact containing the labeled design, test summary, and major improvement justification. items.title: Problem Definition, Criteria & Constraints
items.description: A Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on problem definition, criteria & constraints.
items.searchText: IED Lesson 0.6: Problem Definition, Criteria & Constraints | LockwoodSTEM IED Lesson 0.6: Problem Definition, Criteria & Constraints | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.6 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.6 Problem Definition, Criteria & Constraints Focus Question: How do engineers define the problem before designing a solution? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Define before designing Separate the need from a preferred solution, then identify the goals and limits that guide design decisions. Need Goals Limits Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Practice writing a problem statement that leaves room for multiple possible solutions. Learning Targets Separate a problem statement from a solution idea. Write a clear problem statement. Identify criteria and constraints for a design challenge. Success Looks Like… Your problem statement identifies the need without choosing the final product too early. Core habit: Define the user, need, criteria, and constraints before generating solutions. Opening prompt Problem vs. solution Criteria + constraints Classification challenge Worksheet Check Exit Opening Prompt What happens when a team chooses a solution too early? A preferred product can hide the real need and reduce the number of possible solutions. Quick class share: What is the difference between “build a rocket stand” and “support a rocket safely during setup”? Reveal the distinction The problem describes the need. The solution is one possible response. Good problem definition leaves room for multiple designs that can be compared against criteria and constraints. Aerospace Context Launch systems solve multiple connected needs Observe the number of structures and interfaces surrounding the rocket. A launch system is more than a rocket. Ground structures must satisfy needs for support, access, stability, safety, and operations. Image: NASA/Aubrey Gemignani, public domain via Wikimedia Commons Mindset Shift Problem vs. Solution Define the need before naming the final product. Solution Too Early “We are going to build a rocket stand.” Names a product immediately Can lock the team into one idea Makes alternatives harder to compare Problem Definition “We need a way to support the rocket safely during setup.” Explains the user and need Leaves room for multiple solutions Guides criteria and constraints Core Vocabulary Criteria, constraints, success, and evidence Use these terms throughout the design challenge. Criteria Goals the design should meet. Example: supports the rocket securely. Constraints Limits the design must follow. Example: approved classroom materials only. Success Criteria How the team knows the design worked. Example: does not tip during the stability test. Evidence Proof used to justify decisions. Example: sketches, photos, data, and observations. Classification Challenge Criterion or constraint? Classify each statement before opening the answer. A. The launch pad must fit the provided rocket. B. The design should include a realistic access feature. C. Teams may use only approved classroom materials. D. The prototype should stand without tipping. Reveal the classification Criteria B and D describe performance goals. Constraints A and C establish required limits or conditions. A statement may function differently in another project. Classification depends on how the challenge is written. Activity Define before brainstorming Complete the worksheet without selecting a final solution too early. Read the scenario carefully. Identify the user, need, and reason. Write the problem in one or two clear sentences. List criteria the design should meet. List constraints that limit the design. Check that the statement does not assume one final solution. Mission Debrief What You Submit Create the definition that will guide later concept work. Defined Design Problem Problem Definition, Criteria & Constraints One completed problem-definition worksheet containing the problem statement, criteria, constraints, and proposed success evidence. items.title: Unit 0 Portfolio Check & Design Reflection
items.description: A Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on unit 0 portfolio check & design reflection.
items.searchText: IED Lesson 0.12: Unit 0 Portfolio Check & Design Reflection | LockwoodSTEM IED Lesson 0.12: Unit 0 Portfolio Check & Design Reflection | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.12 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.12 Unit 0 Portfolio Check & Design Reflection Focus Question: How does reflection help engineers prepare for the next design challenge? View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Audit the evidence and reflect Verify that the Unit 0 portfolio shows a complete design process and use specific evidence to explain growth. Audit Reflect Transfer Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Close the unit by checking evidence quality and identifying habits to carry into technical sketching. Learning Targets Organize the complete Unit 0 notebook portfolio. Verify that launch-pad documentation is complete. Reflect on teamwork, testing, improvement, and design-process growth. Success Looks Like… Your portfolio shows the path from problem definition to tested prototype, and your reflection cites specific evidence. Core habit: Reflection is strongest when it names a specific decision, result, challenge, or improvement. Opening prompt Portfolio audit Complete evidence Reflection Self-check Carry forward Close Opening Prompt How can a portfolio show growth? A portfolio is not a pile of finished pages; it is an evidence trail across the design process. Quick class share: Which piece of Unit 0 evidence best shows a change in your thinking or design? Reveal the portfolio purpose A strong portfolio shows the path from idea to evidence-based improvement. Reflection helps identify which habits should carry into the next challenge. Portfolio Audit Check the full evidence trail Use the list to find missing, incomplete, or unclear work before writing the reflection. 1 Notebook and course-resource routines are established. 2 Paper-airplane worksheet is complete, numbered, and revised. 3 Problem definition, criteria, and constraints work is complete. 4 Individual and team launch-pad concepts are present. 5 Build plan is labeled and build-ready. 6 Prototype build notes and change evidence are complete. 7 Testing and improvement evidence is complete. 8 Final design review and reflection are included. Reflection Use specific evidence—not generic praise A reflection should explain decisions, challenges, improvements, and future actions. Explain How the team used the design process Your strongest contribution The biggest challenge The improvement with the biggest impact What you would change with more time Support with Specific examples Test results or observations Clear connection to notebook evidence Honest discussion of problems Recognition of teamwork Quick Check Which reflection is stronger? Vote before opening the answer. A. “The project went well and our team worked hard.” B. “Our first base tipped during the stability test. I suggested widening it by 2 in, and the revised prototype remained upright in the retest.” Reveal the stronger reflection B is stronger. It names the problem, contribution, change, and result. A may be true, but it does not provide evidence of learning or improvement. Carry Forward What Unit 0 established These habits become the foundation for technical sketching, CAD, prototyping, and later design reviews. Define Start with the need, criteria, and constraints. Document Make thinking and decisions visible. Test Use repeatable checks to create evidence. Improve Revise based on specific results. Communicate Defend the final design clearly. Mission Debrief What You Submit Close Unit 0 with a complete portfolio and individual reflection. Unit 0 Portfolio and Reflection One complete chronological Unit 0 portfolio with an updated table of contents. One individual reflection on evidence, revision, and growth. items.description: A Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on engineering notebook setup & course resources.
items.searchText: IED Lesson 0.2: Engineering Notebook Setup & Course Resources | LockwoodSTEM IED Lesson 0.2: Engineering Notebook Setup & Course Resources | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.2 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.2 Engineering Notebook Setup & Course Resources Focus Question: How will you organize evidence so your engineering work can be understood later? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Build an evidence system Set up a chronological engineering notebook and verify access to the digital resources used throughout IED. Organize Access Name Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Set up the physical and digital systems that will keep engineering evidence organized all year. Learning Targets Set up the binder-based engineering notebook system. Explain chronological organization and table-of-contents routines. Locate course resources, templates, downloads, and submission locations. Success Looks Like… Your binder and digital files are organized so another person can find and understand your work. Core habit: Record work in order and use consistent names so decisions remain traceable. Opening prompt Notebook purpose Binder setup Resource access File naming Readiness check Debrief Opening Prompt What makes a notebook useful later? Think beyond neatness: what must another person be able to find or understand? Quick class share: Name one piece of engineering evidence that would be difficult to recreate if it were not recorded. Reveal the working definition An engineering notebook is a chronological evidence record. It captures what happened, when it happened, and why decisions changed so the work can be reviewed, repeated, or improved. Notebook System Build the binder in the correct order The table of contents is the map; numbered documents are the evidence trail. Binder Setup Required structure Place the printed Table of Contents first. Do not number the Table of Contents. Start page numbering with the first actual document. Add new work in the order it is completed. Update the Table of Contents as documents are added. Why It Matters Professional habits Makes design thinking visible Helps teams trace decisions Creates evidence for design reviews Supports revision and inspection Prevents lost or disconnected work Live Setup Notebook Readiness Check Complete the physical setup before moving to digital resources. 1 Binder has six dividers and a clear place for Unit 0. 2 Table of Contents is placed first and left unnumbered. 3 Lined and graph paper are available. 4 Name and course are clearly identified. 5 First numbered document location is ready. Digital Access Confirm the course systems work Do the access check now so project time is not lost later. Access sequence Log in to Google Classroom. Open and bookmark the LockwoodSTEM IED Course Hub. Locate lesson pages, downloads, templates, and certifications. Confirm that required Drive or submission locations open correctly. Ask for help now if any account or permission fails. Where information lives Projected agenda Warm-up, announcements, and today’s sequence Google Classroom Assignments, submissions, and posted resources LockwoodSTEM.org Lesson pages, downloads, references, and course tools File Naming Make digital work findable A useful name should make sense before the file is opened. Required format: LastName_FirstName_Unit_AssignmentName Which name is stronger? 1 finalfinal2.pptx 2 Lockwood_Jonathan_Unit0_PaperAirplaneEvidence.pptx Reveal the stronger file name Best answer: 2 It identifies the student, unit, and assignment without opening the file. Avoid vague names such as final , new , or thing . Check: Save files in the correct location and keep a backup when work is important. Mission Debrief What You Submit Most of today’s evidence is verified live rather than uploaded. Course Setup Check A completed binder/table-of-contents setup and verified access to the required course resources. No formal digital submission unless your teacher gives a separate direction. items.title: Launch Pad Build Plan
items.description: A Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on launch pad build plan.
items.searchText: IED Lesson 0.8: Launch Pad Build Plan | LockwoodSTEM IED Lesson 0.8: Launch Pad Build Plan | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.8 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.8 Launch Pad Build Plan Focus Question: How does planning make a prototype easier to build and test? View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Make the concept build-ready Convert the team concept into a labeled, dimensioned, material-aware sequence another person could follow. Label Sequence Check Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Reduce improvisation by deciding how parts, materials, dimensions, and steps fit together before building. Learning Targets Refine the team launch-pad concept into a build plan. Add labels, approximate dimensions, materials, and construction steps. Complete a build-readiness check before construction begins. Success Looks Like… Another team could understand what to build, what materials to use, and what order to follow. Core habit: Plan enough detail to reduce avoidable problems during construction. Opening prompt Plan requirements Materials planning Refine plan Readiness check Peer check Exit Opening Prompt Could another team build from your sketch? A concept communicates an idea; a build plan communicates how to make it. Quick class share: What information is usually missing from a rough concept sketch? Reveal the planning goal A build-ready plan reduces improvisation during construction. It identifies parts, approximate sizes, materials, connections, order of work, and likely weaknesses. Engineering Example Plans communicate structure before fabrication Observe how multiple views make the platform easier to understand. Technical diagrams make relationships, dimensions, and structure easier to communicate before construction. Image: NASA/KSC, public domain via Wikimedia Commons Plan Requirements What the build plan must include The goal is not artistic perfection; the goal is clear construction information. Refined Sketch Show the chosen team concept clearly. Labels Name the base, supports, guides, braces, and features. Approximate Dimensions Show important sizes and spacing. Materials Identify approved materials for each major part. Build Sequence List construction steps in a logical order. Risk Check Identify one likely weak point or build problem. Materials Planning Design with available materials in mind Match material properties to the job each part must perform. Structure + bracing Cardboard / paperboard Bases, walls, support surfaces Craft sticks Frames, reinforcement, angled supports Straws / tubes Guides, lightweight supports, alignment Connections + fit String / rubber bands Tension or temporary holding when approved Tape / glue / hot glue Connections used only as directed Provided rocket Used for fit checks; not modified Quick Check Build-ready or vague? Vote before opening the answer. A. “Base: cardboard, approximately 8 in × 8 in, with two craft-stick support columns.” B. “We will make the bottom strong somehow.” Reveal the build-ready statement A is build-ready. It identifies a part, material, approximate size, and support approach. B does not give enough information to build or inspect. Readiness Check Pause before construction begins Use the plan to find problems while they are still easy to change. 1 The build is realistic in one class period. 2 All materials are approved and available. 3 Rocket fit and support locations are shown. 4 The base and main structure are clear. 5 At least one possible weakness is identified. Mission Debrief What You Submit Leave with a plan that is ready to review with your teacher before construction. Launch Pad Build Plan One refined team build plan containing the labeled sketch, materials, and ordered construction steps. items.title: Launch Pad Testing & Improvement
items.description: A Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on launch pad testing & improvement.
items.searchText: IED Lesson 0.10: Launch Pad Testing & Improvement | LockwoodSTEM IED Lesson 0.10: Launch Pad Testing & Improvement | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.10 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.10 Launch Pad Testing & Improvement Focus Question: How does testing show what a prototype needs next? View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Turn tests into improvements Test the launch pad against the challenge criteria, record specific results, revise one weakness, and retest. Test Record Revise Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Run criterion-based tests and use the results to guide a documented design change. Learning Targets Test the prototype against challenge criteria. Record observations, strengths, weaknesses, and failure points. Make at least one evidence-based improvement. Success Looks Like… You can connect one design improvement directly to a test result. Core habit: A test result should lead to a clear decision: keep, change, or investigate. Opening prompt Test criteria Run tests Analyze results Improve + retest Document Exit Opening Prompt What makes a test useful? A test should answer a specific question connected to a design requirement. Quick class share: What is the difference between “try it” and “test it”? Reveal the testing standard A useful test has a criterion, a repeatable action, and evidence to record. The result should guide a clear next decision. Aerospace Context Testing happens before commitment Real launch systems are checked as integrated structures, not only as separate parts. Before launch, integrated systems are checked against specific operating requirements. Classroom tests should also connect directly to criteria. Image: NASA/Aubrey Gemignani, public domain via Wikimedia Commons Test Criteria Match each test to a requirement Record what actually happens—not what the team hoped would happen. Stability Test Does the pad stand without tipping? Record: pass/fail, wobble, tipping direction, photo. Rocket Fit Test Does the provided rocket sit securely? Record: contact points, slipping, movement, alignment. Support Test Does the structure hold without bending or collapsing? Record: weak joints, bending, sliding, deformation. Feature Check Can the team explain the function of realistic launch-pad features? Record: labels and functional explanation. Test Cycle Test → record → revise The improvement must connect to an observed weakness. 1 Test Run the criteria checks consistently. → 2 Record Identify strengths, weaknesses, and failure points. → 3 Revise Make one evidence-based improvement and retest. Improvement Options Choose changes that address test results Do not add parts without a reason. Widen the base to improve stability. Reinforce weak joints or support columns. Adjust rocket-support spacing or angle. Add bracing to reduce bending or twisting. Improve alignment so the rocket sits securely. Remove parts that add weight without function. Scenario Response The pad holds the rocket but wobbles Choose the strongest next step before opening the answer. A Keep it because it did not fall. B Add realistic-looking details. C Record the wobble, locate the weak area, revise the base or supports, and retest. D Repeat the same test without recording anything. Reveal the evidence-based next step Best answer: C The wobble is a specific weakness. The team should record it, target the likely cause, and collect new evidence after revision. Mission Debrief What You Submit Finish with a tested, improved, and documented prototype. Launch Pad Test and Revision One test-results record for the assigned criteria. One documented design improvement with evidence from the retest. items.title: Course Launch & Engineering Mindset
items.description: A Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on engineering mindset, aerospace connections, and evidence-based design decisions.
items.searchText: IED Lesson 0.1: Course Launch & Engineering Mindset | LockwoodSTEM IED Lesson 0.1: Course Launch & Engineering Mindset | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.1 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.1 Course Launch & Engineering Mindset Focus Question: How do engineers think, document, and make evidence-based decisions? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Think like an engineer Define the problem, test the idea, and use evidence to make and communicate decisions. Define Test Decide Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A complete opening lesson that launches the engineering mindset you will use throughout IED. Learning Targets Describe the purpose of IED through an aerospace lens. Explain how engineering problems differ from typical assignments. Identify evidence engineers use to support design decisions. Success Looks Like… You can explain a design decision using more than “I think.” Core habit: Connect each design claim to evidence another person can inspect. Opening prompt Engineer-actions vote IED + aerospace Mindset shift Evidence challenge Quick check Exit debrief Opening Prompt What do engineers do? Think about actions, habits, and decisions—not job titles. Quick class share: Give one short answer using an action word such as design, build, test, fix, invent, solve, measure, or improve. Reveal the working definition Engineers use knowledge, tools, and creativity to solve problems under real constraints. 1 Define Clarify the need, user, criteria, and constraints. 2 Generate Create multiple possible solutions before choosing one. 3 Test Collect evidence from models, prototypes, data, and feedback. 4 Communicate Document decisions so others can understand and improve the work. Interactive Vote Engineer Actions: Which One Fits? Hold up fingers 1–4 or vote silently. Then justify your choice. Which action sounds most like engineering work? 1 Copying exact instructions to make the same model as everyone else 2 Choosing the first idea because it seems easiest to build 3 Testing two versions and comparing data before deciding 4 Making a design look impressive without checking if it works Reveal the strongest engineering choice Best answer: 3 Testing two versions and comparing data before deciding uses comparison, data, and a decision based on evidence. The other choices prioritize copying, ease, or appearance rather than proof. Carry-forward idea: In IED, an answer becomes stronger when it connects to evidence. Course Launch IED Through an Aerospace Lens Build transferable engineering habits through aerospace contexts and projects. Core Engineering Skills Sketching and visual communication Engineering notebook documentation CAD modeling and technical drawings Prototyping, testing, and data analysis Design reviews and evidence-based explanations Aerospace Connections Rocket launch pad design challenge Rocket models and assemblies Aircraft, drones, satellites, and rovers FabLab tools and manufacturing routines Human-centered aerospace capstone Turn + Talk Aerospace Connection Map Choose a rocket, drone, satellite, rover, or aircraft . Identify one design choice an engineer must make, then connect it to one kind of evidence. Sketch What features or shapes matter? Model What could be represented in CAD? Measure What dimensions or data matter? Test What would prove it works? Share-out target: one system + one design decision + one kind of evidence. Mindset Shift Assignment vs. Engineering Problem The goal is not just to finish; the goal is to make a design claim you can defend. Completion Mindset Typical Assignment Often has one expected answer Can be completed and put away Usually judged as correct or incorrect Mistakes are avoided Evidence Mindset Engineering Problem Has multiple possible solutions Must satisfy criteria and constraints Uses testing to compare designs Mistakes become evidence for improvement Key Idea Evidence-Based Engineering Engineers connect what they claim to proof that others can inspect. 1 Claim What you believe about the design → 2 Evidence What proves or challenges the claim → 3 Decision What you do next because of the evidence Evidence can include: sketches; measurements; test data; observations; photos; prototypes; user feedback. Mini Challenge What Evidence Would You Need? Select the two pieces of evidence that best support the claim. Claim: “Our launch pad design supports the rocket safely and is ready for testing.” A A labeled sketch showing where the rocket contacts the support B A photo that makes the prototype look finished C A stability test showing the pad does not tip with the rocket placed on it D A teammate saying the design is probably strong enough E A list of the materials used to build the base and support Reveal the best evidence pair Best support: A + C A shows design intent and the support locations. C provides direct performance evidence against a safety and stability criterion. Photos, material lists, and teammate opinions can support the story, but they do not prove the claim by themselves. Scenario Response What Should the Engineer Do Next? Choose the strongest next step and explain your reasoning. A team builds a small rocket support. During the first test, it stands up, but the rocket leans to one side. A Keep it because the prototype did not fall over. B Add decorations so the design looks more complete. C Record the lean, identify where the support is uneven, revise, and retest. D Start over without writing down what happened. Reveal the strongest next step Best answer: C Record the lean, identify where the support is uneven, revise, and retest. Record Write down what happened during the test. Identify Find the likely cause of the lean. Revise + Retest Change the design and collect new evidence. Engineering move: Use the problem as evidence, not as a reason to hide or restart the work. Quick Check Evidence or Opinion? Vote on all three statements before revealing the answers. A. “Our design is the best because it looks strong.” B. “Version 2 traveled 12 ft farther than Version 1 in the official test.” C. “We changed the wing fold because the first test curved left three times.” Reveal the evidence check A Opinion-heavy Uses a vague judgment: “looks strong.” B Evidence-based Uses a measurable result: 12 ft farther. C Evidence-based reasoning Connects a change to repeated test observations. Takeaway: Claim + specific evidence = stronger engineering communication. Mission Debrief Exit Ticket Show that you understand the mindset before moving into notebook setup. Engineering Mindset Exit Ticket One response explaining how engineering problems differ from typical assignments and naming one form of design evidence. Next Mission Lesson 0.2 Engineering Notebook Setup & Course Resources Set up the binder-based engineering notebook and verify access to the digital tools used throughout the course. items.title: Safety Acknowledgment, PPE & FabLab Orientation
items.description: A Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on safety acknowledgment, ppe & fablab orientation.
items.searchText: IED Lesson 0.3: Safety Acknowledgment, PPE & FabLab Orientation | LockwoodSTEM IED Lesson 0.3: Safety Acknowledgment, PPE & FabLab Orientation | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.3 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.3 Safety Acknowledgment, PPE & FabLab Orientation Focus Question: How do safe habits make engineering work possible? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Protect people and the workspace Recognize the behaviors, PPE, and permission systems required before using tools, machines, and materials. Notice Protect Report Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Connect safe behavior to engineering quality, shared responsibility, and permission to use equipment. Learning Targets Identify major safety expectations for the engineering classroom and FabLab. Explain PPE and safe behavior expectations around tools and materials. Understand the signed acknowledgment requirement before tool use. Success Looks Like… You can recognize an unsafe condition, stop, and explain the correct next action. Core habit: When something seems unsafe, stop immediately and ask before continuing. Opening prompt Why safety matters PPE + behavior FabLab orientation Scenario vote Acknowledgment Debrief Opening Prompt What can go wrong before a tool is even turned on? Safety begins with awareness, preparation, and behavior—not only with emergency response. Quick class share: Identify one unsafe condition that could affect a person, a tool, a material, or the quality of a project. Reveal the engineering connection Safety is an engineering requirement. Unsafe behavior can injure people, damage equipment, waste materials, and make test results unreliable. Professional Workspace Safety protects more than people Technical spaces use controlled procedures because quality and safety are connected. Professional technical spaces depend on controlled behavior, clear procedures, and attention to the work area. Image: NASA Glenn Research Center, public domain via Wikimedia Commons Non-Negotiables Know the baseline expectations These expectations apply before activity-specific tool rules are introduced. PPE Prepare yourself Wear safety glasses when directed or required. Wear closed-toe shoes for fabrication activities. Tie back long hair. Secure loose clothing and dangling jewelry. Use gloves only when appropriate and directed. Behavior Protect the workspace No horseplay, rushing, or distracting others. Use tools and materials only with permission. Keep work areas and walkways clear. Respect active build zones. Report damage, injuries, and unsafe conditions immediately. Scenario Vote What should happen first? Vote before opening the answer. A student notices that a cutting tool has a loose handle, but the class is already behind schedule. A Use it carefully and tell the teacher later. B Ask a teammate to test it first. C Stop, keep others from using it, and report it immediately. D Put it back without saying anything. Reveal the safest response Best answer: C Stop, prevent use, and report the condition. Schedule pressure never overrides safety. Stop Do not continue with unsafe equipment. Protect Keep others away from the hazard. Report Tell the teacher immediately. Access Requirement Signed acknowledgment comes before tool use Orientation does not replace individual equipment certifications. 1 Review Student and parent/guardian review classroom and FabLab expectations. 2 Return Submit the signed paper acknowledgment as a graded completion item. 3 Certify Complete separate tool certifications before operating specific equipment. Until the acknowledgment is returned: you may participate in class, but you may not use FabLab tools or machines. Mission Debrief What You Submit Complete the safety-readiness requirement before future fabrication work. Safety Acknowledgment The completed safety acknowledgment with required student and parent/guardian signatures. items.title: Launch Pad Prototype Build Day
items.description: A Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on launch pad prototype build day.
items.searchText: IED Lesson 0.9: Launch Pad Prototype Build Day | LockwoodSTEM IED Lesson 0.9: Launch Pad Prototype Build Day | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.9 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.9 Launch Pad Prototype Build Day Focus Question: How do teams turn a design plan into a physical prototype? View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Build function first Construct from the approved plan, check fit and stability during the build, and document changes as they happen. Build Check Document Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use most of the period for careful construction, with required checkpoints and evidence capture. Design Brief Rocket Launch Pad Design Challenge Brief Review the challenge background, problem statement, criteria, constraints, required evidence, and evaluation expectations for the launch pad project. Download DOCX Learning Targets Build a first prototype from the approved plan. Check rocket fit and stability during construction. Document changes, problems, and solutions as they happen. Success Looks Like… The prototype stands on its own, supports the rocket, and includes a clear record of changes made during construction. Core habit: Pause and document when the physical build differs from the plan. Safety launch Plan check Prototype build Fit + stability Document changes Cleanup Exit Opening Prompt What should be built first? Build order affects stability, access, fit, and the amount of rework required later. Quick class share: Why might decoration be a poor first priority for a prototype? Reveal the build priority Build function before decoration. Establish the base, support the rocket, and verify fit before adding research-informed details. Aerospace Build Context Complex systems are assembled in planned stages Use the photo to notice temporary supports, work access, alignment, and controlled work zones. Large aerospace systems are assembled in deliberate sequences, with access, support, alignment, and documentation considered throughout the build. Image: NASA Kennedy Space Center, public domain via Wikimedia Commons Build Priorities Base → support → features Do not advance to the next layer until the current one performs its job. 1 Base First The launch pad must stand on its own. → 2 Support Next The rocket must sit securely without tipping or collapsing. → 3 Features Last Add realistic details after the main structure works. Build Day Protocol Construct carefully and document changes The plan guides the work, but the notebook records what actually happened. During construction Gather only approved materials. Compare the build to the plan regularly. Pause for fit and stability checks. Do not force parts or ignore unsafe conditions. Keep the work area organized. Evidence to capture Photo or sketch of work in progress Materials actually used Changes from the plan One problem encountered How the team solved or plans to solve it Scenario Response The support bends during a fit check Choose the strongest next step before opening the answer. A Ignore it until the final test. B Add decoration to hide the weak area. C Pause, record the problem, reinforce the support, and document the change. D Force the rocket into place. Reveal the engineering response Best answer: C Continuing would create unreliable evidence and could damage the prototype. Pause, document, revise, and check the result. Mid-Build Checkpoint Stop before the final minutes A quick checkpoint prevents a finished-looking prototype that cannot perform. 1 The base stands on its own. 2 The rocket fits without being forced. 3 Main supports do not bend or collapse. 4 Changes from the plan are recorded. 5 The team has time for cleanup and evidence capture. Mission Debrief What You Submit Document the prototype as it exists at the end of build day. Prototype Build Record One progress photo or labeled sketch with a brief note describing a build change or unresolved problem. items.title: Redesign the Rocket Launch Pad
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Redesign the Rocket Launch Pad IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.1 Redesign the Rocket Launch Pad Redesign the launch pad to use less material while maintaining stability, rocket fit, and safe classroom handling. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Your original launch pad proved that a free-standing structure can support the classroom rocket. A launch systems team now wants a lighter, easier-to-build version that still protects and supports the vehicle. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply criteria and constraints to a redesign Generate and compare multiple concepts Collect stability test evidence Justify a final design using data Materials What You Need Original launch pad or drawings Provided 3D printed rocket Approved classroom build materials Ruler or tape measure Scale if available Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the original design and list three specific weaknesses. Measure and record the original mass, footprint, and rocket contact points. Create two new annotated concept sketches. Each concept must show how the rocket is supported. Use a decision matrix with at least four criteria to select a concept. Build the selected concept using fewer materials than the original. Test the pad on a level surface and on a 5-degree inclined surface. Place the rocket on the pad and perform three gentle disturbance tests from different directions. Record results, revise one feature, and repeat the test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Support the provided rocket without assistance Stand on its own for at least 60 seconds Remain upright during three disturbance tests Use at least 20% less material by mass or measured quantity Include at least one research-informed launch pad feature Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved classroom materials No adhesives or fasteners may contact the rocket body Must fit within a 30 cm by 30 cm footprint Must be completed within two class periods Deliverables What You Submit Problem statement and criteria/constraints Two annotated concept sketches Decision matrix Before-and-after material comparison Test table with at least six trials Photo of final prototype One-paragraph design justification Reflection Reflection Questions Which criterion had the greatest influence on your final design? What failed or moved during testing? What tradeoff did you make between mass and stability? What would you test next if the pad were used outdoors? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Move material away from low-stress areas and keep support members near the rocket contact points. Common Mistake Reducing material everywhere usually weakens the base. Remove material strategically instead of simply making every part smaller. Stretch Goal Reduce material use by 35% while keeping the same test performance. Career Connection Aerospace ground-support engineers design stands, fixtures, and launch equipment that protect vehicles before flight. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.title: Emergency Communications Tower
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 0 Emergency Communications Tower IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.3 Emergency Communications Tower Build the tallest free-standing paper tower that supports a 200 g payload for 30 seconds. Intermediate 45 minutes Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context After a hurricane, a temporary communications antenna must be raised above nearby debris. The emergency team has limited materials and needs a structure that is tall, stable, and quick to deploy. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply structural design principles Plan within strict material limits Test and improve a prototype Use measurements to compare performance Materials What You Need 20 index cards 30 cm masking tape Scissors Ruler or tape measure 200 g test mass Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Study the materials without building for two minutes. Sketch one tower concept and label the base, vertical supports, and payload platform. Predict the tower height and identify the most likely failure point. Build for 15 minutes using only the issued materials. Measure the height before adding the payload. Place the 200 g mass on the top platform for 30 seconds. If the tower fails, document the failure location and make one repair using remaining material. Retest and calculate a performance score: successful height in centimeters divided by grams of material used. Requirements Engineering Requirements Stand without being attached to the table or floor Support 200 g for 30 seconds Use no more than 20 cards and 30 cm of tape Include a platform that prevents the payload from sliding Provide a measured final height Constraints Constraints & Safety 15-minute initial build time No glue, staples, string, or added materials Payload must be placed by hand without holding the tower Height is measured from table surface to top of payload Deliverables What You Submit Initial sketch and height prediction Photo before testing Measured height and material use Failure observation or success evidence Performance score calculation Three-sentence redesign recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions How did the base width affect stability? Where did compression or bending appear? Which material use produced the most strength? What would you change with five additional cards? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Folded card sections resist bending better than flat cards. Test triangular, tubular, and layered shapes. Common Mistake A very tall narrow tower may score well before testing but fail under the payload. Stability is part of performance. Stretch Goal Rebuild with only 12 cards and attempt to achieve at least 80% of your original height. Career Connection Structural and civil engineers design temporary towers, supports, and deployable structures for emergencies and field operations. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.searchText: IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.10 | Patterns and Symmetry: Rocket Fins | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.10 | Patterns and Symmetry: Rocket Fins | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.10 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.10 Patterns and Symmetry: Rocket Fins Focus question: How can patterns create repeated features accurately? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive Video Help What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Focus Repeated features are evenly spaced and controlled by a pattern rather than rebuilt one at a time. Pattern Mirror Verify Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: All fins are equally spaced, aligned, and generated from one controlled source feature. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Create an Accurate Fin Pattern. Learning Targets Use patterns to repeat features accurately. Explain why symmetry matters in aerospace parts. Check count, spacing, and alignment. Success Looks Like Repeated features are evenly spaced and controlled by a pattern rather than rebuilt one at a time. Launch Learn Model Check Submit Opening Prompt Why should rocket fins be patterned instead of copied by hand? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Create an Accurate Fin Pattern. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move A pattern controls spacing and alignment consistently. Manual copies are easier to misplace or make uneven. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Patterns create consistent repeated features. Key Idea 2 Symmetry improves alignment and reduces modeling errors. Key Idea 3 Rocket fins must be evenly placed for balanced design. Fusion & Fabrication Help Video Help Fusion 360 Circular Patterns - The Right Way to Automate Your Designs Review how circular patterns repeat a feature around an axis and how pattern choices affect design intent. Open on YouTube Pause, replay, or open the tutorial in a new tab while you work. Follow the lesson requirements when the video uses a different example. Lesson Interactive Build an Equal Rocket-Fin Pattern Choose the fin count and pattern axis, then verify the angular spacing around the rocket body. Pattern Preview Number of fins Equal angular spacing 120° Pattern axis Choose Rocket body center axis Source-fin edge Global X axis Check Pattern Create four fins from one source feature around the central rocket axis. Your Task Create an Accurate Fin Pattern Use symmetry or a circular pattern to repeat one fin at equal spacing around the rocket body. Model or identify one correctly positioned source fin. Select the rocket axis as the pattern axis. Set the required number of repeated fins. Inspect spacing and orientation from the top and isometric views. Quality check: All fins are equally spaced, aligned, and generated from one controlled source feature. What You Will Submit Rocket Fin Pattern A saved model showing the completed repeated fin arrangement. A screenshot from a view that clearly proves equal spacing. Submission standard: All fins are equally spaced, aligned, and generated from one controlled source feature. Sketch Extrude Inspect Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The solid has the intended footprint and thickness, with no unintended extra bodies or open profiles. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Turn a Closed Sketch into a Solid. Learning Targets Identify a closed sketch profile. Use extrusion to create a 3D solid. Check extrusion distance and direction. Success Looks Like Your 2D sketch becomes a clean 3D feature with intentional depth. Launch Learn Model Check Submit Opening Prompt Why does an extrusion need a closed profile? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Turn a Closed Sketch into a Solid. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move A closed profile gives Fusion a clear region to turn into a solid feature. Open geometry usually cannot form a clean solid extrusion. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Extrude adds depth to a closed profile. Key Idea 2 Extrude distance controls thickness, length, or height. Extrusion Preview Distance: 8 mm Direction Choose Positive Symmetric Negative Operation Choose New body Join Cut Check Extrusion Create a 12 mm positive extrusion as a new body. Your Task Turn a Closed Sketch into a Solid Use an extrusion to create the first solid body while keeping the source sketch and feature history understandable. Confirm the profile is closed and selected correctly. Choose the correct extrusion direction and distance. Create a new solid body. Inspect the body from multiple views and rename the feature if required. Quality check: The solid has the intended footprint and thickness, with no unintended extra bodies or open profiles.
