items.title: Fillets, Chamfers, and Design Intent
items.description: IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.8: Fillets, Chamfers, and Design Intent. How do edge features improve function, safety, and printability?
items.searchText: IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.8 | Fillets, Chamfers, and Design Intent | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.8 | Fillets, Chamfers, and Design Intent | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.8 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.8 Fillets, Chamfers, and Design Intent Focus question: How do edge features improve function, safety, and printability? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive Video Help What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Focus Your edge features have a reason beyond appearance. Smooth Bevel Print Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: Each edge treatment has a stated design reason and does not remove a critical feature. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Refine Edges with Fillets and Chamfers. Learning Targets Distinguish between fillets and chamfers. Apply edge features intentionally. Explain how edge treatment affects function or manufacturing. Success Looks Like Your edge features have a reason beyond appearance. Launch Learn Model Check Submit Opening Prompt When might rounding an edge make a part worse instead of better? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Refine Edges with Fillets and Chamfers. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move If the edge controls fit, alignment, or contact with another part, changing it without a reason can reduce accuracy or function. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Fillets and chamfers can improve safety, strength, fit, and printability. Key Idea 2 Edge treatment should support the function, not just appearance. Key Idea 3 Design intent explains why a feature exists. Fusion & Fabrication Help Video Help Introduction to Fusion 360: Fillet and Chamfer Tool Basics Review when to round an edge with a fillet and when to bevel an edge with a chamfer. Open on YouTube Pause, replay, or open the tutorial in a new tab while you work. Follow the lesson requirements when the video uses a different example. Lesson Interactive Select Edge Treatments by Function Decide whether each edge should receive a fillet, chamfer, or no treatment based on safety, assembly, and inspection needs. Design Scenarios Hand-contact edge you will handle this edge repeatedly. Assembly lead-in A shaft must enter a printed opening without catching. Inspection datum A caliper must reference a precise flat edge. Hand-contact edge Choose Fillet Chamfer No treatment Assembly lead-in Choose Fillet Chamfer No treatment Inspection datum Choose Fillet Chamfer No treatment Check Design Intent Use edge features intentionally; not every sharp edge should be modified. Your Task Refine Edges with Fillets and Chamfers Apply edge treatments only where they improve safety, function, assembly, or printability. Identify one edge that benefits from rounding and one that benefits from a bevel, when appropriate. Apply a fillet or chamfer using an intentional value. Inspect nearby dimensions and faces after the feature is added. Compare the refined model with the unmodified edge condition. Quality check: Each edge treatment has a stated design reason and does not remove a critical feature. What You Will Submit Edge Treatment Evidence A screenshot showing the completed edge feature. A one-sentence justification for the selected fillet or chamfer. Submission standard: Each edge treatment has a stated design reason and does not remove a critical feature. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 2 Design for 3D Printing IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.4 Design for 3D Printing Redesign the part to improve printability while preserving its function. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A part was designed in CAD without considering how it would be printed. It requires excessive supports, wastes material, and takes too long. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize common additive manufacturing limitations Modify geometry for reduced supports Compare slicer estimates Justify design-for-manufacturing decisions Materials What You Need Teacher-provided CAD part Fusion 360 Slicer software Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Import or open the baseline part. Write the part’s intended function and identify features that must not change. Slice the baseline in the most reasonable orientation and record print time, material, and support amount. Identify at least three printability problems. Create two redesign sketches and select one. Modify overhangs, holes, wall thickness, orientation surfaces, or part segmentation. Slice the redesign using the same printer and comparable settings. Compare estimates and check that all functional dimensions remain correct. Requirements Engineering Requirements Reduce support material by at least 50% or eliminate supports Reduce print time or material use by at least 15% Preserve specified functional dimensions Maintain minimum printable wall thickness Document all slicer settings used for comparison Constraints Constraints & Safety Use the same printer profile and layer height for baseline and redesign Do not remove functional features No print is required unless approved Use classroom-safe geometry and scale Deliverables What You Submit Baseline slicer screenshot and estimates Three identified printability problems Two redesign sketches Revised CAD file Final slicer screenshot Before/after comparison table Design explanation Reflection Reflection Questions Which geometry caused the most support? What change produced the largest improvement? Did reducing print time create a new tradeoff? How would injection molding change the design rules? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Before changing the part, rotate it in the slicer. Sometimes orientation solves more than redesign. Common Mistake Comparisons are invalid if the baseline and redesign use different layer heights or infill settings without explanation. Stretch Goal Create a two-part version that prints even faster and compare assembly complexity. Career Connection Additive manufacturing engineers adjust geometry, orientation, supports, and process settings to improve quality and cost. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive Video Help What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Focus Your finished print is inspected and documented before fit data are trusted. Inspect Finish Record Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The tester is safe to handle and the evaluated surfaces have not been altered in a way that invalidates the test. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Inspect and Finish the Printed Tester. Learning Targets Identify common post-processing needs. Explain how cleanup can affect dimensions and fit. Document inspection and post-processing steps. Success Looks Like Your finished print is inspected and documented before fit data are trusted. Launch Learn Model Check Submit Opening Prompt Why might a print not be “done” when it comes off the printer? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Inspect and Finish the Printed Tester. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move Supports, brim, stringing, rough edges, or dimensional issues may need careful cleanup and inspection before the part can be used as evidence. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Supports, brim, stringing, and rough edges can affect the final part. Key Idea 2 Post-processing can change dimensions and fit. Key Idea 3 Cleanup should be documented as part of fabrication. Fusion & Fabrication Help Video Help These Tools Make 3D Print Cleanup Easy Use this video to review support removal and cleanup tools before handling or finishing printed parts. Open on YouTube Pause, replay, or open the tutorial in a new tab while you work. Follow the lesson requirements when the video uses a different example. Lesson Interactive Protect the Fit Evidence During Cleanup Choose the correct action for each condition so the tester becomes safe to handle without changing the surfaces being evaluated. Inspection Findings Support tab Sacrificial support remains under an overhang. Loose stringing Thin strands connect two outside edges. Fit slot surface Surface is rough but is the feature being tested. Warped corner One corner lifted 1.2 mm from the plate. Support tab Choose Remove carefully Leave attached Sand all fit surfaces Loose stringing Choose Trim loose strands Ignore all loose material Melt the part surface Fit slot surface Choose Leave unchanged for valid testing Sand until the mating part fits Enlarge with a drill Warped corner Choose Document as a test limitation Bend it flat by hand Do not report it Check Cleanup Plan Remove only sacrificial or loose material; do not tune the measured fit surfaces. Your Task Inspect and Finish the Printed Tester Remove supports or surface artifacts carefully, then inspect the tester without changing the fit features being evaluated. Photograph or inspect the part before cleanup. Remove only the required supports, brim, or loose material. Check for warping, layer separation, or damaged test features. Record any cleanup that could influence the fit results. Quality check: The tester is safe to handle and the evaluated surfaces have not been altered in a way that invalidates the test. What You Will Submit Post-Processing Record One inspection photo with any defects or cleanup areas identified. A short cleanup note stating whether the fit surfaces remained valid. Submission standard: The tester is safe to handle and the evaluated surfaces have not been altered in a way that invalidates the test. items.title: Lightweight Bracket Redesign
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lightweight Bracket Redesign IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.3 Lightweight Bracket Redesign Redesign an Teacher-provided bracket to reduce modeled mass by at least 20% while preserving interfaces and basic load capability. Advanced 2-3 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context An aerospace bracket meets the required shape but is heavier than necessary. Every gram matters in flight hardware. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply design-for-lightweighting strategies Use CAD mass properties Preserve functional interfaces Document design tradeoffs Materials What You Need Starter bracket file or drawing Fusion 360 Material property assignment Engineering notebook Optional 3D printer Procedure Instructions Open the baseline bracket and record material, mass, envelope dimensions, and interface locations. Highlight no-change zones such as mounting holes and contact surfaces. Sketch two lightweighting concepts using ribs, pockets, tapered walls, or pattern changes. Select one concept and predict the mass reduction. Create the redesigned model using parameters. Assign the same material and measure final mass. Inspect minimum wall thickness, sharp internal corners, and print orientation. Create a before/after comparison and explain how load could travel through the redesigned part. Requirements Engineering Requirements Reduce modeled mass by at least 20% Preserve all mounting hole locations and interface dimensions Maintain minimum 2 mm wall thickness unless approved Avoid unsupported features that make printing impractical Use at least one rib or load-path feature Constraints Constraints & Safety Use the same assigned material for both mass calculations Do not simply scale the entire part Part must remain printable on classroom equipment No formal claim of structural safety without testing or analysis Deliverables What You Submit Two concept sketches Baseline and final mass-property screenshots Fusion file Before/after visual comparison Manufacturability check Design justification Reflection Reflection Questions Where did you remove the most material? How did you preserve the load path? What new failure risk did the redesign create? What physical test would you perform next? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Keep material along likely load paths and remove it from large low-stress areas. Common Mistake Cutting random holes may reduce mass but can create stress concentrations and weak connections. Stretch Goal Print both versions and compare mass, print time, and a simple non-destructive stiffness test. Career Connection Aerospace mechanical engineers use topology, ribs, pockets, and material selection to reduce mass while maintaining function. Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive Video Help What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Focus Your final recommendation names a clearance and supports it with fit data or observations. Review Recommend Reflect Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The recommendation cites specific tester results and acknowledges any limitation that could affect the conclusion. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Recommend a Rocket Assembly Clearance. Learning Targets Collect fit evidence from the tolerance tester. Compare tight, loose, and acceptable fits. Write a recommendation supported by evidence. Success Looks Like Your final recommendation names a clearance and supports it with fit data or observations. Launch Learn Model Check Submit Opening Prompt What makes a clearance recommendation stronger than a personal preference? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Recommend a Rocket Assembly Clearance. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move A strong recommendation uses repeated fit tests, measurements, photos, and observations to justify which clearance should be used next. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 A recommendation should be based on fit evidence. Key Idea 2 Testing should identify too tight, too loose, and acceptable fits. Key Idea 3 The final conclusion connects Unit 2 to the rocket assembly unit. Fusion & Fabrication Help Video Help How to Design a Print with Perfect Tolerance Every Time Use this tutorial to compare printed evidence with intended clearances and support a final tolerance recommendation. Open on YouTube Pause, replay, or open the tutorial in a new tab while you work. Follow the lesson requirements when the video uses a different example. Lesson Interactive Recommend a Rocket Assembly Clearance Use the simulated fit results to choose a secure clearance that can still be removed by hand, then cite the matching evidence. Tester Results Clearance Observed fit 0.10 mm Will not assemble 0.20 mm Assembles only with high force 0.30 mm Usable snug fit; removable by hand 0.40 mm Free sliding fit 0.50 mm Loose with visible movement 0.60 mm Too loose for alignment Target: secure, aligned, and removable by hand 0.20 mm 0.30 mm 0.40 mm Evidence result to cite Choose High-force assembly Usable snug fit, removable by hand Free sliding fit Check Recommendation Match the recommendation to the stated assembly goal, not simply the loosest fit that works. Your Task Recommend a Rocket Assembly Clearance Use the printed tolerance tester to compare fit conditions and recommend a clearance for the next rocket assembly project. Test each labeled fit condition using the same method. Record whether each fit is too tight, usable, loose, or inconsistent. Compare the results with printing defects or cleanup notes. Write one recommended clearance and support it with the strongest evidence. Quality check: The recommendation cites specific tester results and acknowledges any limitation that could affect the conclusion. What You Will Submit Tolerance Recommendation A completed fit-results table or annotated photo. A one-paragraph clearance recommendation for Unit 3. items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 2 Thirty-Minute CAD Sprint IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.2 Thirty-Minute CAD Sprint Model a randomly assigned object accurately within 30 minutes, then evaluate which modeling choices improved speed and quality. Intermediate 30 minutes plus review Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Rapid CAD work is useful when engineers need a concept model for a meeting or prototype decision. Objectives What You Will Practice Plan an efficient feature sequence Use constraints and parameters quickly Prioritize critical geometry Review CAD quality under time pressure Materials What You Need Fusion 360 One approved object or dimension card Calipers or ruler Timer Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Draw or receive an object such as a LEGO-style brick, die, battery spacer, USB shell, or simple bracket. Spend three minutes identifying the base feature, repeated features, symmetry, and likely parameters. Record a short modeling plan before opening a sketch. Model for 25 minutes. Use the final two minutes to rename features, check constraints, and inspect dimensions. Export one screenshot showing the browser and completed model. Compare the model with the object or dimension card. Record one shortcut that helped and one rushed decision that caused rework. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use at least one named parameter Keep all major sketches fully constrained Include every critical feature Use patterns or symmetry where appropriate Finish within 30 minutes Constraints Constraints & Safety No imported models No help from another student during the timed period Accuracy is more important than decorative details Object must be teacher-approved Deliverables What You Submit Modeling plan Fusion file Final screenshot Accuracy checklist Short time-management reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which feature should have been created first? Where did you lose the most time? Did a pattern or parameter improve speed? What would you change in a second attempt? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Spend a few minutes planning. A strong feature order saves more time than sketching immediately. Common Mistake Fast modeling is not the same as careless modeling. Unconstrained sketches create hidden problems later. Stretch Goal Remodel the same object in 20 minutes using lessons from the first attempt. Career Connection CAD designers frequently create rapid concept models before detailed engineering work begins. Profile Revolve Inspect Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The revolved body is continuous and matches the intended axial shape. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Model a Rotational Rocket Feature. Learning Targets Sketch a profile for a revolved feature. Use an axis or centerline correctly. Connect revolve features to aerospace parts. Success Looks Like Your revolved model is built from a clear profile and axis. Launch Learn Model Check Submit Opening Prompt Why is a nose cone a good example of a revolve feature? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Model a Rotational Rocket Feature. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move A nose cone is rotationally symmetric. A 2D side profile can rotate around a centerline to form the full 3D part. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Revolve creates circular parts from a profile and axis. Key Idea 2 Profiles must be planned around the centerline. Key Idea 3 Nose cones and nozzles are natural revolve examples. Fusion & Fabrication Help Video Help Fusion 360 Revolve Tool Tutorial Use this tutorial to review profiles, axes, revolve angles, and the common errors that prevent a revolve. Open on YouTube Pause, replay, or open the tutorial in a new tab while you work. Follow the lesson requirements when the video uses a different example. Lesson Interactive Configure a Revolved Nose Cone Set up the profile, axis, and rotation needed to create a continuous axisymmetric rocket part. Half-Profile and Axis Axis of rotation Choose Centerline Outer profile edge Base edge Profile status Choose Closed profile Open profile Rotation angle: 180° Check Revolve A solid nose cone requires a closed half-profile rotated fully around the centerline. Your Task Model a Rotational Rocket Feature Create a nose cone or nozzle form by revolving a half-profile around a center axis. Sketch a clean half-profile of the rotational shape. Create or select the intended axis of rotation. Revolve the profile through the required angle. Inspect the resulting solid for gaps, self-intersections, or an incorrect axis. Quality check: The revolved body is continuous and matches the intended axial shape. What You Will Submit Revolved Rocket Part The saved revolved part model. One screenshot showing the profile and axis used to create it. Submission standard: The revolved body is continuous and matches the intended axial shape. items.description: IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.11: Parametric Rocket Part Modeling. How can parameters make a model easier to revise?

Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive Video Help What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Focus A design change can be made by editing a value instead of rebuilding the model. Parameterize Revise Update Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The selected value changes the intended geometry without breaking unrelated features. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Make a Rocket Part Parametric. Learning Targets Identify values that should become parameters. Use editable dimensions to control a model. Test whether the model updates predictably. Success Looks Like A design change can be made by editing a value instead of rebuilding the model. Launch Learn Model Check Submit Opening Prompt Which dimensions in a rocket part might need to change later? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Make a Rocket Part Parametric. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move Diameter, wall thickness, fin spacing, hole size, clearance, and overall length are likely to change as fit or performance requirements evolve. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Parameters allow key values to update the model. Key Idea 2 A parametric model is easier to revise than a fixed model. Key Idea 3 Useful parameters connect to real design requirements. Fusion & Fabrication Help Video Help Fusion 360 for Beginners - Parametric Modeling Tutorial Use this tutorial to connect dimensions, constraints, features, and parameters into an editable model. Open on YouTube Pause, replay, or open the tutorial in a new tab while you work. Follow the lesson requirements when the video uses a different example. Lesson Interactive Test a Parametric Wall Relationship Change the body diameter and wall thickness while keeping the inner opening driven by a meaningful expression. Editable Design Values Body diameter Wall thickness Outer diameter Driven Wall Driven Inner diameter 38.0 mm How should inner diameter be controlled? Choose bodyDiameter − 2 × wallThickness Fixed independent number Drag until it looks correct A useful parametric model stores design intent in relationships, not just isolated numbers. Check Parameter Logic Keep the inner opening between 25 and 40 mm while using the correct expression. Your Task Make a Rocket Part Parametric Identify important design values and make at least one of them easy to revise without rebuilding the model. Select a dimension that controls a meaningful feature. Give the value a clear parameter or dimension role. Change the value to test how the model updates. Restore or set the final required value and inspect downstream features. Quality check: The selected value changes the intended geometry without breaking unrelated features. What You Will Submit Parametric Revision Test The saved model with at least one clearly identifiable editable design value. Before-and-after screenshots or a short note documenting the revision test. Submission standard: The selected value changes the intended geometry without breaking unrelated features. items.title: 3D Print Failure Detective
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 2 3D Print Failure Detective IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.5 3D Print Failure Detective Inspect failed prints, identify likely causes, and recommend a controlled correction for each failure. Beginner 45-60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A print farm has produced several failed parts. Before changing settings, the team needs evidence-based diagnoses. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize common print defects Use physical evidence to diagnose causes Separate printer, material, model, and setup issues Plan controlled troubleshooting tests Materials What You Need Set of failed prints or failure photographs Magnifier Ruler or calipers Failure inspection sheet Slicer access Procedure Instructions Number each failed sample and photograph it from two angles. Describe only visible evidence before naming a cause. Classify the failure as adhesion, extrusion, temperature, support, geometry, layer shift, stringing, or another category. Identify the most likely cause and one alternative cause. Locate the slicer or printer setting connected to the likely cause. Recommend one controlled change; do not change multiple variables at once. Rank the samples from easiest to hardest to correct. Choose one sample and outline a three-print troubleshooting sequence. Requirements Engineering Requirements Analyze at least four samples Include visible evidence for every diagnosis Provide one likely and one alternative cause Recommend only one primary change per test Use correct printing vocabulary Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not operate or service a printer unless authorized Do not touch hot components Do not claim certainty when evidence is incomplete Deliverables What You Submit Failure inspection sheets Annotated photographs or sketches Cause/evidence/correction table Ranked correction list Three-print troubleshooting plan Reflection Reflection Questions Which failure had the clearest evidence? Which diagnosis was most uncertain? Why should only one variable change at a time? What information from the original print job would improve your diagnosis? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Describe the defect before diagnosing it. “The first layer detached at one corner” is stronger evidence than “bad adhesion.” Common Mistake Changing temperature, speed, bed level, and material at once may fix the print but prevents you from learning the cause. Stretch Goal Slice a small test coupon that isolates the suspected problem and predict the result. Career Connection Additive manufacturing technicians and quality engineers diagnose defects using visual evidence, process data, and controlled testing. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.title: CAD Model Check and Revision
items.description: IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.12: CAD Model Check and Revision. How do engineers check a model before fabrication?
items.searchText: IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.12 | CAD Model Check and Revision | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.12 | CAD Model Check and Revision | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.12 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.12 CAD Model Check and Revision Focus question: How do engineers check a model before fabrication? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive Video Help What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Focus Your model is checked before it becomes a printed mistake. Check Revise Explain Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The model is organized, matches the requirements, and contains no known geometry errors. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Complete a CAD Model Quality Review. Learning Targets Check model size, units, features, and printability. Compare CAD evidence to design intent. Document at least one revision or confirmation. Success Looks Like Your model is checked before it becomes a printed mistake. Launch Learn Model Check Submit Opening Prompt Why is checking a CAD model before printing usually faster than fixing a bad print? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Complete a CAD Model Quality Review. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move CAD changes are usually faster and cheaper than wasting print time, material, and queue space on a part with avoidable errors. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 CAD review prevents printing the wrong part. Key Idea 2 Models should be checked for size, units, features, and printability. Key Idea 3 Revision is normal engineering work. Fusion & Fabrication Help Video Help Analyze and Validate Your Design | Getting Started with Autodesk Fusion Review inspection tools and model-validation habits before completing the CAD quality check. Open on YouTube Pause, replay, or open the tutorial in a new tab while you work. Follow the lesson requirements when the video uses a different example. Lesson Interactive Audit a CAD Model Before Export Select every issue that should be corrected before the model moves into the fabrication workflow. Model Browser and Timeline Evidence Body1 Primary part body still uses the default name. Body2 Small accidental body remains outside the intended part. Fillet3 ⚠ Timeline feature reports a failed reference. Overall width: 79.2 mm Requirement specifies 80.0 mm. Issues that require correction Default body name Unintended extra body Failed timeline feature Critical dimension mismatch Timeline contains many valid features Model is currently shown isometrically Complete Audit Select problems that affect organization, geometry, or requirements. Your Task Complete a CAD Model Quality Review Inspect the completed model for geometry, feature order, naming, dimensions, and fabrication readiness before export. Review the model from standard and isometric views. Check the browser and timeline for extra bodies, failed features, or unclear organization. Verify critical dimensions against the assignment requirements. Correct and document at least one issue or confirm the model passed each check. Quality check: The model is organized, matches the requirements, and contains no known geometry errors. What You Will Submit CAD Review Record A completed model-review checklist. A final screenshot showing the corrected model. Submission standard: The model is organized, matches the requirements, and contains no known geometry errors. items.title: Sketch Constraints
items.description: IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.4: Sketch Constraints. How do constraints control design intent?
items.searchText: IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.4 | Sketch Constraints | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.4 | Sketch Constraints | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.4 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.4 Sketch Constraints Focus question: How do constraints control design intent? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive Video Help What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Focus Your sketch changes in a controlled way when dimensions are edited. Constrain Control Revise Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The sketch maintains its intended relationships during a drag test without unnecessary or conflicting constraints. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Control a Sketch with Constraints. Learning Targets Apply common sketch constraints. Explain how constraints control sketch behavior. Check whether a sketch changes predictably. Success Looks Like Your sketch changes in a controlled way when dimensions are edited. Launch Learn Model Check Submit Opening Prompt Why is a sketch that “looks right” not always good enough? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Control a Sketch with Constraints. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move A sketch can look correct but still be under-controlled. Constraints make relationships intentional so the sketch behaves predictably during revisions. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Constraints describe relationships between sketch entities. Key Idea 2 A fully defined sketch behaves predictably. Key Idea 3 Uncontrolled sketches can shift unexpectedly. Fusion & Fabrication Help Video Help Fusion 360: Sketch Constraints Review how geometric constraints control sketch behavior and help create stable, fully constrained profiles. Open on YouTube Pause, replay, or open the tutorial in a new tab while you work. Follow the lesson requirements when the video uses a different example. Lesson Interactive Constrain the Slot Sketch Select the geometric constraints needed to keep the slot square, connected, and symmetric without adding a redundant relationship. Sketch to Control Drag test should preserve shape Constraints to apply Horizontal top and bottom edges Vertical side edges Coincident corner endpoints Equal side lengths Parallel top and bottom after horizontal constraints Check Constraints Choose only the relationships that control the intended geometry without redundancy. Your Task Control a Sketch with Constraints Add geometric relationships so the sketch keeps its intended shape when geometry is moved or edited. Identify lines or points that should remain horizontal, vertical, connected, parallel, or equal. Apply only the constraints needed to communicate those relationships. Drag-test the sketch to find uncontrolled geometry. Correct conflicts or missing relationships and save the sketch. Quality check: The sketch maintains its intended relationships during a drag test without unnecessary or conflicting constraints. What You Will Submit Constraint Check A screenshot of the constrained sketch with constraint symbols visible. A brief note identifying one constraint that protects the design intent. Submission standard: The sketch maintains its intended relationships during a drag test without unnecessary or conflicting constraints. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 2 Reverse Engineer a Tape Measure Hook IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.1 Reverse Engineer a Tape Measure Hook Measure and model a tape measure hook as a fully constrained, parametric CAD part. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A maintenance department needs a replacement tape hook, but the supplier no longer provides the part file. Objectives What You Will Practice Use calipers to collect part dimensions Create fully constrained sketches Build a parametric model Compare CAD geometry to a physical part Materials What You Need Tape measure hook or similar flat metal part Calipers Fusion 360 Engineering notebook Optional flatbed photo with scale Procedure Instructions Identify the part’s datums and create a measurement plan. Measure overall length, width, thickness, holes, slots, bends, and feature spacing. Create a parameter table before sketching. Build the base profile with geometric and dimensional constraints. Add holes, slots, fillets, and bends or approximations in a logical feature order. Verify that every sketch is fully constrained. Create a technical drawing with the dimensions needed for inspection. Compare at least five CAD measurements with the physical part and calculate error. Requirements Engineering Requirements Fully constrained sketches All critical dimensions driven by parameters Five comparison measurements within +/-0.5 mm Realistic fillets and feature order Complete drawing and STL export Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not disassemble a tape measure spring mechanism Model only the approved hook component Use metric units Complete within two class periods Deliverables What You Submit Measurement plan and table Fusion 360 file Parameter list Technical drawing PDF STL file CAD-to-part error table Reflection Reflection Questions Which measurement controlled the most geometry? Where was the largest error? How did constraints make revision easier? What manufacturing process likely created the original part? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Photographing the part next to a ruler can help verify overall proportions, but use calipers for final dimensions. Common Mistake Do not trace a photo and assume it is accurate; camera perspective can distort geometry. Stretch Goal Redesign the hook for easier grip while preserving all connection dimensions. Career Connection Reverse-engineering and sustaining engineers recreate legacy parts when drawings or suppliers are unavailable. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.description: IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.3: Sketch Planes and 2D Sketching. How does a 2D sketch become the foundation of a CAD model?

Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive Video Help What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Focus Your sketch begins on a plane that matches the part’s intended shape and view. Sketch Constrain Build Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The profile is closed, readable, and located on a plane that makes the next modeling step straightforward. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Build the Base Sketch on the Right Plane. Learning Targets Choose a sketch plane intentionally. Create a readable 2D base sketch. Explain how sketch orientation affects the final model. Success Looks Like Your sketch begins on a plane that matches the part’s intended shape and view. Launch Learn Model Check Submit Opening Prompt What could go wrong if you start sketching on the wrong plane? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Build the Base Sketch on the Right Plane. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move The model can become hard to orient, edit, document, or assemble because the geometry begins from a confusing reference. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 The sketch plane controls where geometry begins. Key Idea 2 2D sketches define the base shape of most 3D parts. Key Idea 3 Poor sketch placement creates confusing models. Fusion & Fabrication Help Video Help Fusion 360 - How to Create Planes for Better Sketching Use this tutorial when choosing an origin plane or creating a construction plane for a new sketch. Open on YouTube Pause, replay, or open the tutorial in a new tab while you work. Follow the lesson requirements when the video uses a different example. Lesson Interactive Choose the Best Sketch Plane The tolerance tester begins as a wide flat profile. Select the plane that captures the most useful base shape before thickness is added. Intended Part The base sketch should show the largest face and the locations of repeated fit features. Select a Starting Plane XY Plane Shows width and depth XZ Plane Shows width and height YZ Plane Shows depth and height Check Plane Choose the plane that shows the full flat footprint before extrusion. Your Task Build the Base Sketch on the Right Plane Create a simple closed profile on an intentional sketch plane and explain how that choice supports the shape of the part. Inspect the intended part orientation. Select the plane that best represents the base profile. Draw the main closed profile with clean connected geometry. Finish the sketch and inspect it from an isometric view. Quality check: The profile is closed, readable, and located on a plane that makes the next modeling step straightforward. What You Will Submit Base Sketch Evidence A screenshot of the completed base sketch. A one-sentence explanation of why the selected plane was appropriate. Submission standard: The profile is closed, readable, and located on a plane that makes the next modeling step straightforward. items.title: Cut Features and Holes
items.description: IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.7: Cut Features and Holes. How do cuts and holes create functional features?
items.searchText: IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.7 | Cut Features and Holes | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.7 | Cut Features and Holes | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.7 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.7 Cut Features and Holes Focus question: How do cuts and holes create functional features? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive Video Help What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Focus Your model includes a functional opening that is placed and sized correctly. Cut Locate Document Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The removed feature is located, sized, and cut in the intended direction without damaging other geometry. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Create Functional Cuts and Holes. Learning Targets Use cuts to remove material intentionally. Create holes or slots that match a functional need. Verify cut depth, direction, and location. Success Looks Like Your model includes a functional opening that is placed and sized correctly. Launch Learn Model Check Submit Opening Prompt Why are holes and slots often more than just empty space? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Create Functional Cuts and Holes. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move Cuts create functional features: clearance for fasteners, alignment, weight reduction, access, or fit between parts. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Cuts create holes, slots, pockets, and clearance features. Key Idea 2 Functional openings must be placed and dimensioned accurately. Key Idea 3 Cut direction and depth affect whether the feature works. Fusion & Fabrication Help Video Help Autodesk Fusion 360 Hole Tool Tutorial Use this tutorial to compare cut extrusions with the Hole tool and select an appropriate hole type. Open on YouTube Pause, replay, or open the tutorial in a new tab while you work. Follow the lesson requirements when the video uses a different example. Lesson Interactive Choose the Correct Cut Extent Match each functional feature to the cut extent that will remain reliable if the part thickness changes later. Feature Purpose Cut extent Bolt hole Must pass completely through the plate Choose Distance Through all To object Shallow pocket Leaves 4 mm of material below Choose Distance Through all To object Label recess Engraves text 0.6 mm deep Choose Distance Through all To object Check Cut Extents Use through-all for a feature that must always pass through; use a controlled distance for partial-depth features. Your Task Create Functional Cuts and Holes Add a pocket, slot, or hole that removes material for a clear functional reason. Select the face or plane where the removed feature begins. Sketch and locate the cut profile. Choose the correct cut depth or through-all condition. Inspect the result from at least two views. Quality check: The removed feature is located, sized, and cut in the intended direction without damaging other geometry. What You Will Submit Cut Feature Model A saved model with one correctly located cut, slot, or hole. A short note stating the function of the removed feature. Submission standard: The removed feature is located, sized, and cut in the intended direction without damaging other geometry. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move Measurements, feature labels, intended function, critical surfaces, and notes about requirements help turn documentation into a reliable CAD plan. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 CAD models should be based on documented measurements, not guesses. Key Idea 2 Unit 1 sketches become a modeling plan. Key Idea 3 Good planning prevents wrong-size digital parts. Fusion & Fabrication Help Video Help Day 1 of Learn Autodesk Fusion in 30 Days! Source Documentation 100 mm Planning principle: Start with the plane that shows the controlling profile and create the largest simple solid before adding cuts and edge details. Choose the Modeling Plan Starting sketch plane Choose Front plane Top plane Right plane First profile to sketch Choose Outer bracket outline Circular hole only Rounded edges Feature order Choose Extrude → Cut → Fillet Fillet → Cut → Extrude Cut → Extrude → Fillet Check CAD Plan Connect the source drawing to a stable first sketch and feature sequence. Your Task Translate Documentation into a CAD Plan Use an existing sketch or measured part as the source for a short modeling plan before opening a new CAD design. Create and save the CAD file using the required name. Quality check: The plan clearly connects source evidence to the first geometry you will create. What You Will Submit CAD Planning Evidence One annotated CAD plan showing the starting plane, base profile, and controlling information. A correctly named Fusion file or screenshot showing the file has been created. Submission standard: The plan clearly connects source evidence to the first geometry you will create. Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive Video Help What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Focus Your sketch uses dimensions to make the model accurate and adjustable. Dimension Control Check Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The sketch is controlled by meaningful dimensions rather than duplicated or unnecessary measurements. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Dimension the Sketch for Design Control. Learning Targets Add dimensions that control size and placement. Identify key dimensions that define design intent. Avoid unnecessary or conflicting dimensions. Success Looks Like Your sketch uses dimensions to make the model accurate and adjustable. Launch Learn Model Check Submit Opening Prompt What makes a CAD dimension different from a note written next to a sketch? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Dimension the Sketch for Design Control. Reveal: useful CAD thinking move A CAD dimension controls geometry. When it changes, the sketch updates, so dimensions become part of the model’s design intent. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Dimensions convert rough geometry into measurable engineering intent. Key Idea 2 Key dimensions should come from sketches, requirements, or measured objects. Key Idea 3 Over-dimensioning can make sketches hard to edit. Fusion & Fabrication Help Video Help Quick Tip: Changing Dimensions in a Sketch Use this video to review how dimensions control size and how changing a dimension updates a sketch. Open on YouTube Pause, replay, or open the tutorial in a new tab while you work. Follow the lesson requirements when the video uses a different example. Lesson Interactive Drive a Sketch with Dimensions Adjust the controlling dimensions until the sketch meets the target requirements. Watch the geometry update as each value changes. Live Dimensioned Sketch 60 mm 25 mm Target: 80 mm wide, hole center 25 mm from left Overall width: 60 mm Hole offset: 15 mm Check Dimensions Use dimensions to control size and feature location rather than dragging geometry by eye. Your Task Dimension the Sketch for Design Control Add dimensions that control the overall size and the location of important internal geometry. Identify the dimensions that define the outside size. Add dimensions that locate the important internal feature. Edit one value and observe how the sketch updates. Return the sketch to the assigned values and confirm it is fully controlled. Quality check: The sketch is controlled by meaningful dimensions rather than duplicated or unnecessary measurements. What You Will Submit Dimensioned Sketch One fully controlled dimensioned sketch matching the assigned requirements. Submission standard: The sketch is controlled by meaningful dimensions rather than duplicated or unnecessary measurements. items.title: Fit and Tolerance Investigation
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 3 Fit and Tolerance Investigation IED Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.3 Fit and Tolerance Investigation Design and test a tolerance coupon that identifies useful clearance, transition, and press-fit dimensions for the classroom printer. Advanced 2-3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Two CAD parts may share the same nominal dimension but still fit differently after printing because of machine and material variation. Objectives What You Will Practice Connect nominal dimensions to physical fit Design a controlled experiment Collect repeated measurements Recommend tolerances from evidence Materials What You Need Fusion 360 3D printer and approved filament Calipers Tolerance data sheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Choose a nominal peg or hole size approved by your teacher. Create a parametric coupon with at least six fit offsets spanning loose to tight. Label each test position in the model. Predict which offsets will produce clearance, transition, and press fits. Slice and print using recorded settings and orientation. Measure printed pegs and holes before fit testing. Test each fit using the same procedure and rate insertion force and retention. Recommend one offset for each target fit and explain uncertainty. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use one nominal size and at least six controlled offsets Keep all non-offset geometry identical Record printer, material, orientation, layer height, and scale Measure at least three printed features Define a repeatable fit-rating method Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not force parts in a way that creates sharp fragments Use only approved print settings Results apply only to the tested machine, material, and orientation unless additional evidence is collected Deliverables What You Submit Parametric coupon file Prediction table Printed coupon Measurement and fit data Recommended clearance/transition/press-fit offsets Short limitations statement Reflection Reflection Questions How did actual dimensions compare with CAD? Which fit category had the widest acceptable range? How did print orientation affect the result? Why should tolerances be based on process capability? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Change only the fit offset. Keep every other feature and test condition constant. Common Mistake One successful fit is not enough evidence. Manufacturing variation requires repeated or carefully controlled testing. Stretch Goal Repeat the best three fits in a second orientation or material and compare. Career Connection Design and manufacturing engineers specify tolerances based on function and process capability, not guesswork. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.title: Simplify the Rocket Assembly
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 3 Simplify the Rocket Assembly IED Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.1 Simplify the Rocket Assembly Redesign the assembly to reduce part count or assembly time while preserving required function and overall envelope. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context The current rocket assembly works, but technicians report too many parts, repeated fasteners, and slow assembly. Objectives What You Will Practice Analyze assembly complexity Apply design for assembly principles Preserve interfaces and motion Compare original and revised assemblies Materials What You Need Existing rocket assembly CAD Fusion 360 Bill of materials Stopwatch or assembly-time estimate sheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Create a baseline BOM and count unique parts, total parts, fasteners, and assembly steps. Identify three assembly pain points. Generate two redesign concepts that combine parts, replace fasteners, improve alignment, or reduce orientation errors. Use a decision matrix to select a redesign. Modify the CAD assembly and update joints or constraints. Create an updated BOM and assembly sequence. Compare predicted assembly time and part count. Check for new manufacturing, repair, or tolerance problems. Requirements Engineering Requirements Reduce total part count or assembly steps by at least 20% Preserve rocket exterior envelope and required interfaces Maintain access to parts that may require replacement Use realistic manufacturing methods Update the assembly and BOM completely Constraints Constraints & Safety No change may interfere with the provided rocket requirements Use only available manufacturing processes Do not hide separate components by merely grouping them in CAD Deliverables What You Submit Baseline BOM and sequence Three identified pain points Two concept sketches Decision matrix Revised assembly file Updated BOM Before/after comparison Reflection Reflection Questions Which assembly step created the greatest difficulty? How did your redesign affect repairability? What tolerance issue could appear in the combined part? What physical test should verify the change? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Every time a technician must pick up, orient, or fasten a part is an opportunity for simplification. Common Mistake Combining parts can make manufacturing harder or prevent repair. Evaluate the full life cycle. Stretch Goal Create a mistake-proof feature that prevents one part from being installed backward. Career Connection Design-for-assembly engineers reduce part count, handling, fastening, and orientation errors to improve production. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 3 Portfolio-Quality Exploded View IED Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.2 Portfolio-Quality Exploded View Create a professional exploded view, BOM, and assembly-order visual suitable for a portfolio or design review. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A technical presentation needs one image that clearly explains how the rocket assembly fits together. Objectives What You Will Practice Create an exploded assembly view Use balloons and a BOM consistently Communicate assembly sequence Improve technical drawing layout Materials What You Need Completed rocket assembly CAD Fusion 360 drawing workspace Drawing checklist Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Inspect the assembly browser and rename unclear components. Create or verify a complete BOM with part numbers and quantities. Plan an explosion direction that keeps parts readable and avoids crossing paths. Create the exploded view with consistent spacing. Add trail lines where they clarify movement. Place the view on a drawing sheet and add balloons linked to the BOM. Add one detail view for a small or hidden connection. Use the checklist to inspect alignment, readability, title block, and consistency. Requirements Engineering Requirements Every modeled component appears in the BOM Every BOM item is ballooned exactly once in the main view or detail Explosion order reflects a logical assembly sequence No part paths overlap in a confusing way Drawing includes title, scale, revision, and author Constraints Constraints & Safety Use the current approved assembly Keep the drawing to one sheet Do not use decorative backgrounds that reduce readability Deliverables What You Submit Updated assembly component names Exploded view drawing PDF BOM Ballooned assembly view One detail view Completed quality checklist Reflection Reflection Questions Which parts were hardest to separate visually? How did you choose the explosion direction? Could a technician infer assembly order? What makes the drawing portfolio-ready? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use larger spacing for large parts and smaller spacing for closely related fasteners, but keep the pattern consistent. Common Mistake An exploded view is not random separation. It should preserve relationships and communicate sequence. Stretch Goal Create a short animation that follows the same assembly order. Career Connection Technical illustrators and mechanical designers create exploded views for assembly, service, sales, and training. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson → A student engineering hub for design, fabrication, and aerospace innovation. items.description: IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.9: Assembly Motion and Functional Checks. How do motion checks reveal interference or alignment issues?
items.searchText: IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.9 | Assembly Motion and Functional Checks | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.9 | Assembly Motion and Functional Checks | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.9 IED Unit 3 • Lesson 3.9 Assembly Motion and Functional Checks Focus question: How do motion checks reveal interference or alignment issues? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 3 Mission Focus You can use motion or interference checks to find problems before printing. Move Inspect Resolve Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The check covers the intended range and documents both successful behavior and any interference. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Run Functional and Motion Checks. Learning Targets Identify when motion or interference checks are needed. Use CAD checks to locate collisions or blocked movement. Record evidence that supports a design decision. Success Looks Like You can use motion or interference checks to find problems before printing. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How do motion checks reveal interference or alignment issues? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Run Functional and Motion Checks. Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: The check covers the intended range and documents both successful behavior and any interference. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Motion checks reveal issues that static views may hide. Key Idea 2 Interference is a design problem, not just a display problem. Key Idea 3 Functional checks should happen before fabrication. Your Task Run Functional and Motion Checks Use available joint motion and visual inspection to identify interference, overtravel, or misalignment in the assembly. Identify the joint or relationship that can be tested. Move the component through its intended range. Watch for collisions, separation, or unexpected rotation. Record the result and any needed correction. Quality check: The check covers the intended range and documents both successful behavior and any interference. Lesson Interactive Find the Interference-Free Motion Limit Move the payload tray through its travel and identify the largest position that does not contact the body wall. Motion Sweep Tray travel 0 mm Status Clear Motion Controls Tray travel Engineering response Choose Ignore the contact Add a motion limit Change the joint to rigid Record Functional Limit Find the maximum clear travel and choose a design response that prevents interference. What You Will Submit Motion Check Record One screenshot, short recording, or annotated note documenting the functional check. Submission standard: The check covers the intended range and documents both successful behavior and any interference. Lesson Interactive Prepare the Rocket Print Submission Choose an orientation and support plan for each component, then verify the parts will be submitted as separate printable files. items.title: Prototype Fit Testing and Revision Notes
items.description: IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.12: Prototype Fit Testing and Revision Notes. How can fit testing guide final documentation?
items.searchText: IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.12 | Prototype Fit Testing and Revision Notes | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.12 | Prototype Fit Testing and Revision Notes | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.12 IED Unit 3 • Lesson 3.12 Prototype Fit Testing and Revision Notes Focus question: How can fit testing guide final documentation? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 3 Mission Focus You can turn prototype fit testing into revision notes for the final design package. Test Compare Explain Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: Each conclusion is linked to a specific physical observation or measurement. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Test Prototype Fit and Record Revisions. Learning Targets Run fit tests against assembly criteria. Compare CAD expectations to physical prototype results. Write revision notes that explain what should change next. Success Looks Like You can turn prototype fit testing into revision notes for the final design package. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How can fit testing guide final documentation? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Test Prototype Fit and Record Revisions. Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: Each conclusion is linked to a specific physical observation or measurement. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Fit testing connects physical evidence to future revisions. Key Idea 2 Strong notes describe the issue, evidence, and recommended change. Key Idea 3 Testing results help explain the limits of the final prototype. Your Task Test Prototype Fit and Record Revisions Evaluate the physical connections systematically and convert the results into specific revision notes for final documentation. Identify each critical connection to inspect. Test fit and alignment using the same criteria for each part. Measure or photograph any gap, interference, or loose condition. Write a revision note or confirm the final condition. Quality check: Each conclusion is linked to a specific physical observation or measurement. Lesson Interactive Use Prototype Data to Select a Revision Review the measured results and identify the part and change most directly supported by the evidence. Prototype Fit Data Feature CAD target Measured average Observed result Body inside diameter 40.00 mm 40.05 mm Within expectation Coupler outside diameter 39.70 mm 40.02 mm Too tight Fin angle 90.0° 89.8° Acceptable Choose the Revision Revise body tube Revise coupler Revise fins No revision Revision action Choose Reduce outside diameter Increase outside diameter Change fin angle Check Revision Decision Use the measured error—not the symptom alone—to identify the component and parameter that should change. What You Will Submit Prototype Fit Results A fit-results table or annotated photo set. One prioritized revision note based on the evidence. Your Task Build the Physical Rocket Prototype Assemble the printed components carefully and document how the real parts compare with the CAD assembly. Inspect each printed component before assembly. Quality check: The prototype is assembled without forcing or damaging parts, and fit issues are recorded rather than hidden. Lesson Interactive Sequence the Prototype Build Put the physical build steps in a safe order that protects the parts and produces useful evidence. Printed Part Set Build rule: Never force an unverified fit. Inspection and dry fitting come before final assembly. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 3 Manufacturing Readiness Review IED Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.4 Manufacturing Readiness Review Perform a manufacturing readiness review of another student’s rocket assembly and identify issues before production. Intermediate 60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A prototype is ready for printing, but releasing unreviewed files can waste machine time and material. Objectives What You Will Practice Evaluate CAD and drawing completeness Check manufacturability and assembly readiness Prioritize production risks Communicate corrective actions Materials What You Need Peer CAD assembly and drawings Readiness checklist Slicer software Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Confirm the correct file revision and project requirements. Inspect component names, missing files, joints, and assembly interference. Check each part for print orientation, unsupported geometry, thin walls, and excessive size. Review drawings for dimensions, tolerances, notes, and BOM consistency. Open STL files in the slicer and check scale, units, manifold errors, and estimated print time. Record every issue as observation, consequence, and recommended correction. Classify issues as release blocker, important correction, or optional improvement. Meet with the designer and verify the top three actions. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use the complete readiness checklist Identify at least five evidence-based observations Classify each issue by priority Check both CAD and slicer readiness Provide actionable corrections Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not edit another student’s files directly Keep feedback professional and confidential within the class Do not approve a design with unresolved release blockers Deliverables What You Submit Completed readiness checklist Issue-priority table Slicer evidence Top-three correction summary Final release recommendation: ready, ready with corrections, or not ready Reflection Reflection Questions Which issue posed the greatest waste risk? Which check was easiest to overlook? How did the slicer reveal problems not obvious in CAD? What would be on your personal preflight checklist? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Write findings as “Observed condition - possible consequence - recommended action.” Common Mistake A readiness review is not a style critique. Focus on issues that affect function, fabrication, inspection, or assembly. Stretch Goal Review the corrected package and document whether each release blocker was closed. Career Connection Manufacturing, configuration, and quality engineers review files before production to prevent defects and wasted resources. items.searchText: IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 3 Prototype Component Upgrade IED Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.5 Prototype Component Upgrade Redesign, print, and compare one component so the revised prototype performs better in a defined test. Intermediate 2-3 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Fit testing has revealed one rocket component that is difficult to assemble, weak, or unreliable. Objectives What You Will Practice Translate test evidence into design changes Revise a parametric part Plan a fair comparison Document prototype improvement Materials What You Need Original component and CAD file Fusion 360 3D printer Calipers Test materials appropriate to the component Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Select one component and define the specific problem using evidence. Choose one measurable performance indicator such as insertion force, alignment error, mass, deflection, or assembly time. Record baseline measurements for the original component. Sketch two redesign options and select one. Revise the CAD while preserving required interfaces. Print the revised component with recorded settings. Run the same test on the original and revised versions. Decide whether the revision should be accepted, modified, or rejected. Requirements Engineering Requirements Define one measurable improvement target Preserve all required interface dimensions Change only features connected to the identified problem Use the same test method for both versions Document print settings and revision Constraints Constraints & Safety One component only unless approved Use classroom-approved materials and test loads Do not claim improvement without comparative evidence Deliverables What You Submit Problem statement and baseline data Two concept sketches Revised CAD and STL Original/revised photographs Comparison data Revision decision and justification Reflection Reflection Questions Did the redesign meet the target? What unintended effect appeared? Was the test sensitive enough to show a difference? What would be changed in Revision B? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Define the test and success target before redesigning. Otherwise, it is easy to declare any result an improvement. Common Mistake Do not change several unrelated features at once; you may not know which change caused the result. Stretch Goal Reduce mass or print time while preserving the performance improvement. Career Connection Prototype and test engineers use controlled comparisons to verify that design changes solve the intended problem. items.description: IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.3: Inserting and Positioning Rocket Parts. How are parts placed accurately in a CAD assembly?
items.searchText: IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.3 | Inserting and Positioning Rocket Parts | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.3 | Inserting and Positioning Rocket Parts | LockwoodSTEM Skip to main content LockwoodSTEM Student Engineering Hub Menu Courses Daily Agenda Resources Certifications FabLab About Challenges Home Courses IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.3 IED Unit 3 • Lesson 3.3 Inserting and Positioning Rocket Parts Focus question: How are parts placed accurately in a CAD assembly? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 3 Mission Focus You can insert and position rocket parts using intentional reference geometry. Insert Position Check Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: Every required component is present once and oriented consistently with the rocket body. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Insert and Rough-Position Rocket Components. Learning Targets Insert required rocket parts into an assembly workspace. Use reference geometry to position parts accurately. Check orientation before adding assembly relationships. Success Looks Like You can insert and position rocket parts using intentional reference geometry. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How are parts placed accurately in a CAD assembly? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Insert and Rough-Position Rocket Components. Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: Every required component is present once and oriented consistently with the rocket body. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Inserted parts are not automatically assembled. Key Idea 2 Orientation errors can hide until later if they are not checked early. Key Idea 3 Reference geometry gives a controlled starting point. Your Task Insert and Rough-Position Rocket Components Bring the major rocket parts into the assembly and place them in a recognizable starting arrangement. Insert the body and establish it as the assembly reference. Insert the remaining major parts from the correct files. Use move or align tools to place components near their intended locations. Inspect the assembly for missing or duplicated parts. Quality check: Every required component is present once and oriented consistently with the rocket body. Lesson Interactive Sequence Part Insertion and Positioning Arrange the CAD steps used to create a stable initial rocket assembly. Assembly Goal Stable reference: The main body should remain fixed while other components are positioned relative to it. Put the Steps in Order Insert the nose-cone component ↑ ↓ Align the component axes and contact faces ↑ ↓ Ground the main rocket body ↑ ↓ Move the nose cone near its intended location ↑ ↓ Check Sequence Use the arrow buttons to place the reference step first and the precise alignment step last. What You Will Submit Initial Rocket Assembly A saved assembly containing all major components. One isometric screenshot showing the initial arrangement. Submission standard: Every required component is present once and oriented consistently with the rocket body.
